Coarse-grained (CG) molecular simulations offer a route to connect this mesoscale bonding to macroscopic response, but existing reactive approaches are constrained, since hybrid molecular dynamics/Monte Carlo methods require reaction-acceptance criteria that are difficult to justify away from equilibrium, while other approaches feature complexities that limit implementation or study. We introduce ReactiveLJ, a reduced-parameter, many-body interaction potential based on the Lennard-Jones form that models associative bonding by weakening sticker attraction when reactive beads are locally crowded. Because the resulting forces arise from a potential energy surface rather than from prescribed reaction rules, the model applies to both equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions. We demonstrate ReactiveLJ by simulating associative polymers in single-chain, melt, and semidilute conditions across a range of cohesive strengths, with characterization of transport, viscoelastic, and kinetic properties. ReactiveLJ thereby provides a simple alternative to existing bondorder models while retaining the ability to capture coordination-dependent reversible bonding among indistinguishable stickers.

papers.title: Photoactivated chlorine dioxide oxygenation of freshly cleaved HOPG surfaces
A Glucopyranosylamine-Based Amorphous Copper Metal-Organic Framework (Cu-aMOF):An Efficient Adsorbent for Chromium ions
papers.abstract: A glucopyranosylamine-derived copper-based amorphous metal-organic framework (Cu-aMOF) was synthesized by the reaction between bis-(4,6-O-ethylidene-β-D-glucopyranosylamine)-1,4- dihydroxy-2,5-dibenzylidene (H 6 L) and Cu(OAc) 2 .H 2 O and evaluated for chromium ion remediation from water. Comprehensive characterization (FTIR, UV-visible, TGA, PXRD) confirmed the amorphous structure and thermal stability of the material. Cu-aMOF exhibited high adsorption capacities for Cr(III) (166 mg/g at pH 5.0) and Cr(VI) (64 mg/g), with strong selectivity in the presence of competing ions. Mechanistic insights from FTIR, FESEM, EDX, XPS, TOF-SIMS, and EXAFS revealed distinct binding interactions between copper centers and chromium species. These findings position Cu-aMOF as a promising platform for advanced water purification technologies.

papers.title: Multiplexed Imaging through Affinity Hierarchies in a Supramolecular Host
papers.abstract: Bioorthogonal chemistry has transformed molecular imaging by enabling highly selective synthetic labeling of biomolecules in their native habitats. However, multiplexed imaging remains fundamentally constrained by the limited number of mutually orthogonal reaction pairs that can operate efficiently under physiological conditions. Here, we introduce an alternative multiplexing strategy in which signal assignment is encoded not through reaction orthogonality, but through programmable differences in molecular affinity. Using the synthetic supramolecular host Cucurbit[7]uril (CB[7]), we established a single-host, multi-guest framework that enables dynamic and reconfigurable multiplexed imaging via affinity-programmed host–guest exchange. Specifically, we exploited the hierarchical binding affinities of structurally distinct guest molecules towards CB[7] to achieve directional and selective fluorophore displacement under physiological conditions. This affinity-governed displacement mechanism enables controlled fluorescence erasure from lower-affinity guests while preserving higher-affinity host–guest fluorescent assemblies intact. Coupling of this exchange cycle with subsequent re-complexation of the liberated lower-affinity guests using spectrally distinct CB[7]–fluorophore conjugates enables programmable signal reassignment, thereby facilitating multiplexed labeling and imaging in cells and multicellular specimens, including live tissues. Moreover, CB[7]-mediated supramolecular recognition operates orthogonally to established covalent bioorthogonal chemistries, enabling integration with click reactions for higher-order multiplexed imaging. Collectively, our results establish affinity encoding as a new scaling dimension for bioorthogonal multiplexing, providing a dynamically reconfigurable framework for high-dimensional fluorescence imaging that complements existing bioorthogonal chemistries and maximizes utilization of the available spectral bandwidth of fluorescence microscopy.

papers.title: Lifetime- and potential-engineered photocatalysts for uphill photoredox catalysis
papers.abstract: Most molecular photocatalysts (PCs) have lifetimes ranging from a few nanoseconds to the low microsecond range suitable for photoinduced electron transfer reactions with driving forces larger than –0.2 eV. Very long excited state lifetimes of the PC can facilitate uphill photoinduced electron transfer reactions. With a PC possessing a high excited state redox potential and a long excited state lifetime, excited state redox processes with very challenging substrates can become accessible. Symmetry considerations and quantum chemical calculations informing on redox potential optimization led to the development of a molecular PC made from non-toxic abundant elements with a high excited state redox potential of +1.76 V vs SCE and a very long excited state lifetime of 2.63 ms. After photoexcitation, this PC reacts with difficultto-oxidize substrates, such as carboxylates, N-oxides, olefins, bromide, alcohols and arenes in so-called endergonic photoinduced electron transfer reactions. Exemplary photocatalytic reactions, namely light-driven decarboxylative oxygenation and fluorination as well as arene amination, illustrate the broad potential of such designer PCs with long-lived excited states.

papers.title: Sb-Doped SrSnO3: a lead free perovskite oxide for sustainable photoresponsive optoelectronics
papers.abstract: Lead free perovskite oxides are emerging as promising alternatives to halide perovskites for stable optoelectronic applications. Building on our previous work demonstrating the potential of 5% Sb-doped SrSnO3 as a transparent conductive oxide, this study explores the effect of varying Sb doping levels (2%, 5%, and 7%) on the functional performance of SrSnO3 thin films in optoelectronic device architectures. To promote sustainability and cost-effectiveness, the films were synthesized via a solution processed sol-gel method. The resulting thin films exhibited high quality, uniform thickness and excellent homogeneity. Structural analysis revealed a phase transition from orthorhombic to cubic with increasing Sb content, accompanied by a reduction in lattice parameters. Simple device structures were fabricated by depositing the films onto p-type silicon substrates, forming n–p heterojunctions. Under illumination, the devices exhibited a clear and reproducible photoresponse, with the 7% Sb-doped film achieving a photocurrent of 6 mA at 10 V, significantly enhanced compared to undoped SrSnO3 devices. These results highlight the potential of Sb-doped SrSnO3 as a low-cost, stable photoactive layer for photodetectors and optoelectronic devices and further validate the sol-gel method as an effective route for integrating perovskite oxides into silicon-based optoelectronic systems.

papers.title: In-context learning meets small molecule property prediction: benchmarking novel machine learning approaches
papers.abstract: Recently, a new category of machine learning approaches for tabular data has emerged: tabular foundation models (TFM), based on in-context learning. A TFM is a neural network (usually a transformer) pre-trained primarily on synthetic data. Its input is an entire dataset: features and labels for training records, along with features for the target records. This study comprehensively benchmarked these methods for predicting the properties of small organic molecules. Several TFM were compared with multiple machine learning methods across 11 datasets (regression, random splits, up to 10,000 molecules each). The evaluation showed that TFM consistently outperform XGBoost, CatBoost, multilayer perceptrons, and other descriptor-based methods, even with careful hyperparameter selection for the baselines. TFM also demonstrate accuracy on par with or better than graph-based methods, including those pre-trained on chemical data. Uni-Mol2, a pre-trained deep neural network operating on 3D atomic coordinates, slightly outperforms TFM in some experiments. However, this comparison deliberately disfavors TFM, as they do not use any chemical pre-training and rely on a minimalistic set of 2D molecular descriptors without feature engineering. The best results for relatively large datasets are achieved using retrieval: for each test molecule, the 500 closest neighbors (by Tanimoto similarity) are selected from the training set, and TFM inference is performed on this local subset. Overall, TFM (particularly the TabPFN family) are highly promising for predicting the properties of small molecules.

papers.title: Solution-state Magnetic Bistability in Cobalt Corrole Complexes with Switchable Sidearms
papers.abstract: Molecular materials having switchable electronic states are crucial for modern applications such as spintronics and quantum information processing. In this direction, Ni(II)porphyrins with switchable internal axial ligands have been shown to be the first examples. Herein, we show that structurally similar tetrapyrrole, namely corrole, can be a better candidate for the purpose due to its versatile coordination chemistry. For the first time, a set of cobalt-corroles have been shown to switch between four- and five-coordinated structures, thereby modulating the electronic structure of the complexes. The new molecules discussed here have been spectroscopically investigated for their switchable behaviour. The conclusions thus arrived have been corroborated by structural characterization and density functional calculations. One of the reported molecules, CoTolPy has been shown to be the first example to have an intramolecular antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic switching in solution.

papers.title: Novel Theoretical Framework for Coupled Transport in Polymer Melt Extrusion
papers.abstract: Coupled transport phenomena in polymer extrusion have been extensively investigated using analytical, constitutive, and numerical models. While these approaches provide detailed descriptions of individual physical mechanisms, a unified theoretical framework that systematically organizes their interactions into a coherent interpretation of system-level transport behavior remains lacking. This work establishes a unified theoretical framework for coupled transport in polymer melt extrusion based on idealized concentric-cylinder representations. The proposed framework systematically organizes geometric abstraction, governing conservation laws, rheological constitutive relations, and transport coupling mechanisms into a hierarchical theoretical architecture that explicitly connects governing physical foundations with system-level transport behavior. Within this theoretical architecture, polymer melt transport is interpreted as the emergent consequence of the continuous interactions among pressure-driven flow, drag-induced transport, shear-dependent rheology, temperature-dependent viscosity, and viscous dissipation. Rather than treating these mechanisms as independent physical processes, the proposed framework interprets their continuous interactions as manifestations of a unified transport organization in which rheological response provides the central connection between momentum and thermal transport, thereby establishing a unified interpretive perspective that understands polymer extrusion as an evolving coupled transport system. Building upon this unified interpretive perspective, the framework further establishes an organizational interpretation of transport regimes by describing regime evolution as the continuous reorganization of coupled transport processes under varying processing conditions, material properties, and geometric configurations. It consequently provides a unified parametric perspective that systematically relates transport coupling, regime evolution, and engineering regulation within a consistent theoretical architecture. Overall, the proposed framework establishes a unified theoretical architecture for systematically interpreting coupled transport phenomena in polymer extrusion by connecting governing physical foundations with system-level transport behavior. Beyond polymer extrusion, the proposed framework therefore provides a transferable theoretical organization for interpreting strongly coupled transport systems.

papers.title: Quasi-Isostructural Alloying of Cu4TiSe4 with Cu3TMQ4 (TM: V, Nb, Ta; Q: S, Se): Tuning ‘Stuffing’ Concentration for Ultralow Thermal Conductivity
papers.abstract: In this study, we adopted a quasi-isostructural alloying strategy between selenotitanate Cu 4 TiSe 4 and sulvanite-type Cu 3 TMQ 4 ( TM : V, Nb, Ta; Q : S, Se). At room temperature, both systems crystallize in the cubic 𝑃4̅3𝑚 space group, where Cu 4 TiSe 4 additionally contains positionally disordered Cu + cations, occupying two Wyckoff sites (1 b and 4 e ) inside the sulvanite framework. Crystal structures of the alloys were determined by X-ray diffraction studies. Substituting Ti 4+ for TM 5+ in Cu 3 TMQ 4 allows additional Cu + to dissolve, maintaining overall charge neutrality. The additional (stuffed) Cu occupy positionally disordered sites (1 b and 4 e ) without effecting the 3D sulvanite frameworks, with their occupancy controlled by Ti 4+ / TM 5+ ratio. Moreover, an ordering tendency of the stuffed Cu + ions is observed within the cubic unit cell of the S-substituted alloys. This alloying leads to a substantial reduction in thermal conductivity relative to the parent sulvanite-type compounds, reaching the ultralow regime, while the optical band gaps vary systematically between 0.9 and 2.62 eV. The combination of this low thermal conductivity and a tunable optical bandgap makes these materials highly attractive for diverse applications.

papers.title: Cation competition and low pH protect protocell membranes from divalent cation disruption
papers.abstract: Divalent cations such as Mg 2+ and Ca 2+ are essential for many modern biochemical processes and likely played similarly important roles during the origin of life. However, these ions are highly disruptive to fatty acid vesicles, creating a fundamental incompatibility between prebiotically plausible membranes and metal-ion-dependent chemistry. Here, we identify two complementary physicochemical mechanisms that enhance fatty acid vesicle stability in the presence of divalent cations. First, we demonstrate that certain metal ions, such as Mn 2+ and Fe 3+ , can shield membranes from the disruptive effects of more destructive cations. Second, we show that lowering environmental pH, thereby increasing fatty acid protonation, substantially enhances membrane stability under otherwise destructive conditions. Together, these mechanisms enable retention of encapsulated contents at divalent cation concentrations exceeding 50 mM and can substantially increase vesicle tolerance to Mg 2+ and Ca 2+ under selected conditions. These findings suggest that the incompatibility between fatty acid membranes and divalent cations can be modulated by environmental context. More broadly, our results expand the physicochemical landscape supporting protocell stability and highlight the importance of solution composition and pH fluctuations in early Earth scenarios. This work advances our understanding of how protocells may have coexisted with essential metal-catalyzed RNA chemistry during the origin of life.

papers.title: L→S2+←L Complexes (Sulfurones) with Unique Architecture: Synthesis, Crystal Structure and Quantum Chemical Analysis
papers.abstract: Many innovative complexes with (NHC)→S (NHC is N-Heterocyclic Carbene) coordination bonds were theoretically designed and synthetically obtained in the past five years. Taking this as a clue, (NHC)→S2+←(NHC) systems were proposed as sulfurones. In this work, the synthesis and crystal structures of a few sulfurones have been reported. The unique (L→S) dative bond characteristics have been established by comparing their electronic character of sulfurones with that of species containing C=S=C bonds using Density functional theory (DFT). The experimental as well as the quantum chemical data clearly indicate the presence of L→S coordination interactions in sulfurones.

papers.title: ChemMate: an autonomous research mate for the full computational chemistry research lifecycle, from ideation to manuscript
papers.abstract: Agentic research systems have split along a line. Systems that automate the research lifecycle, from ideation to manuscript, now reach flagship venues, but their experiments are machine-learning runs, biomedical hypotheses, or self-written software, not physical simulation. Systems that drive real computational-chemistry engines stop at the calculation and rarely leave a single cluster. Here we present ChemMate, an autonomous research mate that joins the two for computational chemistry. Riding a general-purpose coding-agent harness, ChemMate adds roughly two hundred expert-protocol skills bound by a machine-checked runtime contract, an idea pipeline spanning applied, method-development, and theory modes, a typed research knowledge graph, and native multi-cluster orchestration designed so that each job leaves a durable, human-readable receipt recording which calculation ran on which machine. Autonomy is bounded by construction: structure-check and submission gates keep a human in the loop exactly where wrong inputs would burn allocation, and the gates are web-actionable, including from a phone, so a researcher can inspect, correct, and approve a job away from the desk. We demonstrate the system through five campaigns spanning electrocatalysis, non-thermal-plasma catalysis, homogeneous asymmetric catalysis, and biomolecular drug discovery, with a concrete result in each: a machine-learned density-functional Hamiltonian whose agent replaced a misleading success metric and cut a band-structure error from 491 to 101 meV; a from-scratch plasma-kinetics model reproducing the measured ethylene-to-acetylene ratio; an enantioselectivity prediction matching the crystallographic assignment at more than 99% enantiomeric excess; a virtual screen returning 100 interference-clean protease hits at 16.5-fold enrichment; and a reconstruction, from a published paper alone, of an isolated-Pd CO-reduction proton-supply mechanism across structural, energetic, and electronic scales. The system is built so that a reported claim can be replayed from its shipped audit trail. The lifecycle, not the calculation, is the unit of automation.

papers.title: Quality over quantity in fluorinated battery interphases
papers.abstract: Fluorination of the solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) is central to achieving high cycling efficiency in lithium metal batteries. However, current approaches often rely on large amounts of fluorinated salts, solvents, or diluents, increasing electrolyte complexity, cost, and environmental footprint. Here, we demonstrate that interphase quality is governed not by fluorine content alone, but by how fluorine is incorporated into the SEI. Using a series of pyridinium-based additives and systematically varying their number of fluorine atoms, we decouple fluorination degree from fluorine content in the electrolyte and show that equivalent amount of fluorine produces fundamentally different SEIs. Increasing the fluorination degree raises the additive reduction potential and facilitates rapid passivation before bulk electrolyte decomposition significantly contributes to interphase formation, yielding robust and homogeneous, LiF-rich SEIs. Tetrafluorinated additive (4FP) reduces at ~2.5 V vs. Li/Li+ and forms a highly passivating and homogenous SEI rich in additive-derived LiF that supports uniform Li deposition and highly reversible Li plating/stripping. In contrast, less-fluorinated additives generate more heterogeneous SEIs containing substantial amounts of anion-derived, yet fluorinated species. Remarkably, 4FP stabilizes Li plating/stripping already at a concentration of 1 mM (0.015 wt%) and under pressure-free conditions. At 3 mM, corresponding to 0.05 wt% fluorinated additive, 4FP enables stable cycling of 20 µm Li||LFP full cells with 99.9 % efficiency for more than 400 cycles. Increasing additive concentration further enriches the SEI with LiF but lowers the Li plating/stripping efficiency, demonstrating that optimal battery performance is determined by interphase quality rather than fluorine quantity.

papers.title: Reinforcement of Polyvinyl Chloride Using Plasma-Activated Aramid Fibers and Surface-Bonded Compatibilizer
papers.abstract: This study investigated the application of a two-step compatibilization procedure to aramid fiber–poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) composites. Aramid fibers were subjected to high radio frequency power air plasma treatment and incorporated into the PVC matrix in the presence of polypropylene-graft-maleic anhydride (PP-g-MA) as a compatibilizer. Plasma treatment substantially increased the nitrogen and oxygen contents of the fiber surface, introduced higher concentrations of functional groups such as amines and carboxylic acids, and significantly enhanced surface roughness. These modifications promoted strong physicochemical interactions between the fibers and the polymer matrix. The resulting composites exhibited substantial improvements in tensile and flexural properties, viscoelastic behavior, and thermal stability, with performance exceeding those previously reported for similar systems. The enhanced compatibility is consistent with covalent bonding between fiber-bound functional groups and maleic anhydride moieties on the compatibilizer, together with possible interdiffusion and entanglement between polypropylene and PVC chains. Unlike the previously-studied thermoplastic polyolefin (TPO) matrix, in which plasma-treatment alone without adding compatibilizers brought notable improvements in composite properties, in PVC enhanced compatibilization only became apparent after both steps. Different reinforcement mechanisms using the same fiber treatment procedure highlighted the role of the host polymer in the effectiveness of interfacial coupling. This work presents a distinctive, environmentally benign compatibilization approach for aramid fiber–PVC systems, addressing a long-standing challenge in thermoplastic composite design. By leveraging surface chemistry modification and targeted interfacial coupling, the method achieves unprecedented property enhancements without resorting to hazardous treatments. The strategy offers a scalable route to high-performance fiber-reinforced thermoplastics with broad applications.

papers.title: Operando observation of immobilized carbonic anhydrase for CO2 conversion
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous catalysis with immobilized enzymes is pivotal for continuous and sustainable industrial bioprocesses. However, the relationship between enzyme dispersion on solid supports and catalytic activity is not well described. Here, we investigate the immobilization of Persephonella marina carbonic anhydrase (PmCA) on multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), combining confocal fluorescence microscopy and high-resolution electron microscopy to correlate enzyme surface loading with CO2 hydration activity. A dual fluorescence labeling strategy enables operando visualization of enzyme location and function, revealing that catalytic activity on the carrier exhibits two distinct regimes: (i) a stochastic regime at low enzyme loadings where activity shows high variability with monolayer coverage yielding the highest perenzyme activity, and (ii) a saturation regime at higher loadings where activity converges on a loading-independent value, attributed to crowding effects. This integrated approach reveals spatiotemporally resolved structure-function relationships for a heterogeneous biocatalyst, establishing a basis for understanding and engineering of advanced enzyme-based catalytic materials.

papers.title: Establishing Quantitative Electrolyte-Solid Electrolyte Interphase Relationships in Lithium Metal Batteries
papers.abstract: Despite the high energy density of lithium metal batteries (LMBs), lithium loss driven by electrolyte decomposition at the highly reductive lithium metal anode to form the solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) remains a critical challenge. Recent studies have established the correlation between an anion derived, inorganic SEI and interfacial stability, motivating electrolyte design strategies which promote preferential anion reduction at the lithium metal anode. Current electrolyte design strategies emphasize the importance of an anion-dominated Li+ solvation structure to promote this inorganic-rich SEI, yet there is a lack of quantitative evidence linking SEI composition with the strength of Li+-anion and Li+-solvent interactions in the electrolyte. Here, we systematically study a series of ether-based solvents with varied dielectric constants in order to connect variation in solvation structure to anion content in the SEI. LiF titration provides a quantitative assessment of the fraction of SEI products derived from anion reduction and demonstrates that an anion-dominated Li+ solvation structure, characterized with nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and Raman spectroscopy, does not necessarily correlate to anion-selective SEI formation. Instead, both an anion-dominated solvation structure and reductively stable solvent are necessary to achieve high anion selectivity. Based on this finding, we develop a descriptor-based model informed by density functional theory (DFT) calculations of both Li+ solvation ability and solvent reductive stability to screen for solvent candidates which enable high anion selectivity. This model aligns with existing examples of ether-based Li metal electrolytes and helped to identify an electrolyte formulation of tert-butyl methyl ether and tert-amyl methyl ether to achieve a Coulombic efficiency of 99.3 %. By demonstrating that both an anion-dominated solvation structure and a reductively stable solvent are necessary to enable high anion selectivity during SEI formation, this work identifies a key solvent design rule for high-performance electrolytes for lithium metal batteries.

papers.title: Electron Activated Dissociation Technique for Middle-Down Mass Spectrometric Analysis of Disulphide Bonds and Free Thiols: Application in Characterising Monoclonal Antibody Biotherapeutic Fragments
papers.abstract: Disulphide bonds contribute to the conformational structure of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and are therefore vital for their stability, biological function and safety. However, the biopharmaceutical manufacturing process can influence these bonds, potentially leading to the formation of free thiols, scrambled configurations, or degradation products, which may negatively impact quality and safety. Current analytical strategies for characterising disulphide bonds and free thiols in mAbs are predominantly based on labelled and label-free bottom-up mass spectrometry approaches. However, these methods are often time-consuming and may generate unwanted artefacts such as disulphide bond scrambled products. As a result, middle-down and top-down mass spectrometry methods are being explored as alternative approaches. However, their broader application remains limited by challenges in achieving sufficient MS/MS fragmentation for reliable characterisation of protein modifications and disulphide linkages. In this study, we evaluated an electron-activated dissociation (EAD) on the Sciex ZenoTOF 7600+ system for middle-down characterisation of intra- and interchain DSB and free thiols in mAbs. The EAD fragmentation generated diagnostic fragment ion patterns that can confirm intra-chain disulphide linkages on the subunits. This approach was applied to assess domain-specific free thiol on the NISTmAb Fc/2 subunit, as well as disulphide-scrambled products generated from mild reduction. Additionally, the method was effective in characterising fragments from antibody degradation. Overall, this EAD-based approach provides a rapid alternative for antibody product characterisation across different stages of the production process.

papers.title: Nickel-Catalyzed Enantioselective Radical C(sp3)–C(sp3) Cross-Coupling
papers.abstract: Enantioselective radical–radical cross-coupling represents a powerful yet largely unsolved strategy for constructing stereogenic C(sp 3 ) centers, because simultaneously controlling cross-selectivity and absolute stereochemistry between two distinct, transient alkyl radicals is exceptionally challenging. Here, we report a nickel-catalyzed C(sp 3 )–C(sp 3 ) cross-coupling that overcomes this limitation by using alkylzirconocenes, readily generated in situ from unactivated alkenes, and α‑halo amides. The reaction proceeds under mild, blue‑light‑driven conditions and provides direct access to chiral α‑aliphatic amides with outstanding efficiency (up to 98% yield) and enantioselectivity (up to 99:1 e.r.). The method exhibits remarkably broad substrate scope: a wide range of functional groups are tolerated on both coupling partners, and the protocol is successfully applied to the late‑stage diversification of complex natural products, including derivatives of cholesterol, estrone, and vitamin E. Furthermore, the reaction is extended to the highly enantioselective construction of quaternary carbon stereocenters, underscoring its practical synthetic value. Critical to this success was the development of a new pyridine–imidazoline (Pyim) ligand through over 140 iterative experimental cycles and deep learning framework for ligand optimization. This systematic screening campaign not only delivered a superior ligand, but also generated a rich, high‑quality dataset that precisely maps ligand structure to catalytic performance.

papers.title: A Density Matrix Theory for Photothermal Two-Dimensional Infrared Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional infrared (2D-IR) spectroscopy can resolve vibrational anharmonicity, mode coupling, and energy transfer. The conventional 2D-IR detects nonlinear polarization that generates propagating photons after sample’s light matter interaction with an infrared pulse sequence. However, photon detection is typically limited by the diffraction limit. The newly developed photothermal AFM-based two-dimensional infrared (AFM-2DIR) spectroscopy changes this fundamental detection endpoint: a femtosecond infrared pulse sequence prepares vibrational excitations in the tip-enhanced nanoscale near field, after which nonradiative relaxation converts the deposited energy into local heat that is read out through AFM’s cantilever’s mechanical response, thereby bypassing the optical diffraction limit. Here, we establish a thermal action theory through propagation of density matrix that formulates photothermal 2D-IR as an action-detected nonlinear spectroscopy. The theory is anchored in a final-state population selection rule: only nonlinear optical pathways lead to excited state populations after the pulse sequence contribute to the detected photothermal 2D-IR signal. Based on this theory, we provide a unified description of the anharmonic ladder response of carbonyl, polariton-to-phonon relaxation in hexagonal boron nitride, and polariton-to-polariton conversion. This framework provides a testable theory for photothermal 2D-IR spectroscopy for nanoscale structural dynamics, interfaces, and energy transfer, as well as to serve as a basis for other photothermal 2D spectroscopy to be developed in the future.

papers.title: Accurate Molecular Properties via Bootstrap Embedding
papers.abstract: We demonstrate the utility of back-transformed bootstrap embedding (BE) one- and two-particle density matrices (1 and 2-PDMs) by computing dipole moments and force gradients for several polar systems. The resulting mean absolute error in atomic force gradients at BE2/CCSD is approximately 0.003 a.u./bohr even in most polar and strained environments. We refer to this approach for generating molecular properties as Bootstrap Embedding – Direct Matrices (BE‑DM). This efficient evaluation of dipole moments and atomic force gradients holds significant promise for machine learning applications, where coupled-cluster-level forces can substantially enhance the quality of machine-learned potentials.

papers.title: In Operando Electrochemical Reduction of Indium Tin Oxide Contacts in Silicon Oxide Memristive Devices
papers.abstract: We report a study of current transient behaviour in silicon oxide memristive devices with indium tin oxide (ITO) top contacts. Constant-current electrical stress reveals that ITO-contacted devices exhibit chaotic conductance fluctuations and a single-phase transient in which the slow decay is suppressed, unlike the smooth, two-phase rise-and-decay response of devices with Au/Ti contacts. Through X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy depth profiling, spectroscopic evidence is provided that proton-driven electrochemical reduction of the ITO electrode decouples the two processes that the gold-contacted transient superimposes, leaving the initial conductance increase attributed to electronic charge-trapping in the bulk oxide while suppressing the slow decay phase normally observed in gold-contacted devices. Binding energy shifts in indium (~0.9 eV) and accelerated interfacial etch rates in stressed devices suggest sub-stoichiometric ITO formation. By suppressing the slow proton screening that masks it in gold-contacted devices, the ITO contact exposes the underlying trap-discharge relaxation, which is dispersive (stretched-exponential, exponent β < 1) with a field-free discharge time of a few seconds. The dispersion is itself bias-dependent, β decreasing with field from a near-single-rate field-free limit, so the strong dispersion measured under bias is in large part field-induced rather than intrinsic. These findings reveal that nanoscale electrode material selection critically determines the physical mechanisms governing conductance dynamics in memristive devices, with implications for neuromorphic computing and reliable nanoelectronic design.

papers.title: Transition-State Analysis Reveals a Noncanonical Multi-Step Pathway for O-GlcNAc Transferase Substrate Recognition
papers.abstract: O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) modifies thousands of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins, primarily within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), yet how it selectively recognizes such diverse substrates remains a central question in O-GlcNAc biology. The canonical model proposes that substrates are recognized through the tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) lumen, where conserved asparagine and aspartate ladders help position substrate peptides for glycosylation. However, many OGT substrates instead contain a short linear motif (SLiM) that binds the OGT intervening domain (Int-D), raising the question of whether these substrates follow the canonical TPR-lumen pathway or employ a distinct recognition mechanism. Here, using the Int-D-engaged substrate SMG9 as a model system, we first show by biolayer interferometry (BLI) that mutations of the canonical TPR-lumen residues N434A and N468A have minimal effects on SMG9 binding, indicating that SMG9 follows a distinct recognition mechanism. To resolve this millisecond-timescale recognition process, we performed 1,283 all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with an aggregate simulation time of 2.1 milliseconds and analyzed the resulting trajectories using Transition State identification via Dispersion and vAriational principle Regularized neural networks (TS-DAR) together with Markov state models (MSMs). The simulations reveal a previously unrecognized, noncanonical multi-step recognition pathway in which SMG9 progresses from the Int-D-binding pocket through a stable TPR-GTD intermediate before reaching the catalytic pocket, revealing that productive substrate recognition occurs through progressive rather than direct loading. Transition-state analysis further reveals that this pathway is driven by two sequential transient hydrophobic anchoring events that first establish the TPR-GTD intermediate and subsequently promote catalytic-site loading. Consistent with the proposed mechanism, mutation of the key TPR-GTD residue F878 disrupted SMG9 recognition in both transition-state mutation simulations and BLI binding experiments. Together, these findings establish a distinct Int-D-engaged recognition mechanism for OGT and suggest that OGT employs multiple recognition pathways to accommodate structurally diverse intrinsically disordered substrates. Beyond OGT, our work highlights transition-state analysis as a powerful approach for uncovering transient mechanistic interactions that govern biomolecular recognition but remain largely inaccessible from static structures and conventional metastable-state analyses.

papers.title: High-throughput multireference calculations of magnetic properties of lanthanide complexes
papers.abstract: Molecular magnets based on lanthanides are promising candidates for quantum information technologies. However, progress toward practical applications is limited by the small number of compounds with useful magnetic properties. Computational screening could accelerate discovery, but accurate prediction of lanthanide electronic and magnetic properties requires multireference electronic structure methods, which remain difficult to perform at scale. Additionally, the calculation of magnetic properties with perturbative approaches following the multireference calculations is sensitive to the number of states included in the spin–orbit treatment, defined as model space, which generally must be selected manually. Here, we develop an automated workflow for multireference calculations of monolanthanide complexes based on complete active space wave functions, followed by state-interaction spin–orbit coupling. The protocol iteratively selects the model space using an energy-based criterion while preserving near-degenerate manifolds. Benchmark calculations on lanthanide hexachlorides show that the approach reproduces experimental ligand-field splittings with mean absolute errors of 100-200 cm −1 across the lanthanide series. We further analyze the effect of model-space size on magnetic anisotropy and g-tensors in representative Dy and Er single-ion magnets.

papers.title: Case Study of Bayesian Batch Optimization Strategies for Heterogeneous Catalysts in CO2 Hydrogenation
papers.abstract: High-throughput and automated experimentation platforms combined with artificial intelligence are increasingly used to accelerate catalyst discovery. Batch Bayesian optimization (BO) (i.e., the simulta neous selection of multiple candidate experiments per iteration) is widely adopted for navigating large compositional spaces; however, its practical behavior under realistic high-throughput and batch con straints remains poorly understood. In this work, we performed a case study on four BO strategies to optimize the catalyst composition for the hydrogenation of CO2 to methanol. For each BO strategy, 48 catalysts were synthesized by co-precipitation, utilizing an automated synthesis platform, and evaluated in high-throughput fixed-bed reactors over seven batch iterations. The composition space comprised up to four metallic elements selected from a pool of nine. Although all BO strategies identified competitive catalyst formulations, most optimization trajectories rapidly converged toward distinct local optima that were strongly influenced by the initial random design and exhibited limited global exploration of the compositional space. This case study provides practical insights into the limitations of BO for batch catalyst optimization and highlights their strong dependence on the initial random design, parameter space definition, and batch execution strategy.

papers.title: NovoExpert-2: State-of-the-Art ADMET Prediction via Gradient-Boosted Trees on MapLight Fingerprints and GIN Embeddings
papers.abstract: We present NovoExpert-2, a dual-method approach to molecular property prediction that achieves state-of-the-art performance on five endpoints of the Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) ADMET benchmark. Our primary model combines MapLight-style fingerprint fea- tures (2,573 dimensions: Morgan ECFP, Avalon, ErG, and RDKit 2D descriptors) with 300- dimensional GIN supervised masking embeddings from the DGL-LifeSci pretrained model zoo, passed to a 5-seed CatBoost classifier/regressor ensemble. We additionally evaluate a Chemprop v2 directed message-passing neural network (D-MPNN) as a secondary method, and for each endpoint report the stronger of the two. Evaluated on all 22 endpoints of the TDC ADMET benchmark using official splits and per-endpoint metrics, NovoExpert-2 exceeds published state- of-the-art on CYP2D6 Veith (AUPRC 0.778 vs. 0.750, +0.028), CYP3A4 Veith (AUPRC 0.916 vs. 0.900, +0.016), CYP3A4 Substrate Carbonmangels (AUROC 0.660 vs. 0.656, +0.0040), Clearance Hepatocyte AZ (Spearman 0.511 vs. 0.487, +0.024), and DILI (AUROC 0.922 vs. 0.916, +0.006). The first four wins use CatBoost+MapLight+GIN; DILI uses Chemprop v2, which exploits end-to-end learned representations that better capture the multi-mechanism drug- induced liver injury phenotype. We additionally present a metric correction for our previously reported NovoExpert-1 CYP2D6 result: prior work measured AUROC (0.864) while the TDC leaderboard uses AUPRC; under the correct metric, NovoExpert-1 would score approximately 0.64 AUPRC on CYP2D6 and would not have beaten SOTA. NovoExpert-2, evaluated with the correct per-endpoint metric throughout, provides a more rigorous basis for leaderboard comparison. All code, trained models, and prediction files are publicly available.

papers.title: California’s plan to decarbonize electricity omits key greenhouse gas emissions
papers.abstract: Regional decarbonization or climate action plans in the US generally ignore the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of renewable electricity generation systems that occur beyond the operational stage. Our analysis of California’s prospective electricity sector changes through 2045 highlights the risks of omitting life cycle GHG emissions and their geographic variability in decarbonization planning. We demonstrate that the total GHG emissions of the proposed power sector in California through 2045 will be over 30% higher than reported by California’s Scoping Plan for Achieving Carbon Neutrality, even with optimal siting. The lack of life cycle accounting in decarbonization planning may lead to massive infrastructure changes and economic investments towards target emissions reductions that are ultimately insufficient to prevent or that may even contribute to worsening climate change.

papers.title: Non-Significant Effect of Water Content and Precursor Concentration on the Synthesis of Monodisperse SiO2@FexOy Colloidal Spheres
papers.abstract: Monodisperse spherical colloidal particles with core–shell structures, such as SiO₂@shell, are the focus of extensive research. However, those coated with iron oxide (SiO 2 @Fe x O y ) have received comparatively little attention, rendering them a promising area for further research. The present study investigates the process of formation of a thin iron oxide shell from an iron nitrate ethanolic solution. The results of this study indicate that the formation of the shell appears to initiate by the attachment of iron cations to specific, though unidentified binding sites on the silica surface. Once these sites are fully occupied, further incorporation of iron appears to cease. In order to examine how synthesis conditions affect shell thickness, a 2² factorial design was utilized to vary the water content in ethanol and the concentration of the iron precursor. Shell thickness was estimated from the diameters of particles measured in scanning electron microscopy images. The results indicate that, subsequent to the initial binding of iron to the silica surface, alterations in the amount of water or the concentration of the precursor do not result in the continued growth of the shell. This finding suggests that the primary factor impeding shell formation is the number of available binding sites on the silica surface.

papers.title: Mind the Driver: Behavior-aware Battery Usage Prediction to Reduce Electric Vehicle Range Anxiety
papers.abstract: Range anxiety remains a major concern for electric vehicle (EV) drivers due to unpredictable charge usage influenced by terrain and user behavior variations. To address this issue, we propose a data-driven approach to provide accurate trip-specific battery consumption for EV drivers. First, we present a new multi-fidelity battery performance dataset with 117 laboratory verified current profiles from 23 velocity-based drive cycles, capturing diverse road conditions, driving and charging patterns. We also introduce charge usage score, a metric comparing battery consumption to a reference trip at constant maximum velocity for same duration. Secondly, we demonstrate that incorporating additional trip-specific features, such as terrain, driving and charging patterns improves charge usage score prediction. The MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) of machine learning prediction reduced from 5.2% to 4.3% for current-based models and 7.5% to 5.3% in velocity-based models. Finally, we show that charge usage scores can be predicted using only 10% of initial trip data, achieving MAPE of 7.4% (velocity-based models) and 4.4% (current-based models), respectively. Using this early prediction capability, we demonstrate that switching from an assertive to a defensive driving style can save 3% more charge over an 800 second trip. Essentially, this closed-loop feedback system allows drivers with sufficient time to adjust their route, charging strategy and driving style in real time, reducing range anxiety. We hope our work offers a framework for advancing battery management systems and enhancing EV adoption.

papers.title: First-Principles Design of a Quantum-Selective Solid-State Hydrogen-to-Electricity Conversion Cell with Catalyst-Free Anode Dissociation (H2DE)
papers.abstract: Traditional Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) fuel cells are limited by the high cost of Platinum catalysts, polymer degradation, and parasitic pumping losses. In this work, we present the first-principles design of a quantum-selective, air-breathing solid-state hydrogen-to-electricity conversion cell (H2DE) utilizing a catalyst-free anode. By sandwiching a monolayer Hexagonal Boron Nitride (h-BN) membrane between a Magnesium (Mg) anode and a Nickel Oxide (NiO) cathode, we establish a permanent contact potential of Vbi = 1.64 V, yielding an intrinsic field of 0.492 V/ Å. To split hydrogen without a precious metal catalyst at the anode, we design tapered Magnesium nanotips on the anode face. These tips concentrate electrostatic lines, amplifying the local field to Eapex = 2.77 V/ Å at the apex, which exceeds the 2.0 V/ Å polarization threshold to dissociate H2 spontaneously. WKB quantum calculations show 100.0% proton transmission with electron leakage suppressed to 0.21%. 3D finite element (CalculiX) and finite volume (OpenFOAM) modeling verify nanoscale structural safety (SF = 2.11) and negligible parasitic pumping power (7.23 μW). This solid-state design provides a durable, high-efficiency pathway for clean hydrogen-to-electricity conversion utilizing earth-abundant materials. Highlights A catalyst-free, Platinum-free anode design for hydrogen-to-electricity conversion is proposed. A built-in Mg–NiO Schottky field (0.492 V/Å) drives spontaneous H2 dissociation at Mg nanotips. WKB tunneling calculations show 475× proton-over-electron selectivity through monolayer h-BN. DFT, FEA, and CFD modeling jointly verify electronic, mechanical, and fluidic feasibility. Key limitations — periodic-boundary effects, ZPE corrections, and H2 embrittlement risk — are identified for future experimental validation.

papers.title: Chiral Separation and Measurement of D- and L-Cysteine in Mammals
papers.abstract: While a number of recent studies explore the link between D-amino acids (D-AAs) and disease, D-Cysteine (D-Cys) is not commonly included in such studies. Recent reports demonstrate that D-Cys levels in mammalian tissues correlate with health; however, limited analytical methods are available to allow its measurement, especially in small volume samples. This lack of approaches limits studies on its role. Here, a robust small volume chiral measurement scheme for the measurement of endogenous D- and L-Cys in mammalian samples is reported using capillary electrophoresis coupled with laser induced fluorescence (CE-LIF) with LOQs of 20 pM from mammalian tissues. We compare D-Cys levels in young and aged mice in both the pancreas and cerebral cortex, where D-Cys levels decrease with age. Average pancreatic D-Cys levels decrease from 0.014 ± 0.003 µmol/g (n = 5) in 3-week-old mice to 0.006 ± 0.001 µmol/g (n = 6) in 24-week-old mice. This is the first report of the relationship between pancreatic D-Cys levels and aging.

papers.title: Compositional heterogeneity drives nanoscale ring formation in optically active one-dimensional van der Waals crystals
papers.abstract: While ubiquitous in nature, synthetic nanostructures that form ring- or spiral-like structures have remained particularly elusive. This has been especially the case for all-inorganic systems, which despite their potential to manifest distinct long-range physical states arising from twisting and inversion symmetry breaking, are generally devoid of twist-inducing interactions such as hydrogen bonding, πstacking, and disulfide bridging. Here, leveraging the non-covalently bound and one-dimensional (1D) 20 van der Waals (vdW) nature of transition metal trichalcogenides, we demonstrate the compositionally driven formation of well-defined spiral nanorings from NbS3 Type I (NbS3-I) chains that spontaneously self-coil through deliberate Ta alloying and S vacancy formation, forming Nb1-xTaxS3-d during vaporphase crystallization. The spiraled nanorings displayed an average circumference of 17 ± 4 µm, with average cross-sectional heights from ~550 nm down to ~20 nm, and widths ~620 nm down to ~40 nm, 25 respectively. We reconcile the compositionally driven spiraling of the chains into nanorings using density functional theory (DFT) calculations on idealized model structures, which revealed that Ta incorporation disrupts the intra-chain Nb–Nb dimerization, weakens the inter-chain bonding, lowers the Young’s modulus by a factor of ~5.6 relative to pristine NbS3-I, and renders the chains more susceptible to spiraling and self-coiling into nanorings during vapor-phase growth. Owing to their high refractive index and 30 nanoscale dimensions, these nanorings exhibit strong optical activity and size-dependent dipolar photonic signatures reminiscent of confined Mie-type resonance. Their nanoring geometry and structural anisotropy further give rise to polarization-dependent light scattering. These findings establish a deliberate and predictable synthetic route to access atypical nanoscale ring morphologies in 1D vdW solids, highlighting the potential of programmed spiraling and twisting of extended lattice nanostructures to realize optically 35 active nanoscale platforms and collective states arising from curved and twisted structures.

papers.title: Resonant Quantum Tunneling Mediated High Chirality Induced Spin Selectivity in the Multilayered Moiré Superlattices of Graphene
papers.abstract: Recent works that focus on developing new layered 2D materials through twisted stacking for fabricating resonant tunneling diode (RTD) and spintronic devices offer promising avenues for future spintronic and quantum devices. The much-studied graphene could be a potent candidate in this regard. Herein, we report the observation of RTD-like characteristics in moiré superlattices of multilayered graphene homostructures at room temperature and observation of chirality induced spin selection with a maximum spin polarizability of 90.47±1.81% under a bias of 1.41 V and at 0.45 T magnetic field. These superlattices were synthesized using a scalable sonication method in liquid dispersion medium where the graphite crystals were exfoliated to form 2D nanosheets that further twist-stacked to form moiré superlattices. We propose that the twisted interface acted as the quantum well, and the 2D nanosheets (consisting of atomic/oxygen defects) served as the tunnelling barrier, eliminating the need for a separate resistive material as a physical barrier, thus allowing for higher tunneling current. The position of the NDR peak had occurred under opposite potential bias when the direction of the magnetic field was reversed. We also report a method to fabricate precisely twist-stacked moiré superlattices of multilayered graphene using sonication of a mixture of graphite crystals with ZnCl2. These results also suggest the possibility to make portable quantum devices based on resonance tunneling.

papers.title: How Ready Are Universal Machine-learned Interatomic Potentials for Carbon Capture Simulations?
papers.abstract: Nanoporous materials offer a tunable platform for selective carbon capture through adsorption, and identifying the best candidates requires computational screening built on accurate and transferable models of host–guest interactions. Classical force fields (FFs) have enabled rapid large-scale screening but fail to accurately describe such interactions for challenging systems, and while universal Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials (u-MLIPs) promise to bridge this gap, their ability to predict macroscopic adsorption observables across chemically diverse frameworks remains largely underexplored. Here we benchmark 25 u-MLIPs against experimental CO2 adsorption data for nine metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) spanning rigid open-pore, open-metal-site, and confined small-pore classes, and find that quantitative isotherm prediction remains out of reach for the evaluated general-purpose models. We show that failures trace to two distinct error sources, the MOF–CO2 and the CO2–CO2 interactions, whose relative contribution shifts with framework chemistry, so that isotherm accuracy cannot be inferred from any single energy metric. In rigid open-pore and confined small-pore MOFs, the MOF–CO2 error dominates, while in strongly interacting frameworks with open metal site (OMS) both MOF–CO2 and CO2–CO2 descriptions become controlling factors, and error cancellation between the two sources can produce simulated accurate isotherms for physically incorrect reasons. Dataset composition, rather than architecture alone, determines whether a model reaches quantitative accuracy, and models trained on explicit MOF–CO2 and multi-molecule CO2 configurations perform most consistently. The evaluation protocol introduced here separates the two error sources and defines concrete paths for advancing u-MLIPs toward reliable computational screening for carbon capture.

papers.title: Algorithm for locating SCF solutions reveals conceptual limitations of the broken-symmetry approach applied to the oxygen-evolving complex
papers.abstract: Broken-symmetry (BS) calculations of polynuclear open-shell transition-metal complexes are widely used but rely on critical assumptions including the existence and stability of the self-consistent-field (SCF) solutions and the Heisenberg structure of magnetic interactions. We develop a new algorithm for systematic generation and analyses of SCF solutions and apply it to the oxygen-evolving complex (OEC). Several of these solutions are either electronically unstable or exhibit non-Heisenberg character, challenging the conventional interpretation of BS calculations. With homotopy continuation, the DFT solutions continuously transform into the Hartree–Fock solutions through an electron transfer in metal–oxo fragments, explaining a strong functional dependence of BS calculations. The Brueckner coupled-cluster method with double excitations establishes which SCF solutions provide the best reference for correlated wave-function treatments. Expansion of the developed methodology further strengthen the understanding of electronic structure in the Kok cycle of the OEC.

papers.title: Identifying Recurrent Mechanochemical Control in Active Cytoskeletal Networks
papers.abstract: ATP-powered cytoskeletal materials move through interactions among molecular motors, filaments, and networks that bind and remodel over time. Existing active-matter theories describe stress generation, flow, force propagation, and collective order. Long-range motion, however, can also arise from passive elasticity or hydrodynamic transmission. These observations therefore do not reveal whether motion is controlled by recurrent mechanochemical feedback. We define Active-Network Entrainment (ANE) to address this ambiguity. Motorized filament contacts are treated as active ports that can be perturbed locally, and the resulting motion is described by an interventional response operator. We compare this response with a matched frozen mechanochemical coun-terfactual that retains filament geometry, passive mechanics, and baseline source structure while suppressing adaptation and topology feedback. The difference isolates the part of the response that depends on endogenous recurrence. We define the Active-Network Entrainment Transition (ANET) as a closedloop stability loss through a distributed mode that is reachable from active perturbations, observable in measured motion, and absent from the corresponding frozen system. ANE thus identifies a redistribution of causal control from local motor actuation and passive transmission to the dynamics of the coupled mechanochemical network.

papers.title: Cheméo Relay, a D-MPNN-based chemical property prediction model family
papers.abstract: A message-passing neural network is a learned group-contribution method only if its readout carries molecular size, which the framework-default mean readout discards. We train directed message passing neural networks (D-MPNN, Chemprop v2) on experimental thermophysical data from the Cheméo database, one model per property, as a general-purpose graph-based alternative to the Joback group-contribution method [14], strongest in the regime where Joback degrades: Joback was fitted on small molecules and, as we show here head-to-head, degrades steadily as molecules grow; those larger molecules are a minority of the corpus (a quarter to a third of a typical set has eleven or more heavy atoms, though the spread is wide, from 11% for the small Gibbs-energy set to 56% for melting point), but they are exactly the regime where a group-contribution method has no good alternative. The contribution is not that sum pooling beats mean pooling, a fact already established in the graph-learning literature [18,19]; it is a property-by-property diagnosis on experimental thermophysical data of how the default silently fails, a reusable release discipline, and a family of released models measured against Joback, a simple descriptor baseline, and external data. The mean readout is size-invariant: it returns the average per-atom contribution, so a molecule and its dimer map to nearly the same vector, and every property that tracks molecular size collapsed toward the training mean; six properties, among them the critical constants and the Gibbs energy of formation, landed at test R2 near zero, and a gradient-boosted tree on plain RDKit descriptors beat the graph network on all six. Replacing the mean with a sum-aware pooling (sum and max concatenated) makes the molecule embedding scale with atom count, and the message passing then learns the higher-order structural corrections that Marrero and Gani add to a classical scheme by hand as second-and third-order groups [15]. The distinction we keep is between a graph-extensive readout (a property of the network) and a thermodynamically extensive target: the sum is needed outright for extensive targets such as critical volume and the formation enthalpies, while intensive targets that rise along homologous series, such as the boiling and critical temperatures, benefit because molecular size is a strong predictor of them, not because they are extensive. Nine of sixteen properties are released under a two-part criterion: a statistical bar (mean out-of-sample R2 above 0.70 with a train-test gap of at most 0.20 under repeated scaffold cross-validation, or state-of-the-art accuracy on a shared external benchmark) and a veto, that the incumbent Joback must not significantly out-predict the model in its tested domain; we lead with mean absolute error, since a small scaffold test set makes R2 noisy: normal boiling point (MAE 13.5 K, RMSE 30 K, 3.5% average relative error), melting point (MAE 30.8 K), critical volume and critical temperature, enthalpies of formation and vaporisation, ionisation energy, aqueous solubility and the acentric factor, each reported against Joback, the published state of the art, and the experimental reproducibility floor of the property. Against Joback on identical held-out folds the graph model significantly wins on five of the nine comparable properties (boiling-point MAE 13.5 vs 26.3 K, formation enthalpy 35.5 vs 70.9 kJ/mol), ties two, and its error grows far more slowly with molecular size than Joback’s, which grows several-fold; it also covers the compounds Joback cannot fragment at all, a few percent of a typical set and up to about 12% for some properties, at undiminished accuracy on the ordinary organics among them; the two properties Joback still out-predicts, Gibbs energy of formation and critical pressure, are exactly the two the veto holds back as beta, with Joback served in their place. We release them as the Cheméo Relay family, one model per property.

papers.title: Collision Induced Unfolding Predicts the Aggregation of Glycoengineered Monoclonal Antibodies
papers.abstract: Monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapeutics exhibit substantial structural heterogeneity, requiring analytical methods capable of rapidly assessing critical quality attributes (CQAs) that influence stability and developability. Non-native aggregation is a key CQA, given its propensity to decrease mAb efficacy and increase immunogenicity. However, current analytical tools commonly used to screen mAbs during drug development provide limited structural insight into aggregation prone monomeric structures. Orthogonal tools such as ion mobility-mass spectrometry (IM-MS), collision-induced unfolding (CIU), and IM-selected CIU (IM-CIU) enable rapid gas-phase structural characterization of proteins, offering the ability to enhance the resolution of complex structural mixtures, bridging the gap left by conventional aggregation analyses. In this study, we establish CIU as a prompt predictor of mAb aggregation propensity. Analysis of IgG1 CIU fingerprints revealed a high-energy bimodal structural population, quantified here as the ‘A/B ratio’, that correlates with pH-induced aggregation observed in our forced degradation studies. IM-CIU and CIU-electron capture dissociation (ECD) further characterized these structural populations, allowing us to localize the A/B ratio diagnostically to the hinge region of the mAb. We conclude by demonstrating that A/B ratio data, collected for glycoengineered mono-disperse mAb glycoforms can be used to test and predict the ability of specific glycans to protect mAbs from aggregation. Together, these results establish CIU-derived structural metrics as rapid predictors of mAb aggregation propensity, enabling higher-throughput structural assessment of biotherapeutic stability and glycoform-dependent effects.

papers.title: N-Substituent Effects on Selectivity in Ni-Mediated Decarbonylation of N-Arylphthalimides
papers.abstract: The nickel-catalyzed decarbonylation of imides and amides is a promising molecular editing strategy for generating C-C and C-N coupled structures commonly found in biologically active molecules. Despite their potential utility, there is limited understanding of the structural features that influence selectivity and catalytic efficiency in this class of reactions. We aim to understand and address this catalytic limitation through the isolation and study of well-defined reaction intermediates. Herein, we report the synthesis and characterization of 5-membered Ni II -metallacycles that are proposed to be key intermediates in the nickel-catalyzed decarbonylation reactions of N-arylphthalimides. Complexes derived from the direct decarbonylation of both N-phenyl and N-pyrrolylphthalimides were synthesized using both 4-dimethylaminopyridine and 2,2’-bipyridyl supporting ligands and demonstrated to be competent intermediates in Ni-catalyzed decarbonylation reactions. Moreover, comparison of their synthesis and reactivity revealed a striking influence of the N-aryl substituent in modulating the decarbonylation and CO reinsertion steps.

papers.title: Ion Mobility-Selected Collision Induced Unfolding Differentiates Biosimilars Based on Glycan Content
papers.abstract: As patents expire for monoclonal antibody (mAb) therapeutics, biosimilar development has emerged as a critical strategy for improving therapeutic accessibility. One critical quality attribute, glycosylation, can alter the efficacy, stability, and half-life of mAbs. Therefore, characterizing glycan microheterogeneity remains crucial during biosimilar development. While there are many methods to resolve the glycans present, it remains challenging to uncover how these glycoforms contribute to mAb structure and stability. Here, we present a middle-down ion mobility-mass spectrometry (IM-MS) workflow that integrates collision-induced unfolding (CIU) and ion mobility-selected CIU (IM-CIU) to resolve glycoform-dependent stability differences within Fc fragments of Rituxan and its biosimilars. Applying this platform across biosimilars with varying degrees of glycan microheterogeneity, we demonstrate that IM-CIU consistently detects glycan microheterogeneity differences that fall below the sensitivity threshold of ensemble-averaged global CIU measurements. In each case, stability differences are localized to the IM-CIU50-2 transition and can be mapped to leading and trailing IM-arrival time distributions (IMATD) subpopulations. Extending this approach to a controlled G2S2 titration series in trastuzumab, we show that trailing IMATD IM-CIU50-2 quantifies sialylated glycoform abundance and retains linearity at the low sialylation levels most relevant to biotherapeutic manufacturing. Together, these results establish IM-CIU as a sensitive, structurally informative platform for resolving glycoform heterogeneity in therapeutic antibodies, with direct implications for biosimilar characterization and critical quality attribute monitoring workflows.

papers.title: Ion Mobility-Collision Induced Unfolding Detects Stability Shifts within Hidden Protein Conformer Families
papers.abstract: Proteins commonly exist in complex mixtures, adopting a diverse ensemble of structural conformations. While some of these conformations are functionally important, others (e.g. pre-aggregative states), can adversely affect protein function. In monoclonal antibody (mAb)-based biotherapeutics such structural polydispersity is essential for native function but requires advanced biophysical and analytical techniques to assess and properly engineer optimal therapeutics. Methods such as native mass spectrometry (MS) and ion mobility-mass spectrometry (IM-MS) have become increasingly valuable for studying protein structure. Collision induced unfolding (CIU), an IM-MS assay, is frequently used to examine global higherorder structures of proteins. However, standard CIU assays are fundamentally limited by the IM resolution achieved for the precursor ion population, which may contain multiple conformers with similar collision cross sections. In this report, we use cyclic IM-MS (cIM-MS) to develop and conduct IM-selected CIU assays, which show dramatically enhanced capabilities for analyzing structurally polydisperse samples. To develop the IM-CIU approach, we investigate the model protein bovine serum albumin under both low and neutral pH conditions, demonstrating that IM-CIU can accurately identify domain III as the most perturbed region of the protein under these conditions. Additionally, we apply IM-CIU to analyze interleukin dimers, previously linked in therapeutic fusion protein constructs, and demonstrate that they exist in two distinct solution-based conformations. We conclude by outlining the fundamental principles of the IM-CIU method, highlighting its ability to resolve proteins with near-identical collision cross sections, and discussing its potential impact on the development of future pharmaceutical applications.

papers.title: A Unified Total Synthesis of Eudesmane-Type Sesquiterpenoid Dimers Chlorahupetenes A, B and E.
papers.abstract: Chlorahupetenes A (1) and B (2) are eudesmane-type sesquiterpenoid dimers that contain unprecedented, rearranged carbon skeletons that were isolated as enantiomeric pairs by Liu and coworkers in 2022. Herein, we disclose the first total synthesis of chlorahupetenes A (1) and B (2) in 8 steps from commercial materials. Our synthesis employs a novel Diels–Alder strategy to rapidly access the decalin-core of the sesquiterpenoid atractylenolide I (3) and, to the best of our knowledge, represents the shortest total synthesis to date. The endgame of the synthesis features a novel proposed biomimetic, base-promoted cascade of chlorahupetene E (8) to afford chlorahupetenes A (1) and B (2) in a ratio that closely mirrors their isolation ratio. This successful rearrangement supports our hypothesis that chlorahupetene E (8) is a direct biosynthetic precursor of chlorahupetenes A (1) and B (2) and serves to correct an error in a previous biosynthetic proposal.

papers.title: A Synthesis of a Fluorinated Tetrapeptide Substrate, (4-Fluoro-F)LQS, to Monitor SARS-CoV-2 Main Protease Activity (Nonstructural Protein 5, NSP5) Supports Cleavage between Leucine and Glutamine
papers.abstract: Severe acute respiratory coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) caused the global pandemic in 2020. The inhibition of NSP5 of SARS-CoV-2, the main cysteine protease, is a strategy to kill the virus. This paper describes in more detail the eSorts that were involved in designing and synthesizing a fluorinated tetrapeptide substrate, 4-fluoro-FLQS, to monitor NSP5 activity through 19F NMR and mass spectrometry. Docking studies predicted cleavage of the synthesized peptide between the canonical Q-S position. However, experimental results supported that the enzyme cleaved between the L-Q position to yield the product, 4fluoroFL. These results suggest the need for future research eSorts to carefully explore the mechanism of SARS-CoV-2 NSP5 (main protease) activity through the synthesis of other peptide substrates followed by analysis of the products through mass spectrometry for the unambiguous determination of the enzymatic products.

papers.title: Ex Situ Kinetic and Thermographic Profiling for Solvent-free Air-tolerant Giese-type Addition of Boronic esters onto Electron-Deficient Olefins
papers.abstract: We describe a dual Lewis base mechanophotocatalytic protocol for Giese-type additions that unites an iridium photocatalyst with Lewis bases under solvent-minimized or solvent-free conditions. The combination of mechanical agitation and visible-light excitation enables a fast and efficient coupling between boronate esters and electron-deficient olefins, delivering near-quantitative NMR yields within 40 minutes when using a liquid-assisted grinding (LAG) agent. Reactions carried out in the absence of LAG agent proceeded more slowly but still gave significant amounts of the desired product. Among the Lewis bases examined, 4-dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP) provided the highest conversions, regardless of whether a LAG agent was used or not. Thermal imaging and solvent-screening experiments revealed that methanol was the optical LAG agent, providing a micro-solvated environment that assists Lewis-base turnover. Together, these results and insights valorise dual Ir/LB mechanophotocatalysis as an efficient, rapid, and solvent-minimized methodology for this class of C sp3 -C sp2 cross-coupling reactions.

papers.title: A Review on F-Block Elements and Their Role in Nuclear Energy and Power Generation
papers.abstract: This paper intends to shed light on the F-block elements and their critical significance in nuclear energy, from their physical and chemical properties to their conventional uses. This paper covers all the F-block elements, with an emphasis on the details of every element in the lanthanide and actinide series. Linking these elements with nuclear energy, the basics of nuclear fission and energy-production reactors are also explained. I have also included the different types of reactors, along with their pros and cons. These elements heavily influence the future, be it in medicine, electronics and magnetics, catalysis in various technical industries, inorganic chemistry, particle physics, nuclear energy, and many more fields.

papers.title: Highly stable microporous water for energy absorption
papers.abstract: Water has poor compressibility. However, introducing hydrophobic porosity into water can make it highly compressible, as water molecules can be squeezed into the hydrophobic pores under pressure. This offers an exciting opportunity to use water to absorb mechanical shock. One straightforward approach to deliver this concept of microporous water is to disperse hydrophobic porous particles in water. However, using highly porous metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) in water poses a stability challenge: whether MOF particles can form a uniform suspension and remain stable over time without degradation. Herein, we propose a strategy that not only addresses stability concerns but also enhances the energy absorption of MOF intrusion under mechanical impact: shielding the MOF crystal with a mesoporous silica shell. The silica shell provides the long-term chemical and physical stability of the MOF particle, and its mesopores also allow external water to enter the MOF pores under pressure, albeit requiring higher mechanical input. Given the nature of the coating method, we envision it can be deployed across many different MOF materials and is a scalable approach to making stable microporous water for energy absorption.

papers.title: Water transport in MOF monoliths under pressure
papers.abstract: Pressurised intrusion into hydrophobic metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) is of considerable interest for energy absorption and fluid transport applications, yet the transport mechanisms in monolithic architectures remain poorly understood. Here, in-situ synchrotron radiographic imaging and powder diffraction have been employed to reveal the mechanism of pressurised water intrusion in ZIF-8 monoliths, through simultaneous visualisation of water transport and monitoring evolution in the crystal structure. The mechanism is dependent on the compactness of the monolith, with denser monoliths exhibiting a distinct edge-to-centre intrusion mechanism, whereas loosely packed monoliths display spatially uniform intrusion across the entire crosssection. Dimensions of the monolith sample also influence the intrusion pressure and extrusion kinetics by altering the transport path length for guest water molecules. These findings provide the first direct experimental evidence of pressure-driven water transport in MOF monoliths and reveal the mechanisms responsible for water intrusion in monoliths with varying dimensions and compacities. Moreover, this is the first study to report simultaneous synchrotron diffraction and imaging at elevated pressures, facilitated by the development of a novel high-pressure sample environment that allows in-situ measurements and has broad potential utility in combined imaging and diffraction studies at elevated pressures.

papers.title: Insight and Optimization Derived from Principal Component Analysis of Free Energy Surfaces
papers.abstract: Application of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to the free energy surfaces of a family of chemical compositions participating in a common reaction mechanism is shown to provide the number of degrees of freedom over which the free energy surfaces vary substantively, a physical interpretation of these degrees of freedom and a workspace for optimizing reaction kinetics. Free energy surfaces for the reduction of CO2 to formate by a family of molecular electrocatalysts (CpX)M(L2)H have been calculated to illustrate the process. In this case, overall electrophilicity, reducibility (particularly at a ligand), and active site accessibility emerge as independent axes responsible for 98.1% of the variance among the free energy surfaces in the data set. Incorporating a microkinetic model, multidimensional volcano plots can be constructed that illustrate peak performance and rate-limiting processes for all compositions bound by the free energy relationships present in the data. Optimization can be intuitively pursued in the principal component space, in which all kinetic parameters are related. The data illustrate that the optimal composition in a set constrained by realistic free energy relationships is not the one whose intermediates are most isoenergetic or which optimizes a single elementary rate.

papers.title: Epimer-Dependent Solid-State Landscapes of Trospium and Exotrospium Halide Salts
papers.abstract: Trospium (TR) and exotrospium (ETR) form a closely related epimeric pair of quaternary ammonium compounds, differing only in the stereochemistry of the tropane ring system. While the solid-state chemistry of trospium has been studied mainly for its chloride salt, no crystal structures of exotrospium salts have previously been reported. Here, we investigate the epimerdependent solid-state landscapes of TR and ETR across the halide series, using matched salt forms to distinguish the effects of counterion selection from those of stereochemical inversion. Two new TR salts and three new ETR salts were prepared and structurally characterized by single-crystal X-ray diffraction, supported by crystal-packing comparison, hydrogen-bond propensity analysis, lattice-energy calculations, morphology prediction, and CSD-Particle surface analysis. Despite their close molecular similarity, TR and ETR display markedly different solid-state behaviour. TR forms anhydrous chloride, bromide, and iodide salts stabilized by direct charge-assisted OH···halide interactions, whereas ETR forms isostructural chloride and bromide dihydrates, with only the iodide obtained as an anhydrate. These differences are reflected in molecular conformation, crystal packing, hydration behaviour, predicted crystal habit, and surface descriptors. The results show that epimerization can substantially alter both bulk and surface features of pharmaceutical molecular salts and demonstrate the value of combining structural comparison with particle-level descriptors when evaluating related solid forms.

papers.title: Spatial placement of half-Salen-bound nickel single-atoms on MOFs governs cooperative photocatalytic hydrogen evolution
