Mechanistic studies and DFT calculations show that water suppresses hydrazine-mediated photocatalyst quenching and promotes six-membered cyclization, while ambient air acts as the terminal oxidant for selective aromatization. The method exhibits broad functional group tolerance, enables late-stage diversification of complex molecules, and scales efficiently to gram scale without yield or selectivity loss. Notably, it affords di-, tri-, and tetrasubstituted pyridazines with complete regiocontrol governed by furan substitution, providing a complementary, sustainable platform for pyridazine synthesis from biomass feedstocks.

papers.title: C2-Arylation of (Hetero)Cyclic Enaminones with Arylboronic Reagents via the Productive Merger of Iodonium Activation and Carbene Coupling
papers.abstract: Despite the success of metal-catalyzed cross-couplings for C−C bond construction, the C2-arylation of cyclic enaminones is made challenging by preferential N-arylation due to their ambident nucleophilicity. Herein, we disclose a new strategy that achieves selective C2-arylation by converting enaminones into NH-iodonium salts, followed by Ru- or Rh-catalyzed arylation with arylboronic reagents. Notably, we demonstrate for the first time that these readily accessible iodonium intermediates, especially heterocyclic ones, serve as novel α-amino metal-carbene precursors. This protocol enables the synthesis of diverse 2-aryl (hetero)cyclic enaminones, and its excellent functional group tolerance is evidenced by the late-stage functionalization of numerous complex substrates. Moreover, both the iodonium activation and the subsequent arylation are amenable to gram-scale synthesis. The utility of this strategy is also demonstrated by: (i) the concise synthesis of an anti-leishmaniasis drug and three process-related impurities of macitentan, and (ii) the formal synthesis of marketed drugs macitentan and aprocitentan.

papers.title: End-to-End Conditions Generation for High-Throughput Experimentation under Practical Constraints
papers.abstract: C–N and C–C cross-coupling reactions are central to medicinal chemistry, but selecting effective conditions remains a major bottleneck because outcomes depend on strongly coupled choices of catalyst/ligand, base, solvent, and additives. In high-throughput experimentation (HTE), these choices must also be translated into concrete plate layouts that obey practical constraints for which components can be combined together. Here we present an end-to-end machine-learning workflow that connects data curation, condition generation, and constraint-aware plate design. We curate and share two industrial HTE datasets for Buchwald–Hartwig amination and Suzuki–Miyaura coupling that include a substantial number of reactions with negative outcomes. Using these data, we develop a conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) that generates candidate conditions while explicitly modelling both productive and unproductive regions of condition space, and we introduce a Frequency Chain baseline that is competitive under limited sampling budgets. The cVAE outperforms the baselines for low-to-moderate (below 100) sampled conditions, with improvements compared to previous cVAEs in six of eight tested metrics on the Buchwald–Hartwig reaction and one of eight on the Suzuki–Miyaura reaction. In single-transformation case studies, moving from a zero-shot to a few-shot regime improves key component recovery from 33% to 75% (Buchwald–Hartwig) and from 25% to 67% (Suzuki–Miyaura). Finally, an integer linear programming (ILP)-based plate design algorithm converts model predictions into executable HTE plates, matching or outperforming greedy positive-condition coverage while reducing predicted negative wells by 6.1 on average across ten evaluated transformations. Our integrated, data-driven plate design that combines machine learning predictions and lab automation has the potential to enable closed-loop optimisation of reaction conditions for rapid hit-to-lead optimisation.

papers.title: ChemicHAL – agentic explainable artificial intelligence platform for deep learning in chemistry
papers.abstract: Applications of machine learning (ML) in the natural sciences and interdisciplinary research typically benefit from downstream analyses using explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to rationalize predictions. We have designed and implemented an AI agent system powered by a large language model (LLM) to seamlessly link various ML and XAI methods for applications in chemistry. To this end, we focused on chemically intuitive XAI concepts. The agent system was carefully evaluated using different prediction tasks combining (deep) ML and XAI that also required discussion and interpretation of the results, without intermediate user intervention. In these proof-of-concept applications, the agent produced accurate results and showed a partly surprising capacity for chemical interpretation, although the central LLM did not undergo specific chemical training. We also detected limitations of the system’s ability to evaluate results from a chemical perspective, for instance, when challenged with comparing learning characteristics of different models. These findings demonstrated that the agent was not “thinking” independently. However, in terms of technical performance and efficiency, adaptability, and the capacity for chemical interpretation, the agent system significantly advances the use of XAI in molecular ML.

papers.title: Simultaneous LC–MS/MS Quantification of four KRAS Inhibitors (RMC-9805, RMC-7977, RMC-6236, and MRTX1133) in Human Plasma: Towards Therapeutic Drug Monitoring in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
papers.abstract: Purpose: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a highly lethal malignancy, with KRASG12D mutations present in approximately 40–45% of cases. Emerging RAS(ON) inhibitors, including RMC-6236, RMC-9805, RMC-7977, and MRTX1133, offer a promising precision medicine alternative to non-specific chemotherapy. However, except for MRTX1133, published methods for quantifying these compounds in human plasma or blood remain unavailable. Methods: We developed a liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) method for simultaneous quantification of MRTX1133, RMC-6236, RMC-9805, and RMC-7977 in human plasma. Plasma proteins were precipitated with ethanol using reserpine, verapamil, and labetalol as internal standards. Before LC–MS/MS analysis, 4,4′-methylenebis(2,6-diethylaniline) was added as a volumetric standard. Volumetric and internal-standard quantification produced comparable results. Due to matrix effects, analytes should be quantified using calibration curves prepared in spiked plasma. Results: The method showed excellent linearity, with r2 > 0.991, across 0.1–50 ng per 0.1 mL plasma. The lower limit of quantification was 0.1 ng for RMC-6236, RMC-9805, and RMC-7977, and 0.02 ng for MRTX1133. Conclusions: This first simultaneous assay for multiple KRASG12D inhibitors in human plasma supports pharmacokinetic studies and biomarker-driven PDAC clinical trials.

papers.title: DockBind: a quality-controlled dataset of modelled protein–ligand complexes associated with affinity data
papers.abstract: Ligand–protein interaction prediction is essential for structure-based drug discovery, but further development of machine-learning scoring functions is limited by a lack of high-quality training datasets. Here, we present DockBind, a curated dataset of modeled protein–ligand complexes paired with experimental binding affinity data, generated through a quality-controlled docking workflow. This workflow was developed based on an expanded docking benchmark, where we systematically evaluated free and template-based docking methods as well as ligand similarity and maximum common substructure (MCS) based pose filtering to generate and identify the most realistic poses. The resulting workflow was then incorporated into a pipeline integrating structural and binding affinity data from Binding MOAD, the Protein Data Bank, ChEMBL, and BindingDB, which resulted in 18,332 complexes across 612 protein targets, with high structural reliability and chemical diversity – the DockBind dataset – providing a valuable resource for training and benchmarking machine-learning scoring functions.

papers.title: Independent Coexistence of Short-lived Excimer and Long-lived Triplet–Triplet Pair Intermediates in a TIPS-Pentacene Cyclophane Dimer
papers.abstract: Singlet fission (SF), the organic analogue to multiple exciton generation (MEG), has gained attention in order to overcome the Shockley–Queisser limit of efficiency in single-junction solar cells. It is well recognized that SF can compete with other pathways that are typically thought of as parasitic or traps, such as excimer production or symmetry-breaking charge separation. Most notably, it has been shown albeit controversially that excimer-like states can control the efficiency and/or dynamics of the SF process by serving as a mediator to either inhibit or promote the intramolecular SF process. Therefore, understanding the precise nature of electronic states and their crossings is essential for developing tailor-made organic chromophores for molecular optoelectronics. Here, we demonstrate that a chloro-substituted TIPS-Pentacene (Cl-PC) cyclophane-type dimer can generate a wavelength-dependent shortlived excimer-like state for the lowest bright state which does not interfere with SF pathways that can be triggered independently via high energy transitions in the same molecular backbone. Our work for the first time shows that excimer states can exist in molecular dimers electronically uncoupled from the 1TT pair state that promotes SF.

papers.title: Microplastic Release from Multicomponent Paints: Analytical Challenges and Environmental Implications
papers.abstract: Paints and coatings are recognized as a potential source of secondary microplastics, yet quantitative experimental data on release mechanisms and rates remain scarce due to the complex, multicomponent nature of these materials. In this study, we developed and validated a stepwise, multi-modal workflow to assess microplastic release from façade paints under environmentally relevant conditions. In one model façade paint formulation, the binder was systematically varied, with one paint based on a pure acrylic binder and the other on a styrene-acrylic binder. The paints were subjected to 3000 h of artificial UV aging, followed by a stepwise sampling protocol with progressively increasing mechanical stress. Released species were comprehensively characterized using pyrolysis-GC/MS for polymer quantification, ICP-OES for inorganic components, analytical ultracentrifugation for nanoscale particles, particle counting, and total organic carbon analysis. A key challenge identified was delamination as model substrate artifact during sample preparation, which can lead to significant overestimation of microplastic release. By refining the protocol to avoid non-environmentally relevant delamination, reproducible mass balances and reliable quantification were achieved. The results demonstrate that UV aging predominantly leads to polymer degradation into volatile products and dissolved organic carbon, while the release of solid polymer-containing fragments remains very low. Measured microplastic releases were 0.59-0.84 mg/m2 per year (worst case from all environmentally relevant measurements) after accelerated aging, which is approximately 112-159 times lower than best case values predicted by commonly used model estimates. Overall, the findings highlight that, under realistic aging and mechanical conditions, paints release predominantly inorganic particles and only trace amounts of microplastics. The presented workflow provides a robust, transferable methodology for distinguishing between degradation products and true microplastic release, thereby supporting improved environmental risk assessment and the development of more sustainable coating systems with minimized microplastic emissions.

papers.title: Gradient-based Curvature-only Time-derivative Coupling for Surface Hopping and Coherent Switching with Decay of Mixing: Application to SO2 and Molecular Tully Models
papers.abstract: Time-derivative couplings (TDCs) are central ingredients in mixed quantum–classical simulations of nonadiabatic dynamics, yet their evaluation remains a key practical challenge when analytic nonadiabatic coupling vectors or wave-function overlaps are unavailable. Curvature-driven approximations provide an appealing alternative by evaluating TDCs from adiabatic potential energies or gradients along nuclear trajectories, motivated by the one-dimensional Baeck–An model. In this work, we examine curvature-based TDC approximations within trajectory surface hopping (TSH) and coherent switching with decay of mixing (CSDM), and introduce a modified gradientbased curvature-only formulation that retains the directional-curvature contribution to the TDC while omitting the explicit acceleration-dependent term at all times in the coupling evaluation. The performance of energy-based, gradient-based, and curvatureonly TDCs is evaluated for four benchmark systems of increasing dynamical complexity: ethylene, DMABN, fulvene, and SO 2 . For ethylene, all curvature-driven schemes closely reproduce reference dynamics obtained with analytic nonadiabatic couplings.

papers.title: Sulfation-enabled Direct Cross-Coupling of Phenols
papers.abstract: Up to 90% of the carbon feedstocks used in chemical manufacturing originate from oil and natural gas, with the remainder derived mainly from coal and biomass. This overwhelming dependence on fossil resources raises pressing sustainability and economic concerns, further amplified by recent geopolitical instabilities. Historically, the chemical industry has been founded on the catalytic oxidation and functionalization of petrochemical hydrocarbons, a paradigm that has shaped modern synthetic chemistry. Transitioning toward renewable carbon feedstocks instead requires an inverse approach: the catalytic deoxygenative functionalization of highly oxygenated biomass-derived substrates such as polyols and phenols. In this context, the emergence of lignin biorefineries has highlighted the growing potential of biomass-derived phenols as abundant, inexpensive and sustainable building blocks for the production of substituted arenes traditionally synthesized from fossil-derived precursors. However, the direct activation of phenolic C–OH bonds remains a long-standing challenge limiting the use of phenols in synthetic chemistry. Here, we report a novel and efficient strategy based on the in situ sulfation of phenols enabling their direct nickel-catalyzed cross-coupling with aryl Grignard reagents. This method provides an efficient, general and sustainable alternative to conventional palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling processes relying on aryl halides, which are less sustainable, non-renewable and more costly starting materials, paving the way to the sustainable synthesis of biaryl derivatives.

papers.title: Agentic, Explainable, and Generative Artificial Intelligence for Structure-Aware Small-Molecule Drug Design
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence for drug discovery is moving from static virtual-screening scores toward integrated decision systems that generate molecules, predict potency, explain model behaviour, quantify uncertainty, and guide experimental prioritisation. This framework presents a simulated, literature-benchmarked AI for drug discovery workflow that combines agentic and explainable machine learning with generative molecular design. The workflow is described at two levels. At the molecular level, the system represents each compound using ligand descriptors, protein-ligand interaction features, docking-like quality, graph-inspired latent variables, and ADME-like properties. At the systems level, these molecular signals are converted into classification performance, pIC50 regression, chemical-space visualisation, uncertainty estimates, applicability-domain flags, multi-objective lead scores, active-learning choices, and agentic medicinal-chemistry actions. The first module generated a focused small-molecule dataset across oncology-relevant targets, including LDHA, ATR, RAD52, POLQ, KRAS G12D, and PI3K alpha. In a representative run, logistic regression achieved ROC AUC 0.868 and PR AUC 0.973 for active-compound classification, while ridge regression predicted pIC50 with RMSE 0.607 and R2 0.598. Explainability highlighted docking-like score, shape complementarity, hydrophobic contacts, hydrogen bonding, polar surface area, and graph-inspired variables as key determinants of predicted activity. The second module extended the system into generative AI using BindingDB-, ChEMBL-, and PDBbind-inspired seed records, n-gram SMILES sampling, fragment recombination, scaffold mutation, and optional recurrent neural network generation. RDKit validation yielded 479 unique generated molecules with a novelty fraction of 0.923 relative to the seed corpus. Generated molecules were scored for predicted potency, activity probability, docking-like compatibility, ADME desirability, hERG-like risk, synthetic accessibility-like risk, uncertainty, novelty, diversity, and applicability-domain status. The final output is a transparent prototype showing how small-molecule AI can move from molecular representation to explainable prediction, generative design, uncertainty-aware prioritisation, and closed-loop experimental decision support. The workflow is synthetic and hypothesis-generating, but it is structured for replacement with real BindingDB, ChEMBL, PDBbind, docking, molecular dynamics, DMPK, and assay data.

papers.title: Oleic acid binding and exchange dynamics on NaYF4 nanocrystals
papers.abstract: Lanthanide-doped NaYF4 nanocrystals (NCs) are widely used for their exceptional photoluminescence properties. Their performance and processability are critically dependent on surface-bound ligands such as oleic acid. While these ligands stabilise NCs during synthesis and in nonpolar solvents, applications often require post-synthetic ligand exchange. Here, we investigate the binding mode, surface location, and exchange dynamics of oleic acid on NaYF4 NCs using a variety of analysis techniques, including infrared spectroscopy (IR), nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR), and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). Our methods distinguish bound and free ligand populations, quantify surface coverage, and detail how common purification steps alter ligand density. These findings offer key insights into NC surface chemistry and provide a foundation for rational NC purification and ligand-exchange strategies, with implications for optimising colloidal stability and functionalisation.

papers.title: Organocatalytic Cascade Assembly of Hyperfunctionalized Electron-Deficient Cyclopentadienones
papers.abstract: Hyperfunctionalized carbocyclic systems have attracted attention by virtue of unique physicochemical properties, yet general synthetic routes for their construction are scarce. The present work describes an organocatalytic cascade approach to the synthesis of 2-hydroxycyclopentadienones with electron-withdrawing substituents. Two cascade schemes are developed and utilized, which provide a high degree of substituent variation and employ readily available starting materials and DMAP as the organocatalyst. Quantum chemical calculations and HRMS monitoring were applied to elucidate reaction mechanism.

papers.title: Probing Solvent Dynamics at the Single-Molecule Limit
papers.abstract: The Electric Double Layer (EDL) that self-organises at electrode-electrolyte interfaces plays a fundamental role in electrochemistry. While its structure has been extensively studied over the last 150 years, its dynamic behaviour is still not completely understood. Here, we present a novel experimental approach to probe the EDL–using single-molecule junctions as ultrasensitive probes–validated by a preliminary study of the Inner Helmholtz Plane (IHP). We measured the current response of single-molecule devices under square-wave bias in various solvent environments, and we found remarkable differences falling into three categories: large non-linear transients in highly polar solvents, capacitor-like responses in solvents of intermediate polarity, and no significant transients (within our frequency limits) in non-polar solvents. By fitting the solvent behaviour to a molecular-level equivalent circuit, our data reveal trends in how the nature of the solvent influences IHP dynamics, and provide insights into the origin of non-linearity.

papers.title: Magnetic Fields Affect Hydroxyl Structure at the Interface of Water and Dysprosium-Treated Alumina
papers.abstract: Resolving magnetic field effects on surface and solution structure at the molecular scale is important to a range of applications, including synthesis, separations, and catalysis. We present direct evidence that paramagnetic rare earth element (REE) ions adsorbed onto alumina surfaces respond to magnetic fields by reorganizing interfacial water and hydroxyl structure. Vibrational sum-frequency generation (vSFG) spectroscopy showed that REE adsorption suppresses free aluminol intensity and increases hydrogen- bonded hydroxyls. Mapping the REE ion distribution revealed surface-bound domains correlated with the underlying alumina lattice. When a 1 T magnetic field was applied, dysprosium-treated alumina interfaces experienced pronounced hydroxyl restructuring, including suppression of free hydroxyls, reorganization of weakly hydrogen-bonded species, and increased ordering and adsorption of strongly hydrogen-bonded hydroxyls. Magnetic-field effects were absent for lanthanum-treated alumina and other non-magnetic controls. Density functional theory simulations showed that Dy 3+ is likely to dynamically occupy inner- and outer-sphere adsorption states that induce long-range spin polarization in water and hydroxyls, substantially quenching its magnetic moment while perturbing hydrogen-bond networks across multiple solvation layers; a result validated by magnetometry measurements. This unexpected magnetic field effect on hydroxyl structure presents opportunities for controlling interfacial phenomena and energy landscapes at the molecular scale, beyond simply using magnets to affect mass transport.

papers.title: Rapid two-step multicomponent synthesis and structure-degradation relationships of selective HDAC6 PROTAC degraders
papers.abstract: This work reports on the development of selective histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) degraders based on a peptoid scaffold. Structure-based design identified the isocyanide-derived cap region as suitable exit vector for linker attachment, enabling rapid generation of CRBN-recruiting PROTACs via the Ugi four-component reaction. A focused library of 12 degraders revealed a strong dependence of activity on linker composition, with octyl-linked compounds (9e-h) showing the strongest HDAC6 degradation with half-maximal degradation values of 17-36 nM in kinetic HDAC6 degradation assays. The lead compounds selectively degraded HDAC6 in MM.1S and MV4-11 cells without affecting class I HDACs and demonstrated clean proteomic profiles. Functionally, compounds 9e and 9f exhibited submicromolar antiproliferative activity in FLT3-ITD-mutated acute myleoid leukemia cells. In immune cells, inhibition of proinflammatory signaling was linked to residual class I HDAC inhibition rather than HDAC6 degradation. Overall, this study establishes an efficient multicomponent strategy for PROTAC synthesis and highlights key structure-degradation relationships.

papers.title: Pilot-Scale Evaluation of Single-Stage Lime Softening for Upgrading Drinking Water 1
papers.abstract: Motivated by the need to modernize a 90-year-old two-stage softening system, this 24-26 month pilot study evaluated a single-stage solids-contact clarifier under varying source water 27 conditions. Water quality was monitored through softening, ozonation, and granular activated 28 carbon (GAC) filtration to assess downstream treatment performance. Lime addition maintained 29 alkalinity below 100 mg/L but did not consistently achieve hardness goals, whereas soda ash 30 addition improved hardness but increased alkalinity above levels desired for scale control. Lime 31 and caustic provided the best balance between hardness and alkalinity targets, with performance 32 varying by coagulants. Metal-based coagulants combined with softening chemicals improved 33 hardness removal through co-precipitation and achieved higher TOC and UV254 control than 34 cationic polymer. With appropriate chemical dosing, softening dampened source-water variability, 35 and downstream GAC filtration achieved stable turbidity removal. Overall, the study demonstrates 36 that chemical dosing and operational control are key to consistent hardness removal and robust 37

papers.title: Convergent synthesis of the minimal macrolide antibiotic narbomycin
papers.abstract: Macrolide antibiotics are a class of structurally diverse polyketides including essential medicines like erythromycin and azithromycin. Structurally minimal macrolides such as narbomycin lack much of the functionality common to other members of the class and exhibit a distinct mode of action wherein they completely inhibit bacterial growth despite only moderate (~50%) inhibition of global protein synthesis. Unfortunately, lack of availability of these natural products has prevented a thorough investigation of their unusual mechanisms of action. Here we report a 10-step synthesis of narbomycin enabled by a Liebeskind-Srogl fragment coupling, a novel macrolactonization by direct displacement of an Evans auxiliary, and a stereoselective late-stage enone reduction. In addition to accessing the natural product, the route enables access to C8,19-unsaturated variants which could serve as useful precursors for late-stage functionalization by conjugate addition.

papers.title: Morphology and Ion Transport in Zwitterionic Polysiloxanes
papers.abstract: energy barriers for ion transport and therefore increase room temperature ionic conductivity. Here, 28 we demonstrate that superionic conductivity is not a universal behavior of doped PZIs, instead 29 demanding strategic design of ion transport pathways. Using a flexible polysiloxane-based PZI 30 doped with LiTFSI salt, we observe that room temperature conductivity remains limited (~10-8 31 S/cm at 293K) despite relatively low glass transition temperature and high dielectric constant. X-32 ray scattering reveals the structural origin of this result: zwitterionic groups aggregate into isolated 33 nanodomains separated by the polymer matrix which slows down ion mobility. Once these clusters 34 start overlapping, doped PZI showed significant enhancement in conductivity. These results 35 demonstrate critical role of percolating ion channels for superionic conductivity in PZIs. 36 37 38

papers.title: Potential-Driven Asynchronicity in C–H Bond Activation Mediated by a New TAML–Iron Chloride Complex
papers.abstract: High-valent iron–oxo complexes are among the most effective oxidants for C–H bond activation; however, the ability of non-oxo high-valent iron species to perform similar transformations remains an emerging area of research. Herein, we report a new generation of bTAML–Fe complexes featuring strategic ligand framework modifications that markedly enhance the redox potential of the iron center. Oxidation of the FeIIICl precursor generates a highly reactive FeIVCl species, which has been characterized by UV-vis, EPR and HRMS. Remarkably, this complex is the first FeIVCl species shown to abstract hydrogen atoms from O–H and weak C–H bonds. Kinetic and thermodynamic studies reveal that substrate oxidation proceeds through an oxidative asynchronous concerted proton-electron transfer (CPET) pathway.

papers.title: From mouth to colon: a framework for engineering food matrices to engage the satiety cascade and endogenous GLP-1 signalling
papers.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have produced the largest pharmacological reductions in body weight yet achieved. Their success is most usefully interpreted not as the discovery of a new target but as validation of an endogenous pathway the gut already possesses, and of appetite regulation as a tractable physiological target. Yet food engages appetite control weakly and inconsistently, and pharmacotherapy alone cannot meet the global burden of metabolic disease. This Perspective argues that satiety is not a single signal but a spatially and temporally distributed cascade—oro-sensory and cephalic at the mouth, volumetric at the stomach, nutrient chemosensing at the duodenum, direct enteroendocrine sensing at the ileum, and fermentative signalling in the colon—and that the food matrix is the common variable that governs engagement at each station. Food processing acts on precisely this architecture, weakening engagement station by station: a softened matrix shortens oral exposure and accelerates eating; lowered viscosity speeds gastric emptying; raised digestibility diverts substrate from the distal small intestine and colon, where the food-responsive L-cell populations and fermentative capacity reside. Recent human work shows that engineering a single structural lever—intact plant cells that carry starch past proximal digestion—elevates and sustains GLP-1 and PYY. This single-station result is interpreted here as evidence supporting the plausibility of a broader and largely unattempted programme: designing real, multi-component food matrices that engage multiple components of the satiety cascade across the gastrointestinal tract rather than acting predominantly at a single site. Drawing on an integrated body of in vivo evidence, the analysis treats structural digestibility as a measurable candidate variable with the potential to predict relationships among matrix architecture, ileal escape, intestinal transit, the colonic site of fermentation, and food intake. It sets out what must be established—structural characterisation as standard practice, model systems that preserve the food-to-signal chain, and fermentation phenotype as a determinant of individual response—to make multi-site, food-based appetite engineering clinically actionable.

papers.title: Investigating Tensile Properties and Pull-Out Behaviour of Novel High-Modulus Glass Fibres and the Impact of Various Sizings
papers.abstract: High modulus glass fibres (HM-GF) offer a promising alternative to carbon fibres for lightweight composite applications, particularly in next-generation > 20 MW wind turbine blades, where high stiffness combined with cost-effectiveness is critical. This study investigates the mechanical properties of four novel HM-GF compositions (T9, T10, V9 and V10) based on the magnesium aluminosilicate (MAS) glass system, modified with Y2O3 and ZnO to increase the Young's modulus. Three sizing formulations (EP1, EP5, EP7) were developed to optimise fibre–matrix compatibility, and a commercial E-glass fibre (E-GF) was included as a reference. Single-fibre tensile tests and single-fibre pull-out tests were used to characterise the tensile properties and the interfacial bonding, respectively. Sizing significantly enhanced the characteristic tensile strength, with V10-GF/EP7 achieving a 91 % improvement (1042 → 1993 MPa) over the unsized fibre. EP7 also yielded the highest apparent interfacial shear strength (58.9 MPa for E-GF, a 65 % increase over the unsized reference), while EP5 performed well for T9- and V9-GF. In contrast, both EP1 and EP5 reduced the local interfacial shear strength below that of the unsized V10-GF, revealing a composition-specific sizing incompatibility unique to the ZnO-containing V10 glass. Overall, the results show that HM-GF combine the high stiffness required for next-generation blades with an interfacial performance that can be tuned through tailored sizing, establishing them as a promising, potentially cost-effective alternative to carbon fibres in renewable energy applications and beyond.

papers.title: Demonstrating Reversible N=N Double Bond Cleavage at a Single Metal Center
papers.abstract: Oxidative addition (OA) and reductive elimination (RE) processes represent fundamental organometallic chemical transformations. These reactions generally break and form single bonds via the formal removal or addition, respectively, of two electrons from a redox-active atom. The capacity of certain transition metal ions to reversibly mediate two-electron OA and RE reactions forms the basis for myriad catalytic chemical transformations essential to the modern chemical synthesis of industrial and fine chemicals. While a wide variety of single chemical bonds readily undergo OA and can be (re)formed via RE, there remains a dearth of examples whereby double bonds are manipulated in a similar manner. Examples of four-electron OA or RE are rare, in part owing to the requirement of a redox-active center that can faithfully accept or release four electrons. This report describes the reactivity of a molecular chromium complex that mediates both a 2-electron OA of a phthalazine derivative and the four-electron OA of the N=N double bond of a benzo[c]cinnoline derivative. Crucially, the latter reaction is shown to be reversible and the heterocycle can be released via a four-electron RE process. This represents the first example of a reversible fourelectron bond activation at a single metal center, and its demonstration provides a blueprint for expanding the toolkit available to organometallic chemists.

papers.title: An Inverse Design Workflow for Solvent Mixtures Based on Hansen Solubility Parameters
papers.abstract: We present SolvPred, an open-source Python framework for inverse design of solvent mixtures based on Hansen solubility parameters (HSPs). SolvPred allows users to control the composition of solvent mixtures while setting essential experimental constraints. We have validated the approach using a polyimide condensation as a model reaction, where hydrogen bonding interactions were selectively tuned. SolvPred identified seven viable ternary mixtures from an otherwise intractable space of 171,871 possibilities. The optimal solvent mixture achieved a fivefold improvement in the product yield at a milder temperature when compared with the conventional single-solvent condition. This work establishes SolvPred as a practical solution for rational solvent mixture design and experimental planning, as well as an efficient tool for property-guided solvent optimization within data-driven experimental workflows.

papers.title: Integrated Hydrodynamic-Reactive Computational Framework for Fischer-Tropsch Slurry Bubble Column Reactors
Current-limited photocatalysis unravels interface-driven band modulation in 2D heterostructures
papers.abstract: Transition Metal Dichalcogenide heterostructures, layer-wise functionalized and separated by atomically sharp interfaces, offer prospects for novel, ultra-compact device concepts. Intertwined in the electronic read-out, layer-sensitive property optimization requires advanced experimental access to spatially separated regions for disentanglement. This study employs nano-droplet Scanning Electrochemical Cell Microscopy (n-SECCM), limiting the current and compensating for intrinsic interlayer resistance. Our results reveal the dominant role of the surface conduction band minimum's alignment in governing photocatalytic activity. Charge recombination and interlayer transfer limitations, while relevant in device performance, are secondary to the alignment effect. The combination of n-SECCM with complementary experimental and computational techniques provides unprecedented insights into the complexity of the surface electronic structure through photocatalysis, charting a pathway toward next-generation solar energy solutions.

papers.title: SuFEx-Enabled Tyrosine Specific Bioconjugation of Near-Infrared Fluorophores
papers.abstract: Sulfur (VI) fluoride exchange (SuFEx) chemistry has been widely applied in small-molecule medicinal chemistry, but its translation to near-infrared (NIR) fluorophores and application to antibody labeling remain largely unexplored. Here, we report a general synthetic approach for the preparation of aryl sulfonyl fluoride-functionalized indolenines and their incorporation into heptamethine cyanine (Cy7) fluorophores. The strategy is compatible with a broad range of indolenine substrates bearing diverse electronic and solubilizing substituents, enabling the synthesis of a library of water-soluble, SuFEx-enabled Cy7 fluorophores. Using SAT-NIR-746-SF as a lead probe, we demonstrate that the aryl sulfonyl fluoride handle is stable under physiologically relevant conditions (t1/2 >18h at pH 7.4) and enables efficient antibody labeling (DOL up to 6.1) under mild aqueous conditions. The degree of labeling can be systematically controlled by varying reaction pH, incubation time, and reagent stoichiometry. The strategy was successfully applied to therapeutic monoclonal antibodies, including trastuzumab, panitumumab, and cetuximab, and the resulting conjugates were stable under acidic, physiological, and serum conditions. Amino acid selectivity assays and tandem mass spectrometry-based proteomics of labeled trastuzumab confirmed modification exclusively at tyrosine residues, establishing the tyrosine-selective nature of this conjugation platform. SAT-NIR-746-SF-conjugated secondary antibodies provided specific labeling of phospho-histone H3 (H3S10P) in confocal immunofluorescence microscopy. These results establish SuFEx-enabled Cy7 fluorophores as a practical platform for tyrosine-selective antibody bioconjugation and demonstrate their utility in fluorescence imaging applications.

papers.title: Ligand-Controlled Chemodivergent β-Methylene C(sp3)–H Heteroarylation of Aliphatic Acids
papers.abstract: Ligand-controlled chemodivergence in C–H activation remains a significant challenge as multiple reaction pathways exist in the presence of multiple C–H bonds. Here we report a Pd(II)-catalyzed chemodivergent β -methylene C(sp³)–H heteroarylation of free aliphatic acids leading to distinct products enabled by two different classes of bidentate pyridone ligands, respectively. These two ligands also overcome a long-standing inhibitory effect of heteroaryl iodides, demonstrating the potential of this protocol to serve as a general C(sp³)–C(sp 2 ) coupling method using readily available aliphatic acids as the alkylating partner. Mechanistic experiments and DFT analyses reveal that quinoline and the imine motifs of the ligands dictate how the carbon-carbon and carbon-palladium bonds of the key intermediates rotate through π-π interaction and steric control, respectively, decisively splitting the catalytic pathways towards either oxidative or reductive Heck products.

papers.title: A Hierarchical MnO/rGO-IrOx Nanocomposite Architecture for Sensitive Detection of Chlorate in Water
papers.abstract: Chlorate is an emerging contaminant originating from industrial processes, disinfectants, and water treatment applications, necessitating the development of rapid and reliable detection methods for environmental monitoring. Conventional chlorate analysis typically relies on laboratorybased techniques that require expensive instrumentation, extensive sample preparation, and skilled operators, limiting their suitability for on-site measurements. In this work, an electrochemical chlorate sensor based on a MnO/rGO–IrOx modified interdigitated gold microband electrode is presented. The hierarchical nanocomposite architecture enhances the electroactive surface area and promotes efficient charge transfer, resulting in high selectivity enhanced sensitivity, improved reproducibility. Using square wave voltammetry, the sensor exhibited a sensitivity of 0.03124 µA ppm-1, a limit of detection of 0.375 ppm. The developed platform demonstrated good selectivity toward chlorate in the presence of common interfering ions, including NO3-, NH4+, SO42-, Mg2+, Fe2+, Zn2+, and K+. These results highlight the potential of the proposed MnO/rGO–IrOx functionalized microelectrode as a simple and cost-effective platform for chlorate sensing and future environmental monitoring applications.

papers.title: Introducing Biocatalysis into the Second-Year Organic Laboratory: Using an Aldolase in the Synthesis of a Sunscreen Ingredient
papers.abstract: Biocatalysis has become an important part of synthetic chemistry, particularly in the pharmaceutical industry. It is therefore important for chemistry students to learn about biocatalysis in their programs. We have developed an experiment for the second-year organic laboratory that uses an aldolase to catalyze an aldol condensation using pyruvate as the aldol donor and 4-methoxybenzaldehyde (p-anisaldehyde) as the acceptor. By coupling this reaction with an oxidative decarboxylation using hydrogen peroxide, the reaction generates para-methoxycinnamic acid. The 2-ethylhexyl ester of this compound is a widely used active ingredient in commercial sunscreens. This procedure is carried out in a 3-hour laboratory session which also includes established techniques such as TLC and extraction using a separatory funnel, and yield and melting point of the product is assessed in the subsequent laboratory period. Student experience was gauged by a brief anonymous survey, which indicated an overall very positive response. This experiment, now delivered to ~150 students per year, promotes principles of green chemistry and encourages interdisciplinary thinking.

papers.title: Co-solvent enhanced solvation shell lability improves ion transport in Li-ion battery electrolytes
papers.abstract: Electrolytes for extreme fast charging (XFC) of Li-ion batteries must combine high ionic conductivity with favorable Li+ transference, yet these transport properties are difficult to improve simultaneously in practical carbonate-based liquids. Here, we investigate a 1.2 M LiPF6 electrolyte series based on ethylene carbonate (EC), ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC), and acetonitrile (ACN), in which ACN progressively replaces EMC from 0 to 40 vol%. Experiment and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations show that increasing ACN content raises conductivity from ∼10 to 23 mS cm−1, lowers viscosity from 3.5 to 2.2 cP, while MD further predicts a modest increase in the Li+ transference number from 0.37 to 0.42. These transport gains exceed what is expected from viscosity reduction alone: the conductivity–viscosity product increases monotonically, whereas ionicity and ion pair fractions change only weakly. At the molecular level, not only does ACN replace EMC in the Li+ first solvation shell, it remarkably shortens the residence time of all solvation shell species, thereby increasing solvation shell lability. Onsager analysis shows that ACN enhances the transport of both Li+ and PF− 6 while reducing persistent Li+–PF− 6 correlated motion over transport-relevant times. Solvent-resolved correlations and PF− 6 entry/exit analyses further show that ACN promotes faster solvent exchange during local ion-pair formation and relaxation, shifting transport away from a more vehicular regime and toward a more exchange-mediated one. These results identify dynamic solvent tuning as a transport design principle for XFC-relevant electrolytes, showing that the experimental measurements of conductivity and cation transference can be improved without requiring a major change in ion association.

papers.title: SPARQC: Spectral and Spatial Assessment for Reproducibility and Quality Control in MALDI Imaging Mass Spectrometry
papers.abstract: Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization imaging mass spectrometry (MALDI IMS) has matured into a leading approach for mapping a wide range of molecular classes at cellular resolution. Its incorporation into large-scale biological and biomedical studies has accelerated the need for standardized instrument assessment and monitoring to ensure imaging reproducibility across instruments, institutions, and time. To address this need, we present SPARQC, an open-source dashboard that pairs monitoring of mass spectrometer (MS) ion optics performance with quantitative assessment of MALDI laser irradiation performance, a spatial dimension of quality control (QC) that is unique to imaging experiments and unaddressed by existing tools. MS performance is tracked through standardized direct-infusion electrospray ionization (ESI) in both positive and negative ionization modes, monitoring signal intensity, resolving power, and mass accuracy. MALDI imaging performance is evaluated by generating ablation patterns on matrix-coated substrates under defined laser power and scan conditions and analyzing the resulting crater morphology using optical microscopy and automated image segmentation. By uniting spectral signal quality with quantitative laser ablation morphometry, SPARQC delivers a semi-automated, standardized framework for longitudinal QC of MALDI IMS systems and other mass spectrometry platforms. We demonstrate this framework across four instruments with distinct configurations over twelve months and present SPARQC as an open-source tool for the imaging community.

papers.title: Adsorption-Transport Coupling in Rice Husk Biomass-Derived Thin-Film Nanocomposite Membranes for Arsenic Remediation: A Mechanistic Insight into Nano-Interfacial Transport and Sustainable Membrane Design
papers.abstract: Arsenic contamination of groundwater remains a persistent environmental and public health issue in South and Southeast Asia, especially in decentralised rural regions where conventional water treatment is difficult to sustain. In the Mekong River Basin of Cambodia, elevated risks are reported in Kandal, Prey Veng, and Takeo provinces. Thin-film nanocomposite (TFN) membranes have emerged as promising solutions due to their coupled adsorption and selective transport behaviour, particularly when incorporating biomass-derived nanomaterials such as rice husk silica nanoparticles. However, mechanistic understanding of adsorption–transport coupling within these systems remains limited. This perspective analyses how nanoparticle functionalisation, dispersion, and IP influence selective layer formation, nano-interfacial energetics, permeability–selectivity trade-offs, fouling resistance, and transport stability. Key arsenic removal mechanisms-steric hindrance, Donnan exclusion, adsorption-mediated retention, hydration-assisted transport, and surface complexation are integrated. The emphasis being on distinct behaviours of As(III) and As(V), a major limitation in conventional polyamide membranes. Functionalised silica nanointerfaces (iron oxide, amine groups) are evaluated for their roles in hydrophilicity, freevolume modulation, and nanochannel formation. A mechanistic framework is proposed linking nanoparticle chemistry, selective-layer architecture, and adsorption–transport coupling in sustainable TFN systems.

papers.title: Impact of Chelate Binding and Structural Configuration on Redox Prediction: Insights from High-throughput Calculations
papers.abstract: Redox chemistry governs the energetic and electronic landscape of chemical transformations central to catalysis, energy conversion, and separations. Predicting the redox behavior in complex metal coordination systems requires a systematic sampling of the configurational space to capture the subtle interplay between molecular geometry, solvation, and electronic structure. This challenge is particularly relevant in actinide chemistry, where redox processes dictate the efficiency of nuclear fuel recycling and waste separations. In this work, we integrate automated structure generation with high-throughput density functional theory to probe the AnO2 2+/+ (An = U, Np, Pu) redox couple in aqueous nitric acid media with representative chelating ligands. By explicitly accounting for diverse coordination environments and ligand-binding configurations, the role of chelator charge, donor-atom identity, and molecular configuration is established. Systematic configurational exploration exposes shifts exceeding 0.300 V arising from ligand substitution and structural isomerization—effects often overlooked in conventional single-structure studies. The observed correlations between coordination number, local electrostatic environment, and frontier orbital energetics establish design principles for tuning redox potentials across f-element systems for a wide range spanning over 1.5 V. These findings highlight the essential role of configurational sampling in quantitative redox prediction and offer molecular-level strategies not only for controlling redox chemistry in advanced nuclear separation workflows, but also towards metal coordination chemistry used in a variety of applications.

papers.title: Theory and Simulations of Atomic-force-microscopy based Two-dimensional Electronic Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Probing excited states and ultrafast dynamics in heterogeneous and interfacial systems requires enhanced spatial and temporal resolution. Coherent two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy (2DES) offers a sub-picosecond temporal resolution but its spatial resolution is restricted by the diffraction limit. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) overcomes the diffraction limit and routinely attains a sub-10 nm spatial resolution. In this article we establish a theoretical framework for the AFM-detected 2DES spectroscopy—a technique that is yet to be experimentally realized but promises to deliver high temporal and spatial resolution simultaneously. AFM-2DES would measure thermal expansion of the sample in response to interactions with multiple time-delayed laser pulses which interrogate electronic states of the system. We illustrate that the information contained in AFM-2DES spectra is complementary to other action 2D spectroscopies, thus establishing AFM-2DES spectroscopy as a valuable addition to the arsenal of ultrafast spectroscopy techniques.

papers.title: Superionic boron diffusion in dense crystalline B2O3
papers.abstract: We report the emergence of a superionic phase of B 2 O 3 revealed by molecular dynamics simulations using a machine-learned interatomic potential trained at the r 2 SCAN level of theory. The phase exists at 3600 K and 50 GPa, with a density of around 3.8 g/cc, and is characterized by rapid boron motion, while the oxygen sublattice is crystalline in the P6 3 /mmc space group. The hopping mechanism of boron motion is ascertained through van Hove space-time correlation functions. Nudged elastic band calculations for boron hopping within a fixed lattice, both explicit DFT-and MLIP-based, reveal it to be activated with a barrier of around 4 eV. Interestingly, the superionic phase is obtained via two pathways: by heating the B 2 O 3 -P2 1 2 1 2 1 crystal reported in recent experiments, as well as from the B 2 O 3 melt at high pressures.

papers.title: Ion Mixtures Defy Additive Conductivity via Quantised-Hydration Clusters in Angstrom-Scale Channels
papers.abstract: Ion transport in sub-nanometre aqueous channels underpins electrochemical energy storage, ion-selective separations and sensing, where confinement can strongly alter the ionic composition and transport. However, composition-dependent transport in confined electrolytes is still commonly interpreted through effective ion mobility, electrostatic screening or ideal mixing, leaving the structural origin of non-ideal transport largely unresolved. Here, using atomistic simulations of NaCl and KCl in graphene nanoslits, we show that mixed electrolytes exhibit superadditive ion transport, with conductivities exceeding those of the corresponding pure salts while retaining tuneable ion selectivity. This transport anomaly is coupled to ion-specific structural reorganisation: Na+ develops quantised, directionally ordered hydration shells that stabilise charge-asymmetric, non-stoichiometric Na+(Cl-)3 clusters under strong confinement, whereas K+ maintains a flexible, isotropic hydration environment that supports the formation of extended ion clusters. These contrasting behaviours establish hydration geometry—the spatial arrangement of hydration waters—as a physically grounded descriptor of nanoconfined electrolytes, identifying quantised hydration as the interaction-level origin of coupled structural and transport anomalies under extreme confinement. More broadly, these findings show that conductivity and selectivity in confined electrolytes can be tuned not only by ion mobility or concentration, but also by the hydration-driven organisation of correlated ion clusters.

papers.title: Inside job: synthetic exocytosis driven by in situ coacervation in polymersome artificial cells
papers.abstract: Synthetic cells can generate macromolecular products but generally lack mechanisms for their controlled export. Whether phase separation alone can drive macromolecular transit across a compartment boundary, without the membrane-fusion machinery that biological secretion requires, remains untested. Here, we report that within a polymeric artificial-cell system, a macromolecule synthesized in situ using the same chemistry that produced the compartment undergoes spontaneous non-lytic export when its phase state is shifted from soluble to condensed, with the synthesized product itself becoming the transport-competent state. Within PEG- b -PHPMA polymersomes assembled by biocatalytic polymerization-induced self-assembly (bioPISA), myoglobin-mediated polymerization of DMAEMA produced the polycation PDMAEMA, which accumulated at the membrane in a frustrated-wetting configuration. Addition of sodium hexametaphosphate (SHMP) induced intravesicular coacervation; the resulting condensates underwent non-lytic transmembrane transit while vesicle morphology remained preserved. Contact-angle analysis and membrane fluorescence profiling revealed localized membrane perturbations at transit sites, and the absence of a detectable membrane-derived envelope on externalized condensates indicated release as a bare dense phase. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)-mediated polyphosphate cleavage then reversed phase separation and dissolved the exported condensates, completing a cycle of in situ synthesis, condensate formation, export, and dissolution. By decoupling cargo synthesis from the export trigger, this work establishes that phase separation can function as a transport intermediate, not merely a packaging mechanism, for exocytosis-like export of macromolecules from polymeric artificial cells without membrane-fusion machinery.

papers.title: Comparative Molecular Docking of Roscovitine, Nutlin-3, and Pifithrin-α at the CDK2 ATP-Binding Pocket: Interaction Profiling and Implications for p53 Pathway Modulation
papers.abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) is a key regulator of cell-cycle progression and has been implicated in cancer-related dysregulation of the p53 signaling axis. In this study, molecular docking simulations using AutoDock Vina v1.2.7 were performed to compare the binding behavior of three pharmacologically relevant compounds — Roscovitine, Nutlin-3, and Pifithrin-α — within the ATP-binding pocket of CDK2 (PDB: 1AQ1; resolution: 2.0 Å). Docking reliability was assessed by comparing results across two exhaustiveness settings (Exh = 8 and Exh = 16), with all affinity differences remaining below 0.1 kcal/mol, indicating stable convergence of the search algorithm. Among the three ligands, Pifithrin-α showed the strongest predicted binding affinity (−8.599 kcal/mol), followed by Roscovitine (−8.388 kcal/mol) and Nutlin-3 (−7.501 kcal/mol). Protein-ligand interaction profiling with PLIP revealed distinct interaction patterns for each compound. Roscovitine formed three hydrogen bonds, ten hydrophobic contacts, and one salt bridge with catalytic residues LYS33 and ASP145, consistent with its known ATP-competitive CDK2 inhibition. Pifithrin-α displayed a parallel π-stacking interaction with PHE80 and a short hydrogen bond with LEU83, suggesting a possible CDK2-binding mode that merits further experimental evaluation. Nutlin-3 showed the weakest predicted affinity and the fewest contacts, in line with its established role as an MDM2 antagonist rather than a direct CDK2 ligand. Overall, these findings provide a comparative interaction-level analysis of three p53-pathway-related compounds at CDK2 and support further structure-guided investigation of Pifithrin-α as a potential off-target binder.

papers.title: Schema-Constrained LLM Planning for Executable Molecular Workflows: An Intent-to-Execution Infrastructure for Cheminformatics
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can interpret scientific intent, but their free-form outputs are often not executable scientific software. We present an intent-to-execution infrastructure for cheminformatics in which an LLM planner proposes machine-runnable molecular workflow objects under explicit schema constraints, a tool registry restricts allowed actions, and a deterministic execution layer performs SMILES parsing, molecular sanitization, and descriptor calculation. The system treats the LLM as a planning component rather than a chemistry executor: RDKit-grounded tools parse and sanitize SMILES, compute descriptors, apply Lipinski filters, rank candidates, and produce workflow artifacts. We evaluated a deterministic rule-based baseline, schema-constrained LLM planners, and weakly structured unconstrained LLM planners on molecular workflow prompts. For google/gemini-2.5-flash, executable workflow rate increased from 1.8% without constraints to 69.1% with schema constraints over 55 prompts; google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite increased from 1.8% to 47.3%; and anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6 increased from 0.0% to 65.0% on a 20-prompt subset. A chemistry case study using Aspirin, Ibuprofen, Caffeine, Paracetamol, and Metformin generated 43 computational candidates and retained 35 single-component candidates after RDKit parsing/sanitization and disconnected-product exclusion. These results support a constrained-planning claim: schema constraints are not cosmetic formatting, but a necessary yet not sufficient reliability layer for executable molecular workflows. The work does not include wet-lab validation; generated molecules are computational candidates only.

papers.title: Spins Afar - Long-Range Pulse Dipolar EPR Spectroscopy Uncovers Curvature in TRIM25’s Coiled Coil
papers.abstract: Pulse Dipolar Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (PDS) is a powerful method for determining nanometer distances in biomolecular systems. This methodology has been successfully used to validate structure hypotheses and to identify disorder. However, inherent distance limitations are under-explored. Many challenging biomolecular applications require long distance information, driving the need for a benchmarking study. We demonstrate distances up to 10.5 nm in TRIM25 reliably extracted from data obtained under standard sample conditions. By protein perdeuteration accurate distance measurements up to 17.3 nm were enabled. Enhancing sensitivity through optimization of the measurement and sample preparation conditions the achievable dipolar evolution time was extended to 150 µs. Thus, distances close to 20 nm should become experimentally accessible, highlighting the potential of advanced PDS methodologies for probing previously inaccessible long-range structural information in complex systems.

papers.title: Approach to γ-Substituted δ-Hydroxy Ketones via Cu-Catalyzed Cyclopropanol-Epoxide Coupling
papers.abstract: Herein, we present Cu-catalyzed cyclopropanol coupling with monoarylated epoxides. The reported approach gives access to δ-hydroxy ketones, which were obtained with moderate to good yields. The reaction presumably proceeds via addition of the epoxide-derived benzyl radical to the cyclopropanol-derived Cu(II)-homoenolate. The employment of the synthesized Cu(I)complex enables one-pot formation of the cyclic acetal.

papers.title: Spiro-helicenoid Carbofluoresceins: A New Family of Biocompatible CPL-Active Emitters
papers.abstract: Chiral fluorescent probes based on small organic molecules present a promising platform for advanced bioimaging applications. Herein, we have developed a helically chiral spiro-shape carbofluorescein with near-infrared emission (λem up to 613 nm). Configurationally stable enantiomers were separated and electronic circular dichroism (ECD) and circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) evaluated. Preliminary results showed cellular permeability and intracellular emission.

papers.title: In Silico Drug Discovery of Novel Fluorinated Phenylpropanoic Acid Derivatives as Tubulin Colchicine Binding Site Inhibitors: A Systematic Lead Optimization Study
papers.abstract: Tubulin, a key structural protein involved in mitotic spindle formation, represents a validated anticancer target. The Colchicine Binding Site (CBS) on the beta-tubulin subunit offers a promising avenue for the development of novel antimitotic agents. In this study, we present a systematic in silico lead optimization workflow starting from a fluorinated phenylpropanoic acid scaffold (Salma-1) and culminating in the identification of Salma-3 as the best-performing analog. Using AutoDock Vina 1.2, QSAR modeling (XGBoost, ChEMBL n=1,180, R2=0.569), pkCSM ADMET profiling, DFT quantum chemical calculations (B3LYP/3-21G), and target fishing analysis via SwissTargetPrediction, we demonstrate that Salma-3 (SMILES: COc1cc(F)c(CC(C(C)C)C(=O)O)cc1F) achieves a binding energy of -6.55 kcal/mol, a predicted IC50 of 6.11 μM, QED of 0.883, and a clean ADMET profile with zero Lipinski violations. Importantly, Salma-3 exhibits superior drug-like properties compared to the reference drug Colchicine, including absence of P-glycoprotein efflux, clean CYP450 metabolism, and favorable molecular weight (258 Da vs. 399 Da). Target fishing analysis revealed potential secondary interactions with FFAR1 (-5.90 kcal/mol) and PPARG, suggesting a multi-target anticancer mechanism. These findings support Salma-3 as a promising lead compound warranting experimental validation.

papers.title: The ”Radical Cannon” Platform: In Silico Blueprinting of BL-CPT-42 as a Bipolar Metallo-D-Peptide Nanodevice Against Leukemia
papers.abstract: Efficient chemodynamic therapy is limited by peptide degradation and slow Fenton kinetics. Here, this project report an in silico-designed, chirally inverted, and fluorinated metallopeptide cascade reactor for amplified tumor eradication: (Ac-cRGDfC-HEHGH-GPGP-HG-DAH-C-C-H*AD*GH*-PGPG-HGH*E*H*-cRGDfC-NH2) (all-D, * = fluorine). Converting all residues to D-configuration enables complete proteolytic evasion while retaining terminal cRGDfC-mediated targeting to αvβ3 integrins. Strategic fluorine modifications optimize local electronic density to accelerate rate-limiting Fe3+/Fe2+ reduction. Triggered by tumor acidity, the compartmentalized Mn2+ and Cu2+ nodes catalyze H2O2 production, which sequentially funnels into the adjacent binuclear Fe2+/Fe2+ pocket to erupt lethal hydroxyl radicals. HDOCK and APBS mapping corroborate its precise cancer-cell targeting capability and multistage redox feasibility, respectively.

papers.title: From DFT to Insight: A Critical Review of Descriptor Discovery Pipelines and Interpretable Machine Learning for Heterogeneous Catalysis
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) has become a central tool in computational heterogeneous catalysis, yet most deployments remain black boxes that predict adsorption or reaction energies without exposing why a catalyst works. This review follows a single conceptual thread: the descriptor-discovery pipeline that runs from density functional theory (DFT) data, through feature construction and model training, to the extraction and physical validation of descriptors. At every stage we ask a pointed question. Are the descriptors that ML uncovers physically meaningful and interpretable, or merely predictive? We organise the literature around the pipeline DFT → features → model → descriptor extraction → physical validation, contrasting black-box, “gray-box” (post-hoc) and “glass-box” (intrinsically interpretable) approaches1,2. We pay particular attention to compressed-sensing and symbolic-regression methods (SISSO, genetic programming) that promise closed-form, human-readable descriptors3–5, to physics-infused neural architectures that hard-wire domain knowledge into otherwise opaque models6,7, and to graph neural networks whose accuracy now rivals DFT for adsorption-energy prediction8,9. Throughout, we audit claims of physical insight against the established scaffolding of scaling relations, the Sabatier principle and d-band theory10,11. We argue that interpretability is not a cosmetic add-on but a prerequisite for transferable catalyst design, and we propose a checklist for rigorous descriptor validation.

papers.title: Catalyst-Aware Regression for Oxidative Coupling of Methane (OCM)
papers.abstract: We present a catalyst-aware regression baseline for oxidative coupling of methane (OCM), trained on a small, experimentally curated dataset of 291 data points. The model extends a simple operational baseline by incorporating one-hot-encoded catalyst composition (M1, M2, M3, Support). Compared with a baseline model using only operational conditions (temperature, CH4/O2 ratio, total flow, PAr), the catalyst-aware model improves R2 from −0.196 to 0.152 and reduces RMSE from 3.83 to 3.22 (≈16%). We report this result for what it is: a reproducible, formulation-aware baseline demonstrating that catalyst identity carries predictive signal beyond operating conditions alone, rather than a production-ready or industrially validated predictive system. Every number in this study was independently re-derived from the original dataset and training scripts rather than taken on faith, and every limitation identified during external review is catalogued with its current status. A minimal FastAPI backend and Streamlit dashboard expose this baseline interactively; their uncertainty estimate is a fixed-variance placeholder rather than a calibrated quantity, and is summarized with that caveat in the Implementation section.

papers.title: Dual-FKAN: Dual-Encoder Fourier-KAN Fusion for Toxicity Prediction on Sparse Molecular Fingerprints
papers.abstract: Predicting chemical toxicity from molecular fingerprints is challenged by extreme sparsity, class imbalance, and SMOTE-induced artefacts in standard benchmark datasets. We propose Dual-FKAN, a dual-encoder architecture with Fourier Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN) fusion for binary toxicity classification, comprehensively evaluated across all 12 Tox21 assays. We systematically evaluate five model variants—including single MLPs, dual-encoder concatenation, transformer interactions, and Spline-KAN versus Fourier-KAN basis functions—under identical 5-fold stratified cross-validation with per-fold preprocessing to eliminate data leakage. Dual-FKAN achieves ROC-AUC of 0.9043 ± 0.0164 and PR-AUC of 0.6445 ± 0.0523, matching or outperforming standard baselines like concat-MLP (0.9035 ± 0.0127 ROC-AUC). Crucially, Dual-FKAN achieves superior calibration (ECE = 0.1686, Brier = 0.1061). Our results demonstrate that Fourier KAN-based fusion layers offer a principled, mathematically robust alternative to standard concatenation for sparse molecular data, with significant benefits in calibration, efficiency, and activity-cliff robustness.

papers.title: Low-Temperature Solid-State Synthesis of Zirconium Dioxide via Thermal Decomposition of ZrOCl2·8H2O–NaHCO3 Mixtures: Kinetics, Morphological Control by In Situ NaCl Matrix, and Comparison with Established Crystalline ZrO2 Phases
papers.abstract: The thermal decomposition of a solid-state mixture of zirconyl chloride octahydrate (ZrOCl2·8H2O) and sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) was investigated by simultaneous thermogravimetry / differential thermogravimetry / differential thermal analysis (TG/DTG/DTA) over the temperature range 90–250 °C. A pronounced synergistic effect was identified: the maximum mass-loss rate (DTG minimum) of the mixture occurs at 120.0 °C—some 35 °C below that of pure NaHCO3 (155.1 °C) and 15 °C below that of pure ZrOCl2·8H2O (135.1 °C)—while the endothermic DTA peak is dramatically attenuated (−14.9 mV vs. −120.1 mV for the pure oxychloride). Activation energies determined by the Friedman isoconversional method are ≈41 kJ mol-1 (mixture), ≈68 kJ mol-1 (NaHCO3), and ≈110 kJ mol-1 (ZrOCl2·8H2O). The low activation energy is attributed to in situ HCl neutralisation by NaHCO3, which prevents back-reaction and drives the equilibrium towards ZrO2. Crucially, NaCl—co-formed in equimolar quantity with ZrO2—acts as a solid-state spacer matrix that suppresses particle sintering and promotes anisotropic, platelet-like ZrO2 morphology, in sharp contrast to the spherical/polygonal particles obtained by high-temperature routes (>800 °C) described in literature [1–3]. The product is characterised against CAS 1314-23-4 and ASTM C1065 reference data. These results provide a low-energy, aqueous-waste-free pathway to nanostructured ZrO2 with controllable morphology relevant to ceramics, catalysis, and nuclear-grade oxide applications.

papers.title: Modulating the reactivity of anionic phosphido‑boranes via π‑conjugated spacers for reversible CO2 capture
papers.abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) capture using phosphine–borane-based systems has emerged as a promising strategy for sustainable carbon utilization and activation. In this study, density functional theory calculations were employed to investigate alkali-metal-assisted azo- and acetylene-bridged phosphine–borane systems for CO 2 capture and activation. The metal-free systems exhibited weak or thermodynamically unfavorable CO 2 complexation, whereas incorporation of alkali metals significantly enhanced CO 2 stabilization, with Li + consistently outperforming the corresponding Na + and K + analogues. Electronic structure and NBO analyses revealed that the acetylene-linked systems possess greater phosphorus nucleophilicity and more efficient electronic communication than their azo-linked counterparts. Reaction-profile analyses showed that CO 2 activation proceeds through favorable geometric distortion and strong donor–acceptor interactions involving the phosphorus center, activated CO 2 fragment, and alkali-metal cation. Substituent effects revealed that modification at the boron centre effectively tunes CO 2 binding, whereas substitution at phosphorus generally weakens or suppresses CO 2 capture by reducing phosphorus nucleophilicity. Among the systems investigated, acetylene-linked and Li+-assisted derivatives exhibited slightly more favorable CO 2 binding characteristics. Furthermore, the calculated reaction profiles indicate that CO 2 release is associated with moderate energy barriers, suggesting the potential for reversible CO 2 capture and efficient regeneration. These findings highlight the critical roles of linker design, alkali-metal coordination, and substituent engineering in developing efficient phosphine–borane systems for CO 2 activation.

papers.title: Effect of Zirconia Formation Temperature on the State of Surface Hydroxyl Groups and the Nature of Carbonate Species as Revealed by FTIR Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: FTIR spectroscopy was employed to investigate the evolution of surface hydroxyl groups, carbonate species, and the crystalline structure of zirconium dioxide (ZrO2) synthesized by a topotactic method at calcination temperatures of 150, 200, 400, and 600 °C. At low temperatures, the broad absorption in the 3650–3300 cm-1 region is attributed to adsorbed water together with bridging ≡Zr2–OH (Type IIa) and tribridging ≡Zr3–OH (Type III) hydroxyls as classified by the Knözinger–Ratnasamy scheme, whereas at 400–600 °C isolated terminal ≡Zr–OH groups of Type Ia (3775–3760 cm-1, pKa ≈ 2–4) predominate. Drawing on recent DFT calculations by Scafuri et al. (2025), the carbonate bands observed at 1520, 1460, 1400, and 1360 cm-1 are assigned predominantly to polydentate surface carbonate species—bridging (BC) and polydentate (PC) types—formed through adsorption of atmospheric CO2 during drying rather than through a solid-state reaction. Monodentate carbonates are thermodynamically unstable on the m-ZrO2 surface and instantaneously rearrange into polydentate forms. The CO2 adsorption energy and the magnitude of Δν3 splitting are governed by the coordination number of surface Zr4+ ions. This conclusion is supported by the increase in carbonate band intensities from 150 to 200 °C in parallel with the growth of specific surface area, and by their disappearance at 400 °C, a temperature well below the decomposition temperature of bulk carbonate phases (480–530 °C). Analysis of the 800–400 cm-1 region confirms the structural evolution from the amorphous state (FWHM > 200 cm-1) through crystallization of t-ZrO2 (bands at ~740 and ~585 cm-1) to a mixture of t- and m-ZrO2 at 600 °C (~500 and ~455 cm-1).

papers.title: Topochemical Synthesis of ZrO2 from ZrOCl2·8H2O and NaHCO3: Thermal Analysis, Kinetic Modeling, and DTA/DTG Study
papers.abstract: The thermal behavior of the ZrOCl2·8H2O + NaHCO3 system in the temperature range 90–250 °C was investigated by simultaneous thermogravimetric (TG/DTG) and differential thermal analysis (DTA) at a heating rate of 10 °C/min in air. Eight competitive and sequential solid-state reactions were identified and characterized. DTA and DTG curves for reactions (1), (3), and (6) were plotted as functions of temperature; minimum values and zero-crossing points were determined. Eleven formal kinetic models (F1, F2, F3, D1, D2, D3, D4, A2, A3, R2, R3) were fitted to experimental conversion data using the Coats–Redfern method. The best fit was obtained for the F2 model (second-order reaction) with an apparent activation energy of Ea = 64.3 kJ/mol for reaction (1). The cascade mechanism is discussed in the context of topochemical ZrO2 synthesis.

papers.title: GROMACS-Agent: Text-to-Workflow Generation for Molecular Dynamics A multi-agent framework for topology-aware GROMACS workflow generation, evaluation, correction, and selected safe execution
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation links atomic structure to thermodynamic, transport, and interfacial properties, but translating a scientific question into an appropriate GROMACS workflow remains a practical barrier. A complete GROMACS workflow spans structure, topology, MDP, TPR, trajectory, energy, index, and output files, and many errors are scientific rather than syntactic, surviving execution while quietly invalidating the result. Prior MD agents have focused on single-script generation, mainly for LAMMPS, which does not capture this multi-file, multi-stage structure. We present GROMACS-Agent, a multi-agent prototype that treats GROMACS automation as text-to-workflow generation rather than text-to-code generation. The system combines a Manager Agent, Planner Agent, Retriever, Gromacs Worker Agent, Gromacs Evaluator Agent, and Code Executor Agent, supported by two curated datasets: GSCF for workflow generation and GEQS for workflow evaluation. For each task, the agent returns required files, a command sequence, expected outputs, validation notes, an evaluator score, and correction suggestions, with selected safe-execution checks for allow-listed commands. In a five-task pilot comparison, GROMACS-Agent improved evaluator-assessed correctness from 6.6/10 for baseline LLM responses to 10/10, and a single-user timing pilot showed a substantial reduction in local workflow-preparation time. These early results position GROMACS-Agent as a practical, human-in-the-loop step toward reliable GROMACS workflow automation, with expert review and physical validation still required before execution.

papers.title: Closed-Loop LLM-Guided Molecular Dynamics Screening of Thermal Transport in Co-Cr-Ni Medium-Entropy Alloys: A Proof-of-Concept Automated Materials Discovery Workflow
papers.abstract: Thermal-transport property screening across the vast compositional space of medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) presents a persistent bottleneck: each candidate requires a manual cycle of composition selection, supercell construction, molecular dynamics (MD) equilibration, production, and data extraction before the next trial composition can be defined. This work reports a reproducible, closed-loop workflow that integrates a large language model (LLM) decision module with LAMMPS reverse non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (reverse-NEMD) to automate this cycle for the Co-Cr-Ni ternary system. Six independent 50-iteration search paths were launched from distinct starting regions of the ternary diagram, covering approximately equiatomic, Co-rich, Cr-rich, Ni-rich, and biased high-Co and high-Ni starting points. Each iteration generated a random face-centred cubic (FCC) supercell, ran a 300 K equilibration followed by a Muller-Plathe kinetic-energy exchange production run, and automatically extracted the heat-flux and temperature-gradient data needed to compute an MD-scale lattice thermal-conductivity indicator. The LLM module then proposed the next composition through atom-conserving element substitutions guided by a scalar thermal score defined as the conductivity indicator minus a half-unit uncertainty penalty. Across 300 total evaluations the search landscape showed structured variability rather than monotonic convergence, with isolated high-score spikes and several moderate-score plateaus. A reliability filter combining uncertainty thresholding and split-branch temperature-gradient fitting was introduced to distinguish physically meaningful candidates from numerical artefacts. The most defensible candidate from the equiatomic-path search, Co15/Co31.9Cr34.7Ni33.3, returned branch-fit R2 values of 0.845 and 0.899 under the two-branch Muller-Plathe geometry, confirming a well-defined imposed thermal field. The study demonstrates that coupling an LLM decision layer to a standard MD simulator converts an otherwise manual iterative search into a logged, auditable screening platform and opens a practical path toward accelerated composition-property mapping in compositionally complex alloys.

papers.title: pH- and Salt-triggered Release of dsRNA from Adipic Acid-Crosslinked Chitosan Microgels
papers.abstract: The increasing use of synthetic polymers in agrochemical formulations is raising concerns about their environmental impact. Chitosan, a naturally derived biopolymer, is a sustainable alternative due to its biocompatibility and biodegradability. The protonable amine groups generating positive charges along chitosan backbone enable high loadings and efficient release of RNA. However, the design of chitosan microgels with tailored release profiles remains challenging. This study presents adipic acid-crosslinked chitosan microgels (100 - 500 µm) for the release of insecticidal dsRNA via chitosanase-triggered degradation. Mechanical properties, swelling degree and enzymatic degradability of the microgels were tunable via crosslinker content. The diffusive release of dsRNA was triggered by high pH and ionic strength. Finally, microbial degradation of chitosan-based microgels in soil was shown by incubation experiments. The experimental results suggest potential use of the developed chitosan microgels as gut-specific delivery systems in insects.

papers.title: Surrogate Machine Learning Models for ADME Prediction: From Synthetic Labels to Experimental Data
