Additionally, we utilized the MDPE auxiliary for the synthesis of heavily glycosylated segments derived from mucin MUC5AC.

papers.title: Generative AI and Structure-Based Workflow for the De Novo Design and Optimization of DprE1 Inhibitor Candidates
Future directions for therapeutic peptide synthesis and manufacture
papers.abstract: In the wake of a significant increase in global demand for synthetic peptides, with increasingly complex structures, renewed attention into the efficiency and scalability of peptide manufacture is required. Key areas for improvement include reducing raw material use, environmental impact, and increasing global production capacity. The currently dominant platform for peptide drug manufacture, solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), offers robustness, streamlined development and a mature raw material supply chain, but manufacturing capacity is limited, and toxic substances are used extensively. Research in academia and industry to reduce the environmental impact of SPPS has made incremental progress but lack transformative solutions. In this perspective, we provide an overview of the current peptide manufacturing landscape and reflect on the most promising technological advancements of SPPS and alternative methods. Furthermore, we highlight bold efforts to re-think peptide synthesis to ultimately benefit both patients and the planet.

papers.title: NIFREC: A Gaussian-Integrated Automated Workflow for Ground-State Geometry Optimization with No Imaginary Vibrational Frequencies
papers.abstract: We present NIFREC, an automated workflow for molecular ground-state geometry optimization without imaginary vibrational frequencies. NIFREC combines a conformer search module based on RDKit and xTB with a Gaussian module for sequential "Opt Freq" calculations, and imaginary-frequency remediation. In Gaussian module calculations, imaginary frequencies are resolved using a two-step process consisting of an RCFC-based procedure and iterative displacement of atomic coordinates along imaginary-mode vectors, followed by "Opt Freq" calculations. NIFREC was evaluated using 948 molecules at PM6, PM7, HF/STO-3G, and B3LYP/6-31G(d) levels of theory. For these molecules, the conformer search module provided at least one xTB-optimized conformer without significant imaginary frequencies, and the Gaussian module automatically resolved all cases detected as having imaginary frequencies. These results demonstrated that NIFREC was robust in ground-state geometry optimization using Gaussian. This tool can be incorporated into an automated workflow of quantum-chemistry-derived molecular descriptors for chemoinformatics applications. NIFREC is available from the GitHub repository (https://github.com/tanaka-hideya/NIFREC); the latest release is v1.2.1 and is archived on the Zenodo repository (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20303948).

papers.title: spTool: An interactive software to generate and navigate in-silico single particle data from ICP-QMS and ICP-TOFMS instruments
papers.abstract: Single particle inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (SP ICP‑MS) provides unique capabilities for the elemental analysis of nano- and microparticles as well as single cells (SC ICP-MS). Both in quadrupole mass spectrometry (QMS) as well as time-of-flight (TOF) MS, data analysis plays a central role in deriving meaningful results, where the reliability and accuracy of outcomes depend on well-characterised analysis algorithms. As a consequence, the demand for benchmarking and comparison of data evaluation workflows is steadily increasing. Currently, both aspects are often limited by the scarcity of suitable reference materials and the stochastic nature of SP ICP-MS event detection. To address these challenges, we introduce spTool, an interactive software with a graphical user interface (GUI) for generating and navigating in‑silico SP ICP‑MS data for both ICP-QMS and ICP-TOFMS datasets. spTool features a user‑friendly graphical interface that promotes the structured input of parameters, rapid “what‑if” exploration and in-silico experiments to test data analysis strategies. A core strength of the platform is its capability to produce multi‑element and multi‑isotope time series, enabling realistic emulation of elemental particle compositions across particle populations of arbitrary complexity. Importantly, it provides realistic particle peak shapes based on a simple yet fit-for-purpose diffusion model. By combining this model with randomised event scheduling and Poisson/compound‑Poisson sampling, the newly developed algorithms reproduce critical features observed in experimental SP ICP‑MS, including, counting noise, detector dead‑time effects and composition‑dependent detectability. The result is a novel way to generate in-silico SP ICP-QMS and SP ICP-TOFMS data, which is embedded in a flexible GUI platform to: (1) benchmark algorithms against datasets with known inputs, (2) evaluate thresholding strategies and false‑negative/coincidence behaviour, and (3) plan experiments by assessing dilution and background levels.

papers.title: Ambient High-Density Hydrogen Storage in Solid Organic Hydrogen Carriers via an Aqueous Redox-Mediated Flow Cell
papers.abstract: Widespread deployment of hydrogen energy is limited by the safety risks and energy penalties of compressed and liquefied storage, whereas alternative hydrogen carriers often require harsh operating conditions or exhibit sluggish kinetics. Here we report a redox-mediated flow cell architecture based on solid organic hydrogen carriers (SOHCs) that enables reversible hydrogen storage and release at ambient temperature and pressure. The system is driven by the rapid, reversible interconversion between hydrogen and proton-electron pairs via the hydrogen oxidation and evolution reactions, while soluble redox mediators shuttle protons and electrons between the electrode and a separate tank containing the solid carrier. This dual-mediator proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) strategy enables rapid charging and discharging under ambient conditions while decoupling electrochemical hydrogen conversion from hydrogen storage. Using this approach, we achieve a volumetric hydrogen storage density equivalent to approximately 120 bar compressed gas without pressurized vessels. These results open a route that combines the high power density of flow cells with the high energy density of solid-phase materials and provides a scalable, safe, and efficient pathway for stationary hydrogen storage. The modularity in this approach provides a general platform in which the solid carrier, redox mediators, and flow-cell operation can be optimized independently, creating pathways to higher storage density, lower voltage hysteresis, improved kinetics, and broader materials compatibility beyond the specific substances demonstrated here, e.g., including inorganic materials exhibiting a PCET mechanism.

papers.title: Conformational Adaptability Enables Efficient Long-Wavelength Through-Space Charge Transfer Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence without Conformational Locking
papers.abstract: Through-space charge-transfer thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TSCT-TADF) emitters typically rely on rigid donor–acceptor architectures to suppress nonradiative decay and maintain efficient excited-state coupling, particularly for long-wavelength emission. Here, we demonstrate that conformational adaptability provides an alternative strategy for efficient orange-to-red TSCT-TADF. An S-shaped donor–π–acceptor–π–donor framework composed of phenoxazine donors, xanthene linkers, and a dibenzo[a,j]phenazine acceptor enables efficient through-space charge transfer without requiring permanent conformational locking. Structural, photophysical, and theoretical investigations reveal that the xanthene linker functions primarily as a conformational regulator, controlling donor–acceptor proximity and orientation while minimizing through-bond charge-transfer contributions. The developed emitters exhibit efficient orange-to-red TADF with rapid reverse intersystem crossing on the order of 105 s−1 with high radiative decay rate (kf > 107 s–1), thereby alleviating the trade-off commonly encountered in long-wavelength TADF systems. Timeresolved spectroscopy and theoretical analyses indicate the presence of multiple emissive conformations and excited-state structural relaxation, supporting a conformationally adaptive TSCT mechanism. Organic light-emitting diodes employing these emitters achieve orange-to-red electroluminescence with external quantum efficiencies up to 13% and suppressed efficiency roll-off at high luminance. These findings demonstrate that access to electronically favorable donor–acceptor conformations, rather than permanent structural locking, provides an effective design strategy for high-performance long-wavelength TSCT-TADF materials.

papers.title: Stochastic kMC modeling enables understanding of the neighboring-group effect in post-polymerization modification of polyamines
papers.abstract: Describing the progress of reactions occurring along the polymer chain remains challenging due to the large number of dynamically evolving reaction sites present during post-polymerization modification (PPM) processes. Herein, we propose a kinetic Monte Carlo (kMC) model describing PPM reactions constrained by steric interactions between neighboring modified repeating units (r.u.), which dynamically modulate the reactivity of adjacent reaction sites. We demonstrate that the large number of potential reaction sites can be reduced to a limited set of kinetically distinguishable reaction centers, whose distribution and frequency of occurrence can be predicted using a stochastic Monte Carlo approach. The proposed model was validated using a series of aza-Michael reactions between acrylic esters and polyamines. Methyl, n-hexyl, and tert-butyl acrylates were reacted with polyethyleneimine (L-PEI) and polytrimethylenimine (L-PTMI) to investigate the influence of substituent size, spacing between reactive centers, and reaction temperature on the PPM process. Apart from describing reaction kinetics, the model also enables prediction of sequence distribution in partially modified polymer. We show that non-exhaustive PPM reactions do not lead to entirely random polymer structures, but instead generate predictable distributions of unreacted reaction centers and repeating units along the polymer chain.

papers.title: A Simplified Transient Spectroelectrochemistry Technique Reveals Super-Reductant Excited State Dynamics
papers.abstract: Super-reductant photocatalysis activates challenging bond transformations, yet mechanistic studies are hindered by inadequate in situ instrumentation. Previous mechanistic investigations relied on ex situ electrochemical reduction or sacrificial electron donors to generate super-reductant catalysts, assuming electrochemical and chemical generation routes are equivalent. Tandem bulk electrolysis-transient absorption (T-BETA) spectroscopy is a simplified approach to transient spectroelectrochemistry presented herein to observe in situ excited state dynamics of an electrochemically reduced PDI 2- super-reductant. The T-BETA spectra and the transient absorption spectra of PDI 2- generated via reduction by CoCp 2 reveal singlet 1 PDI 2- * and triplet 3 PDI 2- * excited states with 6 ns and 130 ns lifetimes, respectively, and formation of a solvated electron and PDI •− in both systems. Importantly, ground-state recovery of PDI 2- is markedly slower under electrochemical conditions, revealing that mass-transport limitations, not intrinsic photocatalyst dynamics, constitute the primary bottleneck in electrophotocatalytic turnover.

papers.title: Rerouting Non-Heme Iron Oxo Chemistry: Mechanistic Basis of Iron-Hydride Reactivity in Enzymatic Mukaiyama Hydration
papers.abstract: Metal–hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) reactivity is well established in homogeneous catalysis, but analogous reactivity in enzyme active sites remains rare and mechanistically underexplored. A recently discovered non-heme Fe/2-oxoglutarate (Fe/2OG) enzyme catalyzes the Mukaiyama hydration of styrene in the presence of NaBH4 and O2, affording a 3:1 mixture of the Markovnikov alcohol and ketone products. Here, we use combined QM/MM and molecule dynamics simulations to uncover how this Fe/2OG scaffold is diverted from its canonical ferryl chemistry into a non-native iron–hydride (Fe–H) manifold. Facile hydride transfer from BH4- to the Fe center initiates a non-canonical Fe–H pathway that outcompetes ferryl formation. The resulting Fe–H species enables Markovnikov-selective MHAT to styrene, followed by O2 trapping to form an Fe–alkylperoxo radical. Branching at this radical intermediate determines the product selectivity: HAT from active-site residue Y131 to the intermediate produces the alcohol, whereas HAT from the intermediate to the iron-oxo center gives the ketone. The calculated barriers for these competing steps are consistent with the experimentally observed product ratio. Subsequent quenching of the Y131 radical by an active-site water molecule generates an Fe–OOH intermediate, and tunnel analysis reveals a persistent, residue-lined proton relay channel that delivers protons to Fe–OOH, favoring oxidase uncoupling over ferryl formation and completing the catalytic cycle. Together, these results provide a mechanistic picture for enzymatic MHAT reactivity and explain how a repurposed Fe/2OG active site supports low-valent Fe–H chemistry in place of its canonical high-valent oxidative manifold.

papers.title: NHC-Supported Metaphosphoric Acids: A Modular Class of Anionic Oxygen-Donor Ligands
papers.abstract: Anionic oxygen-donor ligands play a central role in coordination chemistry, yet the development of new, modular ligand families remains limited. Herein, we report a series of N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC)-supported metaphosphoric acids (NHC→PO 3 H) spanning three distinct carbene structures. These compounds are prepared on gram scale in two steps via NHC phosphorylation followed by ester cleavage, affording air- and water-stable metaphosphate esters and their corresponding oxoacid derivatives. Singlecrystal X-ray diffraction and density functional theory reveal closely related structures across the series, featuring conserved C–P bonding alongside flexible PO 3 geometries. Protonation affords well-defined (NHC→PO 3 H 2 )+ species, one of which was characterized by contraction of the C–P bond and increased pyramidalization at phosphorus, consistent with enhanced carbene–phosphorus interaction. In aqueous solution, these metaphosphoric acids behave as monoprotic oxoacids with tunable Brønsted acidity spanning more than three pK a units (pK a = 4.07–7.14). The chemical behavior of these ligands is further demonstrated by carbene-dependent reactivity in phosphoanhydride formation and by coordination to Cu(I), yielding discrete dicopper and tetracopper complexes supported by μ 2 -η 1 :η 1 and μ 3 -η 1 :η 1 :η 1 binding modes, respectively. Together, these results establish NHC-supported metaphosphates as a versatile and tunable class of anionic oxygen-donor ligands with adaptable structural, electronic, and coordination properties.

papers.title: Unraveling the ultrafast photodynamics of molecular photoswitches in β-adrenergic receptors by first-principles non-adiabatic dynamics simulations
papers.abstract: Understanding how protein environments regulate the photodynamics of chromophores is a central task in quantum biology and remains a major challenge. This challenge is particularly significant for G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), which are natively non-photochromic but can be optically controlled via synthetic photoswitchable ligands. Such artificial photoreceptors are new and important because they not only enable the photo-control of signaling processes beyond those regulated by rhodopsins but also deepen our fundamental understanding of quantum effects in light-protein interactions. However, the ultrafast nonadiabatic dynamics of these ligands in GPCRs remain difficult to resolve experimentally, while traditional computational approaches fail to describe these processes accurately and efficiently. Here, we employed a multiscale framework to comprehensively investigate how receptor binding, mutations, receptor subtype, chemical substitution, and binding pocket electrostatics regulate the photodynamics of photoswitchable agonists (OPs) of β-adrenergic receptors (β-ARs). This framework integrates extensive first-principles ground-state conformational sampling, absorption-spectrum calculations, and non-adiabatic dynamics simulations. Chemical substitution controls how excitation energy, excited-state lifetimes, and quantum yields (QY) respond to receptor binding, subtype changes, and binding-pocket mutations. The F289A and Y199A mutants generally accelerate excited-state dynamics, whereas the D113E mutation slows the dynamics of OP2 in β 2 -ΑR by reducing the excited-state driving force. Neutralizing the charge of the counterion D113 residue via protonation increases the QY of OP2 in β 2 -ΑR by altering the local electrostatic and hydrogen-bonding environment. The ultrafast photoisomerization of the ligands does not require large-scale binding-pocket expansion. Overall, this work provides new insights into how binding-pocket environments regulate the photochemical properties of photoswitchable ligands targeting GPCRs.

papers.title: Ultrasonic Cryoporometry: Determining Pore-Size Distributions from Acoustic Measurements
papers.abstract: The standard experimental approaches for determining pore size distribution (PSD) are gas adsorption (e.g., nitrogen porosimetry) and mercury intrusion porosimetry. While widely used, these methods have limitations: gas adsorption experiments often require high-temperature heating and are less sensitive in macropores, whereas mercury intrusion is destructive and involves hazardous materials. Therefore, there is always a demand for alternative methods for characterization of porous materials. Thermodynamics of fluids confined in nanopores depend on the pore size. In particular, both the capillary condensation pressure and the freezing/melting point are shifted relative to their bulk values due to confinement. Capillary condensation is the basis of gas adsorption porosimetry, while the melting/freezing temperature shift can also be used for PSD determination through the Gibbs-Thomson equation, which links the transition temperature to the pore radius. This is the main idea of thermoporometric methods such as differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) based thermoporometry, and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) cryoporometry. Both techniques, however, typically require complex and costly instrumentation. Ultrasonic measurements provide an alternative route to probe phase transitions in porous materials. In ultrasonic pulse-transmission technique, speed of an ultrasonic wave depends on the density and elastic moduli of the composite system. When a fluid confined within nanopores freezes, the shear modulus of the composite increases, and the difference between the liquid-like and solid-like states reflects the contribution of the confined phase to the overall modulus. In this work, we analyze literature ultrasonic data for fluids (heptane, nonane, argon) confined in nanoporous media using a phenomenological model by Denoyel and Pellenq for phase transitions under confinement. We demonstrate that the temperature-dependent ultrasonic response provides information on the fraction of solidified fluid and, consequently, used to extract the pore size distribution. Our results suggest that ultrasonic data on porous materials can be used for determining PSD, providing an alternative to the methods based on NMR or DSC.

papers.title: Hyphenated Mass Spectrometry-based Strategies for Characterizing Oligomers of α-Synuclein in Parkinson’s Disease
papers.abstract: The pathological aggregation of α-synuclein (α-syn), an intrinsically disordered protein that regulates synaptic vesicle trafficking in the brain, is a defining molecular feature in Parkinson’s disease (PD). Early oligomeric assemblies are widely considered the most neurotoxic species, yet their structural features remain unexplored due to their low abundance, transient, and fragile nature. Here, we establish a trapped ion mobility-mass spectrometry (TIMS-MS) strategy that enables direct detection and structural interrogation of these oligomers. Low-flow size exclusion chromatography provides MS-compatible desalting and reveals broad ensemble-level differences between fresh and aggregated α-syn. Native TIMS-MS measurements uniquely probe numerous higher-order oligomers, thereby revealing a reduced conformational heterogeneity with increasing oligomer size, supporting a linear β-strand-type assembly pathway. These findings show that oligomerization drives a transition from dynamic monomers to increasingly ordered intermediates. This progressive rigidification is relevant to models in which α-syn oligomerization alters normal membrane engagement during PD-associated aggregation.

papers.title: Thermally Controlled Polymorphism and Doping Gradients in Poly(dodecyl-quaterthiophene) (PQT) for Functionally Graded Organic Thermoelectrics
papers.abstract: Conjugated polymers are essential for flexible organic thermoelectrics (OTEs). Herein, we demonstrate that polymorphism in poly(dodecyl-quaterthiophene) (PQT) significantly dictates doping efficiency and charge transport upon tetracyanoquinodimethane (F4TCNQ) vapor doping. Using X-ray scattering, ellipsometry, and molecular dynamics simulations, we characterize how thermal annealing induces distinct side-chain and backbone orientations. 130 °C annealed samples reach a conductivity (σ) of 8.6 ± 0.1 S/cm, while 100 °C samples only exhibit a conductivity of 0.3 ± 0.2 S/cm due to inhibited doping from the polymorph with stronger interdigitation of the side chains. Leveraging these findings, we fabricated functionally graded (FG) PQT films using a custom thermal annealing station to induce spatial microstructural gradients. Modeling the cooling performance via linear constitutive relations and experimental transport profiles reveals that FG films outperform equivalent uniform (EU) counterparts in cooling performance (∆Tc = TH – Tc). Overall, this work establishes a robust strategy to enhance OTEs performance by leveraging thermally induced microstructural gradients in semiconducting polymers.

papers.title: Porous Peptide Frameworks with Tertiary Structures
papers.abstract: Complex functions such as selective molecular recognition and catalysis arise from the precise three-dimensional arrangement of functional groups that are best exemplified in the protein tertiary structure. Reproducing this level of structural precision and chemical modularity in abiotic materials remains a fundamental challenge. Here, we show that peptide self-assembly into porous crystalline frameworks can result in tuneable tertiary structures composed of helix, loop, and βstrand motifs within a single chain that is only 15–19 amino acids in length, which is less than 6% the size of the average protein. These peptide frameworks were designed by hybridising a framework-forming 11-residue α-helix with variable sequence fragments, yielding extended lattices with channels lined by 8–10 distinct side chains, as confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SC-XRD). As a proof-of-principle, these pores can be programmed to encode various constellations of functional groups capable of selective molecular recognition, including nearquantitative discrimination of ATP over ADP and chain-length-dependent recognition of perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids. These results demonstrate that a well-defined tertiary structure can exist in very short peptides and can impart programmable, protein-like function to synthetic porous materials.

papers.title: Unraveling the ion transport mechanisms of isoquinolinium and pyridinium-based liquid crystal electrolytes
papers.abstract: Ionic liquid crystals are emerging as a promising class of quasi-solid-state electrolytes for the next generation of batteries, where the combination of the self-assembly behavior of liquid crystals and the high ionic mobility of ionic liquids is of significant research interest. In this work, several isoquinolinium and pyridinium salts are described as ionic conductors throughout the entire stability range of the smectic A mesophases. The cationic and anionic units organize into segregated layers that serve as two-dimensional conduction pathways, where the mesophase enhances the transport of the chloride counterions. It is shown that the ionic conduction mechanism is reversible in salts with greater thermal stability, i.e. ionic conduction is detected both in the mesophase formed from the solid upon heating and in that formed from the liquid phase upon cooling. Ionic conductivity is higher in the latter case, where the mesophase forms highly continuous and well-ordered conduction pathways that enhance the ion conductivity, exhibiting activation energies as low as 0.84 eV. The commonly employed strategy of increasing the number of chloride anions to enhance the ionic conductivity was evaluated but proved ineffective, instead leading to an increase in the activation energy. In contrast, modulation of the pyridinium substituent revealed a pronounced structure–property relationship: positioning the nitrogen atom at the 3-position significantly enhances mesophase fluidity and, consequently, improves the ionic conductivity of these species.

papers.title: Rechargeable Batteries with Water as the Electrolyte
papers.abstract: Aqueous batteries typically rely on water-based electrolytes containing dissolved ionic compounds to supply mobile charge carriers, establishing a design paradigm in which water functions primarily as an electrochemically inert solvent. Within this framework, the intrinsic self-ionization and ion-conducting capabilities of water remain largely overlooked in battery operation. Here, we demonstrate that water can serve as the sole electrolyte, offering a wide stability window, for a water-dissociation battery by pairing a hydroxide-hosting cathode with a proton-hosting anode. The resulting water-battery full cell exhibits the potential as a storage battery with an active mass loading of 31 mg·cm–2. In addition, water can serve as an electrolyte for a rocking-chair proton battery, even in its frozen state—ice—as a solid electrolyte. These results reveal the underappreciated ion-transport capability of water and open an avenue toward safe, sustainable, and low-cost aqueous batteries.

papers.title: Bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide anion decomposition initiated by the Solid Electrolyte Interphase
papers.abstract: Lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) is widely regarded as the leading salt for stabilizing lithium metal anodes, owing to the formation of an inorganic-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) and enabling Coulombic efficiencies (CE) >99.5%. Here, we identify sulfur–fluoride exchange (SuFEx) click chemistry as a previously unrecognized pathway governing the stability of FSI under cycling and aging conditions. We show that O-nucleophiles abundant at the lithium surface, including Li2O and lithium alkoxides, react with FSI to produce bis(sulfonato)imide derivatives, establishing a self-driven SEI degradation pathway. Through a detailed kinetic and crystallographic study, we isolate critical SuFEx intermediates and identify their chemical fingerprints in SEI layers. We demonstrate that methoxide-substituted FSI anions are particularly detrimental: being soluble and reduced at potentials less cathodic than FSI, they alter the SEI formation mechanism and decrease CE. These findings reframe electrolyte design strategies and suggest that suppressing SuFEx reactivity is essential for achieving sustained CE >99.9%.

papers.title: Engineering potent SNAr biocatalysts from de novo proteins featuring an activated arginine
papers.abstract: Arginine side chains play important roles in the catalytic sites of many natural and engineered enzymes. This versatility is further exemplified by the recent development of artificial enzymes for S N Ar processes, which rely on a key catalytic arginine embedded within a haloacid dehalogenase scaffold. Although powerful, the catalytic proficiency of these first generation S N Arases remains limited, meaning their activity is restricted to highly activated electrophile and nucleophile coupling partners. Here we address these limitations by developing miniature de novo S N Arases that offer far greater catalytic potency and synthetic scope. To this end, a computationally designed NTF2-like protein featuring an activated arginine embedded within its hydrophobic core was optimized over successive rounds of directed evolution. The enhanced catalytic proficiency offered by these optimized designs allows them to operate efficiently on poorly activated substrates and has enabled the development of unprecedented regio- and enantioselective S N Ar transformations. Structural and biochemical analysis of the most active enzyme reveals a remarkably sophisticated active site, whereby a key catalytic Arg17 embedded in an extended polar network works in synergy with an aromatic-rich substrate binding pocket to accurately position and activate the S N Ar coupling partners. This study provides new insights to guide the design of arginine-containing catalytic sites that will enable the future development of de novo enzymes for diverse chemical transformations.

papers.title: Directed attachment of catalysts into the extended environments of soft photoelectrodes for hydrogen evolution
papers.abstract: We present a detailed mechanistic investigation of early stage photoelectrochemical deposition of platinum nanoparticles (Pt-NPs) on (PEC) platforms for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) using electrochemical, spectroscopic, and microscopy characterization, combined with density functional theory (DFT) modeling. The photoactive junction—formed from a blend of conjugated donor (PTB7-Th) and acceptor (P(NDI2OD-T2)) polymers—exhibits HER efficiencies that increase exponentially with Pt-NP loading (ca. 8.0 x 101 to 2.5 x 104 ng/cm2) of highly faceted Pt-NPs. The blended heterojunction demonstrates vertical phase segregation, with acceptor-rich domains driving photoelectrochemical Pt-NP deposition heterogeneously via progressive nucleation, at sites which we posit are the termini of “fast transport pathways.” X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and DFT modeling suggest that Pt-S interactions involving the bi-thiophene groups in (n-doped) P(NDI2OD-T2) dominate at the earliest stages of Pt deposition, while larger 14- and 38-atom Pt clusters also demonstrate Pt–C and Pt–O=C interactions on naphthalene diimide cores. Collectively, our findings reveal that sub-micron environments in soft photoelectrode materials function as integrated architectures where charge transport and catalytic sites operate in concert. The hierarchical assembly of these nanoenvironments will provide a transformative framework for scalable energy conversion that extends beyond hydrogen evolution to more complex energy carriers, such as multielectron and proton redox reactions.

papers.title: Distributed Polarization Enables Volumetric Electrochemical Promotion of Brønsted Acid Catalysis
papers.abstract: Temperature and pressure are conventional handles for promoting thermochemical reaction rates and are readily applied to catalytic active sites over the entire volume of a reactor. Electrical polarization has recently been recognized as a powerful complementary strategy for promoting thermochemical Brønsted acid catalysis, but is generally confined to the surface area of an electrode. Herein, we utilize collision-mediated electron transfer and design a reactor to polarize dispersed Brønsted acid catalysts across a reactor volume. This design increases polarizable active-site density 10,000-fold relative to 2D electrodes while preserving rate-potential scaling. While this enhanced volumetric scaling enables Brønsted acid catalyzed acylation reactions at room temperature, at 55°C, we drive acylation and olefin isomerization reactions to >50% conversion at >100 mM concentrations, improving upon open-circuit rates by up to 25-fold with pseudo-Faradaic efficiencies >1000%. Distributed polarization therefore provides a volumetrically-scalable complement to temperature and pressure to promote thermochemical Brønsted acid catalysis.

papers.title: Evaluating the Link Between Lipid Management and Cognitive Impairment: A Short Review on Cholesterol Lowering Medications and Brain Function
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are recognized as the leading cause of mortality worldwide, so lipid management is established as a cornerstone of preventive medicine. Because the brain is known as the most cholesterol-rich organ, a "Heart-Brain Paradox" is created when blood cholesterol is aggressively lowered. In 2012, a safety label change was mandated by the FDA due to reports of memory loss and confusion among statin users. In this review, the connection between medications like statins, PCSK9 inhibitors, and ezetimibe and cognitive function is evaluated. It is understood that lipophilic statins can pass through the blood-brain barrier, while hydrophilic statins are generally excluded. Additionally, the potential impacts of pharmaceutical excipients and environmental pollutants on the gut-brain axis are explored. It is concluded that the benefits of vascular protection are generally found to be much greater than the risks of cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Rational Design of Heteronuclear Dual-Atom Catalysts for Enhanced CO₂ to Formate Conversion
papers.abstract: The development of efficient catalysts for CO₂ hydrogenation is essential for sustainable hydrogen storage and carbon utilization. Herein, heteronuclear dual-atom catalysts (HDACs) were rationally designed on adenine-derived nitrogen-doped carbon (NC) supports with a high surface area of 3338 m² g⁻¹ and nitrogen content of 8.32 wt.%. Ruthenium was combined with transition metals (Fe, Co, and Ni) to investigate synergistic effects on catalytic performance. HRTEM-STEM and XPS analyses confirmed atomically dispersed metal species predominantly in the +3 oxidation state. Catalytic evaluation demonstrated that transition metal incorporation significantly enhanced CO₂ hydrogenation to formate. Among the catalysts, RuFe/NC (1:2) exhibited the highest activity, achieving a specific activity of 268 mmolFA gcat-1 within 2 h, compared with 107 mmolFA gcat-1 for monometallic Ru. Enhanced performance was attributed to electronic interactions and dual-site catalytic effects that promote CO₂ activation and intermediate stabilization. The catalysts also showed excellent stability over five reaction cycles.

papers.title: Single-Fluorophore FLIM Multiplexing and STED Nanoscopy in Live Cells with a Hydroxyl-Tunable Near-Infrared aza-BODIPY Platform
papers.abstract: Fluorophores that simultaneously enable stimulated emission depletion (STED) nanoscopy and fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) multiplexing within a single spectral channel remain scarce, particularly within a single, synthetically accessible scaffold. Here we report a family of hydroxyl-functionalised 3,5-tert-butyl BF 2 -azadipyrromethene fluorophores as a synthetically accessible platform for advanced live-cell imaging. We establish that hydroxyl content determines subcellular localisation, and that asymmetric derivatives distribute across organelles of distinct physicochemical character, generating two resolvable lifetime populations. This enables discrimination of lipid droplets and membrane-rich organelles using a single fluorophore, without genetic manipulation or multiple probes. All derivatives are compatible with 775 nm STED depletion, enabling super-resolved visualisation of membrane architectures. Further sulfonation of one derivative affords a water-soluble plasma membrane probe with robust photostability that retains STED and FLIM capabilities, demonstrating the post-synthetic versatility of this scaffold. This work introduces a single-fluorophore approach for targeting and resolving complex cellular environments via concurrent nanoscopy and intrinsic lifetime-based sensing.

papers.title: A Non-equilibrium Statistical Mechanics-Based Diffusion Theory: Hydrogen Spillover Driven by Chemical Potential Gradient on Support Surface (I)
papers.abstract: Hydrogen spillover is an interfacial transport phenomenon widely present in heterogeneous catalysis, and the fluctuation and discreteness of active hydrogen on the support surface renders modeling particularly challenging. In this work, an interfacial transport model for hydrogen spillover driven by the chemical potential gradient is developed within the framework of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, by integrating random walk and linear response theories. The constitutive relationships between the transport characteristics of active hydrogen (Onsager phenomenological coefficient, characteristic length, characteristic diffusion rate and chemical potential gradient) and the support properties (reducibility, oxygen vacancies, and surface hydroxyl groups) are analyzed. The model is extended to the water phase and the subsurface of support, establishing a mathematical model that describes the cross-phase transport of active hydrogen. The theory of hydrogen spillover inherits and advances the classical surface diffusion equation and the Langmuir-Hinshelwood model, providing a paradigmatic theory for the spillover of active species (hydrogen, oxygen, CO, ammonia, etc.) and other interfacial diffusion phenomena.

papers.title: Controlling defect density in two-dimensional colloidal crystals using low-frequency AC electric fields
papers.abstract: Colloidal crystals are promising platforms for structural color due to their ability to modulate light through periodic structures with lattice spacings comparable to visible wavelengths. In two-dimensional systems that generate color via grating diffraction, the optical response is strongly influenced by the density and distribution of defects. While assembly directed by electric fields provides a versatile route to fabricate such structures, understanding of the kinetics of assembly and its impact on the density of defects remains limited. Here, we establish low-frequency AC electric fields as a rapid and tunable approach for assembling micron-sized particles into two-dimensional colloidal crystals. Using small-angle light scattering (SALS), confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM), and quantitative image analysis, we characterize the structural evolution and kinetics of assembly across a range of frequencies and voltages. Assembly occurs on timescales of a few seconds, substantially faster than many existing field-directed approaches. We find that faster assembly, achieved at lower frequencies or higher voltages, leads to increased defect densities, demonstrating a direct relationship between kinetics and microstructure. Guided by these insights, we implement time-modulated electric fields (duty cycles) to control crystallization dynamics. By selecting on/off times comparable to characteristic assembly and melting times, we enable particle rearrangement and grain coarsening, doubling the average grain size and reducing defect fractions by up to 50% relative to steady fields. The resulting structures exhibit tunable diffraction patterns relevant for applications using reconfigurable structural color. These results highlight the role of kinetics as a key design parameter for field-directed colloidal assembly.

papers.title: WITHDRAWN
papers.abstract: Withdrawn at the authors' request to address a third-party concern regarding the subject matter of the manuscript. The withdrawal does not reflect any issues with the scientific validity, integrity, or originality of the research.

papers.title: Diagnosing Quantum Tunneling at Ambient Temperature through Rate–Driving Force Responsiveness
papers.abstract: Quantum mechanical tunneling can strongly influence chemical reactivity, yet experimental diagnostics for tunneling contributions remain limited. Here we derive a new diagnostic principle, identifying ratedriving force relationship as a general experimental observable of tunneling. We show that tunneling fundamentally reshapes the scaling relationship between reaction rate and thermodynamic driving force. Whereas classical transition state theory links this responsiveness solely to barrier height, tunneling depends on both barrier height and barrier width, producing responsiveness that exceeds classical predictions. This principle provides a simple experimental diagnostic for tunneling based on responsiveness analysis within a reaction family, complementing existing diagnostics that often rely on cryogenic temperatures or isotopic substitution. We demonstrate this derived principle using the syn elimination of selenoxides as a model system at room temperature. Because the diagnostic framework relies only on standard kinetic measurements, it is expected to be broadly applicable to reactions with measurable elementary kinetics.

papers.title: The Heisenberg Fingerprint: Physics-Informed Molecular Similarity from Neural Network Potential Hidden States
papers.abstract: Scaffold hopping, the identification of functionally equivalent molecules with different chemical scaffolds, is among the most valuable and difficult operations in medicinal chemistry. Topological fingerprints are blind to it: Morgan fingerprints assign near-random similarity (mean Tanimoto 0.20) to confirmed scaffold-hopping pairs. Here we introduce the Heisenberg fingerprint (HFP), a 256dimensional molecular embedding derived from the hidden representations of pre-trained neural network potentials (NNPs) that reliably identifies scaffold hops. Per-atom features from a DFTtrained NNP backbone are pooled via multi-head attention and trained to correlate with 3D shape overlap, electrostatic potential similarity, and pharmacophore feature matching simultaneously, using 2 million molecular pairs with computed overlap targets. On 147 known scaffold-hopping cases, HFP assigns mean cosine similarity of 0.83 to pairs that Morgan fingerprints rate at 0.20. On 24 approved drugs spanning 12 therapeutic targets, including clinically validated scaffold hops such as Imatinib/Dasatinib and Sertraline/Escitalopram, same-target pairs are separated from cross-target pairs with Cohen’s 𝑑 = 1.83 (Mann-Whitney 𝑝 < 10−6), with 100% of scaffold-hop pairs scoring above the cross-target median. HFP improves virtual screening AUROC over Morgan fingerprints on LIT-PCBA (0.524 vs 0.481, winning 10 of 15 targets) and MUV (0.596 vs 0.534, winning 14 of 17 targets, non-overlapping 95% CIs). The approach is backbone-agnostic: we validate two NNP backbones (Egret-1 and MACE-OFF23) and show both produce effective embeddings with complementary strengths. The entire pipeline was completed for under $400 on cloud infrastructure. These results establish NNP hidden states as a practical source of physics-informed molecular descriptors, with particular utility for scaffold-hopping campaigns where topological methods fail.

papers.title: A Continuous-Space Analytical Framework for Committor Functions from Molecular Dynamics
Strategies to predict and design spin defects for quantum technologies
papers.abstract: The design of materials with functionalities optimally suited for quantum information applications is a critical need in the field of quantum science and engineering. This Perspective focuses on a specific class of systems, spin defects in semiconductors and insulators, and on the manipulation of their electron spins, which can provide controllable qubits with long relaxation and coherence times, and can be coupled to nuclear spins for long-lived quantum memories. We summarize our recent contributions to the development of integrated theoretical frameworks and high-performance codes to predict and design spin defects and present examples of validated predictions and interpretations of experimental results. Starting from a brief description of the structural and charge stability at zero temperature using density functional theory, we present simulations to understand the mechanism of spin defect formation with first-principles molecular dynamics and machine-learned potentials. We then discuss two classes of properties that are essential for the prediction of spin defects' functionalities: electronic and coherence properties. The discussion of computational frameworks is followed by that of results for specific systems illustrating successes, open problems, and future applications, with examples for heterogeneous solids, inclusive of surfaces and mesoscopic defects, and with a focus on quantum sensing and communication applications.

papers.title: Reassessing monomer fractions in SAFT: Quantifying the extent of hydrogen bonding in solvating mixtures using MCR-ALS
papers.abstract: The monomer fraction, X, or the molecular fraction of a component’s molecules not participating in hydrogen bonding, is an explicitly calculable quantity in the SAFT thermodynamic framework. Researchers have long proposed the measurement of X using FTIR spectroscopy and incorporating these data into parameterisation algorithms to overcome parameter degeneracy issues, particularly for polar, solvating species. This work looks to address the lack of monomer fraction data, and indeed the lack of an unbiased approach to its generation, by drawing on spectral processing techniques well-established in the spectroscopic literature. Multivariate Curve Resolution with Alternating Least Squares (MCR-ALS) is investigated as an approach to generate monomer fraction data in solvating mixtures. MCR-ALS resolves spectra for different compositions into statistically significant spectral and concentration profiles, which can be physically interpreted to justify a full range of hydrogen bond interactions, while simultaneously quantifying monomer fraction. This overcomes the inherent bias and spectral ambiguity associated with curve fitting approaches used in previous thermodynamic studies of monomer fractions. The method was validated using the widely studied ethanol/n-hexane system before considering the ethanol/acetone binary mixture as a case study in solvating systems. The acetone monomer fraction was quantified across the compositional space, while the expected low fraction of ethanol monomers could not be elucidated from the instrument noise and signal processing. An initial assessment of polar-SAFT models to simultaneously predict phase equilibrium and monomer fraction data with previously published parameter sets highlighted valid approaches for incorporating these data in model parameterisation and development in future work.

papers.title: Embedded Amide in π-Conjugation as a Tunable Double-Bond Motif for Controlling Optical Properties
papers.abstract: Replacing C=C bonds in aromatic molecules with heteroatom-containing double bond motifs ( e.g. C=N, B–N, C=P) is effective for their electronic modulation. However, structurally modifying these motifs is difficult, making the tunability of their electronic properties challenging. To overcome this limitation, we propose using the amide C–N bond as a tunable double-bond unit. We synthesized a series of amide-embedded pyrenes ( AmPy s) incorporating cis -amide bonds within the π-framework. The degree of C–N double-bond character of the amide was modulated through covalent modifications ( O - and N -methylation), non-covalent interactions (hydrogen bonding), and protonation. Spectroscopic studies revealed that as the C–N bond lengthens, T 1 state energies increase while S 1 state energies remain relatively constant, narrowing the S 1 –T 1 energy gap (∆ E ST ). Computational analysis clarified that short C–N bonds promote localized π-conjugation within two fused K-region rings containing C–N bonds, acting as an electronic insulator that spatially separates unpaired electrons to lower the T 1 state energies. Conversely, long C–N bonds weaken such π-conjugation, leading to more delocalized spin densities, raising the T 1 state energies. This work establishes the amide as a versatile double-bond unit where the C–N bond length serves as a design parameter for tuning electronic properties.

papers.title: Computer Vision Enables Spatiotemporal Monitoring of UV-promoted Polyurethane Foam Degradation Kinetics
papers.abstract: The UV-A photodegradation of toluene-diisocyanate-based polyurethane (TDI-PU) foams is monitored in real time by spatiotemporal computer-vision analysis of single-camera video. Periodic on/off oscillation of the 365 nm UV torch produces two complementary chromatic readouts of the same foam from each recording: an ambient-light b ∗ channel that tracks visible yellowing, and a UV-on b ∗ channel that tracks the loss of UV-excited blue fluorescence. A time-implicit phase-plot analysis of the upper-vs-lower b ∗ relationship resolves an oxygen-mediated coupling step invisible to single-channel ∆E 76 : the linear coupling observed in air (R 2 = 0.93) collapses entirely under nitrogen (R 2 = 0.09). FT-IR difference spectroscopy localises the dominant photo-oxidative bond loss at the polyol-soft-segment ether near 1100 cm −1 –itself atmosphere-independent–and identifies the bonded-urea-region C=O at 1640 cm −1 as the oxygen-controlled chromophore class responsible for the cross-channel coupling. At 3 wt% loading, a benzotriazole UV absorber halves the cumulative colour change, while a tris(1-chloro-2-propyl) phosphate flame retardant confers no photoprotective benefit and slightly accelerates ether-region scission, illustrating the method’s utility as a rapid, lowcost screen for distinguishing photoprotective additives from those that act on a different failure mode.

papers.title: SpectraGuard: A Unified Deep Learning Framework for Spectroscopic Signal Enhancement and Chemical Image Authenticity Verification
papers.abstract: Spectroscopic analysis is a cornerstone of modern chemistry, yet the quality of spectral measurements is often compromised by various noise sources, while the growing sophistication of AI-generated content threatens the authenticity of chemical images and molecular structure diagrams. In this paper, we propose SpectraGuard, a unified deep learning framework that simultaneously addresses spectroscopic signal enhancement and chemical image authenticity verification. SpectraGuard comprises two synergistic modules: an Adaptive Spectral Denoising (ASD) module that combines analytical priors with a filtered feature recycling network for iterative noise suppression, and a Chemical Image Verification (CIV) module that employs reasoning-aligned representation learning for detecting and localizing forgeries in chemical imagery. The two modules share a spectral-image feature encoder, enabling parameter sharing and knowledge transfer within an end-to-end training framework. We evaluate SpectraGuard on three publicly available benchmarks: the RRUFF Raman spectral dataset, the NIST infrared spectral database, and the ChemForged chemical image forgery dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that SpectraGuard achieves an SNR improvement of 16.8 dB on spectral denoising, outperforming the state-of-the-art data-free method SPADE by 1.5 dB, while attaining a detection AUC of 0.981 and localization F1 of 0.867 on chemical image verification, surpassing existing forgery detection approaches. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each proposed component, and human evaluation by domain experts further validates the practical utility of our framework.

papers.title: WITHDRAWN
papers.abstract: Withdrawn at the authors' request because it contained data that was disclosed prematurely.

papers.title: Designing Cooperative Molecular Glues for FKBP12-MAPRE1 with Enhanced-Sampling Molecular Dynamics Simulations
papers.abstract: Molecular glues (MGs) offer a unique modality for inducing protein-protein interactions (PPIs), yet their rational design is often hindered by the limitations of static structural data. Here, we present a computational pipeline for the design of cooperative MGs for the FKBP12-MAPRE1 system using replica exchange with solute scaling (REST2) for enhanced sampling in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. By sampling the conformational ensembles of binary and ternary complexes, we identified a "stabilized configurational space" that facilitates ternary-complex formation through a combination of conformational selection and induced-fit mechanisms. Based on the simulations, we developed a model that correlates the induced PPI information from the simulations with the experimental cooperativity. This model was subsequently used to select and rank a small library of compounds prospectively, of which five were selected for synthesis and testing. Three of the five new compounds exhibited apparent cooperativity equal to or greater than that of the best previously known variants, achieving a hit rate of 60% in prospective design. This study demonstrates that targeting shared configurations within dynamic ensembles is a viable strategy for the rational optimization of cooperative molecular glues.

papers.title: Efficient Bayesian Optimization of Separation Chemistry in the Scarce-Data Regime Using Kinetic Reaction Networks
papers.abstract: Chemical process optimization is a critical and challenging task relevant to a broad range of industrial applications. Bayesian optimization (BO) has emerged as a powerful framework for navigating complex solution spaces, often with substantially greater efficiency than conventional experimental design approaches. While BO is commonly implemented using domain-agnostic Gaussian processes, its performance can potentially be further improved by incorporating domain knowledge. In this work, we propose a model-based BO framework that combines data-driven kinetic reaction networks with the pointwise optimal parameter sets (POPS) approach for improving uncertainty quantification. We apply this framework to the optimization of liquid-liquid uranium extraction using two monoamide ligands, N,N -dihexyloctanamide (DHOA) and N,N -di(2-ethylhexyl)-isobutyramide (DEHiBA). We evaluate the performance of the kinetic-model-based BO framework relative to a traditional Gaussian process counterpart, with particular emphasis on the scarce-data regime. We find that the kinetic reaction networks provide consistent and reliable predictions and that the POPS approach yields well-calibrated uncertainty estimates that can be effectively leveraged to guide the Bayesian optimization process. These features improve optimization efficiency, particularly in the scarce-data regime. Additional performance gains are obtained by regularizing the kinetic reaction networks using quantum mechanical calculations.

papers.title: Agentic crystallography: the crystallographer who never sleeps
Aggregation-Induced Radical
papers.abstract: Over the past three decades, organic semiconductors have achieved remarkable progress in various optoelectronic fields. Traditionally, the classic donor-acceptor (D-A) type organic semiconductors were considered to have a closed-shell singlet ground state, with electron spin resonance signals typically attributed to impurities, defects, or external doping. However, the group of Yuan Li discovered that the D-A organic semiconductors universally exhibit an intrinsic openshell quinoidal singlet and triplet diradical ground state in 2017 for the first time, and they further put forward the descriptive concept of aggregation-induced radical (AIR) in 2019. In 2021, systematic mixed-solvent experiments were performed to mechanistically disclose the key driving force for the formation and stabilization of these diradicaloids. Different from the 118-year-old Chichibabin-type diradicaloids stabilized by the recovery of aromaticity, AIR promotes radical generation and stabilization through ground-state charge transfer, intermolecular π-π interaction and radical-radical pancake bonds in their aggregated state. This review systematically summarizes our recent research progress of the AIR mechanism, multi-dimensional experimental evidences, diverse potential application and future development directions, aiming to provide a comprehensive understanding of this emerging research field on the open-shell ground state of D-A materials and guide the design of novel materials for organic electronic and spintronic devices.

papers.title: Where Foundation Machine-Learning Potentials Fail for Iron-Sulfide Defect Kinetics: Four Failure Modes and a DFT Benchmark of Vacancy-Anchored Hydrogen Migration in Pyrite, Marcasite, Mackinawite, and Greigite
papers.abstract: Foundation machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise cheap, near-DFT energetics, but their reliability for defect kinetics in magnetic transition-metal sulfides is largely untested. We benchmark MACE-MP-0 (medium) and CHGNet-v0.3.0, zero-shot, against plane-wave DFT (Quantum ESPRESSO) for vacancy-anchored proton migration across four iron sulfides (pyrite, marcasite, mackinawite, greigite), plus a pentlandite structural-motif diagnostic. The proton is modelled as a neutral H0 defect in dry bulk supercells, a benchmark proxy rather than an interface calculation. A single unified PBE (U = 0) protocol gives the DFT reference barriers: pyrite V_S2 dimer hop 95 meV and V_Fe + S–H 268 meV; mackinawite 43 meV; marcasite 208 meV; greigite 1.86 eV (ferrimagnetic). We report the first harmonic zero-point corrections for *bulk proton migrationthe stiff reactant S–H stretch becomes the imaginary saddle mode—lowering rate-relevant barriers by 66–94 meV and rendering mackinawite effectively barrierless. The foundation potentials fail in four distinct, diagnosable ways: a flat or wrong-topology PES (pyrite V_S2), [Fe4S4] cubane motif collapse (pentlandite), unphysical energies and non-convergence on the inverse spinel (greigite), and false-positive band-collapse warnings (marcasite); where they converge (pyrite V_Fe) they underbind DFT by 1.2–1.5×. Greigite’s barrier places bulk H migration in the kinetically-forbidden regime (τ ≈ 90 Gyr), excluding inverse-spinel Fe–S phases from proton conduction. Foundation MLIPs are reliable only as topology screeners, with mandatory pre-flight checks, and cannot replace DFT for quantitative barriers in magnetic, defect-rich sulfides. An ASE IDPP minimum-image-convention fix is contributed upstream; the spin-polarized pentlandite barrier is a companion study.

papers.title: Interplay of polaron hopping and Jahn–Teller dynamics defines the mechanism of electronic transport in LiMn2O4
papers.abstract: In electrode materials with Jahn-Teller active transition metals, the mobile charge is itself a Jahn-Teller polaron inseparable from the cooperative distortive order of the surrounding lattice. Polaron transport and Jahn-Teller dynamics have each been characterized in isolation, yet the mechanistic link between them has remained conceptual. Combining first-principles calculations with nanosecond machine-learning molecular dynamics, we resolve this link in the spinel cathode LiMn2O4. Polaron migration is coupled to Jahn-Teller pseudorotation, which transiently reorients the local distortion to open a low-barrier hopping channel, the two events occurring sequentially within tens of femtoseconds. Both barriers scale in parallel with cooperative order, from 0.12 and 0.04 eV in the cubic phase to 0.27 and 0.12 eV in the tetragonal phase. In the orthorhombic phase the polaron is confined to charge-saturated heterocubane clusters, so long-range transport is rate-limited by rare inter-cluster transfer. The coupled dynamics give rise to measurable x-ray and neutron scattering signatures that distinguish pseudorotation from polaron hopping. These results establish cooperative Jahn-Teller order as a tunable parameter governing electronic transport.

papers.title: Fast and Detailed X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy Imaging from Low Resolution and Obscure Images with Deep Learning
papers.abstract: XPS is the workhorse for chemical characterization of functional surfaces, with depth sensitivity of less than ~5 nm, but at the expense of a large collection area of hundreds of micrometers wide, incompatible with prevailing micro-fabrication. Commercial XPS manufacturers have offered imaging XPS with spatial resolution down to ~5 μm for decades, yet it is rarely practiced due to prolonged acquisition times needed to overcome poor signal-tonoise ratios. Here we report a deep learning model trained to reconstruct high-resolution XPS images from rapid, low-resolution, noisy input images. Model accuracy was quantified against ground-truth high-resolution XPS images using structural and spatial metrics. The model was trained on powder grains of various chemicals and demonstrates promising generalization to unseen samples of different compositions, supported by an expert survey. The method produces high-resolution XPS images for low-weight elements at non-destructive X-ray power (75 W) within minutes, making XPS imaging a viable screening tool for follow-up analyses such as small-area XPS localization. It is particularly advantageous for sensitive materials where fast acquisition is critical for non-destructive, sample-authentic spectroscopy.

papers.title: First-Principles Mechanistic Study of Transition Metal-Doped Copper Carbonate Hydroxide Electrocatalysts for C-N Coupling
papers.abstract: Electrochemical C-N coupling has emerged as a sustainable route to organonitrogen synthesis, with copper carbonate hydroxide (CCH) identified as an efficient electrocatalyst. Here, a firstprinciples mechanistic study is performed to investigate the effects of transition metal (TM) doping on the C-N coupling performance of CCH-based catalysts. A volcano plot using d-band center as the optimal descriptor shows that early TM-doped catalysts usually exhibit higher selectivity for C-N coupling, among which Nb-CCH delivers the best performance. A contour plot correlating the C-N coupling performance with the adsorption characteristics of TM-CCHs reveals that enhanced selectivity generally arises from weaker *CO adsorption coupled with stronger *NO adsorption. The bonding analysis further elucidates that TM doping tunes the surface electronic structure and optimizes the adsorption properties of CCH-based catalysts, thereby improving the C-N coupling performance. This work provides theoretical insights into the rational design of C-N coupling electrocatalysts, contributing to the development of green synthesis and pollution control.

papers.title: Ambient rapid phase transformation in zeolitic-imidazolate frameworks monitored by water intrusion
papers.abstract: Rapid phase transformations at ambient conditions are useful in manufacturing porous materials for industrial applications. Such phase transformations are of particular interest between materials with distinct pore properties or synthesis yields. Herein, we report a new mechanism to transform hydrophilic ZIF-L into hydrophobic ZIF-8; unlike existing methods that require days at elevated temperatures, this new approach achieves conversion within a few hours at room temperature, thereby facilitating a more sustainable and economical route to producing ZIF-8. The two ZIFs comprise the same building blocks, but ZIF-L has a two-dimensional layered structure, whereas ZIF-8 has a three-dimensional framework. The transformation is achieved in Zn2+-containing methanol solutions via a two-step process that starts with the dissolution of ZIF-L, followed by the crystallisation of ZIF-8. Interestingly, because of their markedly different pore surface properties, pressurised water intrusion is proposed as a new method to monitor the extent of phase transformation. This method, in addition to being quick and non-destructive, demonstrates high sensitivity to small sample sizes or low transformation percentages and, in principle, can be used to examine the phase transformation of any material with distinct pore properties.

papers.title: FORMULA‑Sigma: a reproducible, machine‑learning‑augmented workflow for pharmaceutical formulation design‑of‑experiments, with retrospective reproduction and analytical transparency
papers.abstract: Background. Pharmaceutical formulation under Quality by Design (QbD, ICH Q8(R2)) relies on design of experiments (DoE), but the dominant analytical practice remains a single low-order response-surface polynomial fitted to a handful of runs, reported by in-sample R², and optimised by Derringer-Suich desirability. Because the per-run data and the exact analysis pipeline are rarely published together, these analyses are difficult to re-examine, and their reported fit statistics are rarely cross-validated. Methods. We present a reproducible, machine-learning-augmented workflow for analysing formulation DoE: cross-validated surrogate selection from a model zoo (linear, quadratic RSM, Scheffé, sparse RSM, PLS, Bayesian Ridge, Gaussian Process, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, MLP, NGBoost, plus an ensemble), Bayesian optimisation, Monte-Carlo probabilistic design space (PDS) aligned with the joint-probability interpretation of ICH Q8(R2), and robust and NSGA-II multi-objective analysis, over eight classical and mixture design families. The workflow is implemented in FORMULA-Sigma; its computations are re-implemented in a standalone, openly released harness so that every result can be regenerated independently of the implementation. We evaluate it on a numerical-soundness check against open tools, a retrospective reanalysis of five published formulation studies, and synthetic ground-truth benchmarks. Results. The classical core agrees with pyDOE3 and statsmodels to within 10⁻¹³ to 10⁻¹⁵. Reanalysis reproduces published optima and ANOVA conclusions across central-composite, mixture-process, Box-Behnken, and categorical D-optimal designs, with the best-fitting model in each case reaching an in-sample R² of 0.96 to 0.99. For every fit the workflow additionally reports a leave-one-out cross-validated Q², which on these small (15 to 22 run) designs is markedly lower than the in-sample R²; the workflow thereby makes a gap visible that R²-only reporting hides, and a systematic audit quantifying this gap across the published literature is reported in a companion study. The workflow also makes explicit the analytical degrees of freedom (model form, significance threshold, term selection, desirability shape) that drive published conclusions, and a cautionary episode shows how an apparent equation inconsistency dissolved once the published coding convention was respected. Synthetic benchmarks confirm that Bayesian optimisation, PDS recovery (Jaccard 0.82), and NSGA-II Pareto search (99.4% of the true hypervolume) recover known answers. Conclusions. A reproducible, machine-learning-augmented workflow for formulation DoE reproduces published work, exposes the analytical choices that single-pipeline reporting leaves implicit, and reports a cross-validated fit metric that small designs make essential. We release the standalone harness and the five case datasets so that the analysis can be checked and extended; the systematic predictive-validity audit that the workflow enables is reported separately.

papers.title: A mechanistic framework to interpret proton-coupled electron transfer kinetics in heterogeneous electrocatalysis
papers.abstract: Mechanistic analysis in heterogeneous electrocatalysis is currently rooted in one of two predominant approaches. Either (i) measured Tafel slopes near cardinal values of 30, 40, 60, or 120 mV dec−1 are interpreted to reflect a single rate-determining step (RDS) or (ii) non-cardinal Tafel slopes and reaction orders are fit by multi-step microkinetic models. While the cardinal approach is mathematically simple and physically intuitive, it is valid only in limiting regimes and neglects complexities such as multiple ratedetermining steps and non-ideal surface isotherms. By contrast, microkinetic modeling can capture these complexities, but requires extensive parameterization and incurs significant computational cost. Here, we present a framework that allies the concepts of degree of rate control and elementary step reversibility to bridge these approaches. We apply these developments to analysis of experimental data available in the literature for H2 evolution, O2 evolution, and CO reduction and demonstrate that jointly constraining noncardinal kinetic observables enables facile identification of rate-determining step(s) and quantification of elementary-step symmetry factors at near-zero computational expense. In doing so, the developed framework transforms non-cardinal kinetic observables from aberrations to invaluable mechanistic descriptors that elicit otherwise elusive molecular-level information.

papers.title: Multi-Objective Formulation Optimization Under Sustainability Constraints
papers.abstract: Chemical formulators routinely face a four-dimensional trade-off — raw-material cost, biobased content, technical performance, and environmental/regulatory impact — that classical linear-programming (LP) tools collapse into a single weighted objective, hiding the trade-off surface from the decision-maker. We present IntelliForm's optimization core, a three-engine architecture that exposes this trade-off explicitly: (1) an LP baseline (PuLP/CBC) for fast, singleobjective minimum-cost formulations; (2) a constrained multi-objective evolutionary engine (NSGA-III) that returns a full Pareto frontier across cost, bio-based %, and performance; and (3) a multi-objective Bayesian optimization engine (qNEHVI, via BoTorch) that treats formulation discovery as a sequential, sample-efficient experiment-design problem over four objectives cost, bio-based %, performance, and a composite EcoMetrics™ sustainability score derived from biodegradability, carbon footprint, ecotoxicity, renewability, and REACH status. A recurring failure mode of evolutionary multi-objective methods on simplex-constrained formulation spaces is reported and fixed: for ingredient pools larger than ~150 candidates, uniform-random population initialization collapses to near-uniform "everything-at-once" blends whose objective values sit at the pool-wide mean — outside any realistic cost constraint causing NSGA-III to report zero feasible solutions. We introduce sparse-prior population seeding, which restores feasibility from generation zero by initializing individuals as compact 3–12 ingredient blends, matching the sparsity of real-world formulations. Beyond the optimization core, we describe and benchmark four downstream decision-support modules that operate directly on optimizer output — QSAR/QSPR property prediction (graph neural network, 5-fold CV R2 up to 0.93), CertificationOracle™ (pre-screening against 10 green-chemistry certifications), an ISO-14067-aligned carbon-credit calculator, and a conformal-prediction stability/shelf-life model — and argue that this integrated stack, not the optimizer in isolation, constitutes IntelliForm's defensible market position relative to both legacy LP tools and general-purpose materials-discovery AI platforms.

papers.title: PDB-Quantifier: Reference-Based Protein Structure Quality Assessment and Prioritization via One-Class Learning
papers.abstract: A curated ADS benchmark set containing 85 protein structures was used as the reference domain. For each structure, feature vectors were constructed from experimentally reported and validation-related descriptors, including resolution, refinement statistics, atom and residue counts, ligand-related variables, and structural validation measures such as clashscore and Ramachandran outliers. Missing values were handled by mean imputation, and an Isolation Forest model was trained to learn the intrinsic distribution of the reference set. The trained model was then applied to two independent external datasets: an MTi benchmark set and a randomly sampled Protein Data Bank set.

papers.title: Electron microscopy identifies protein conformational substates in liquid environment
papers.abstract: Protein functions are closely linked to their dynamic behaviors, particularly involving low-abundance transient states. Quantifying these interconversions remains experimentally challenging, especially for proteins containing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). In this study, we utilize low-dose electron microscopy using graphene liquid cells (GLCs) to image and quantify interconversions between protein conformational states under optimized electron beam conditions and confinement effects. Applied to four proteins in solution: CRISPR-associated protein (Cas9), DNA binding protein (GapR), restriction enzyme (EcoR1), and an RNA binding protein with IDRs (FUS), we visualized low abundance transient structures distinct from crystalline forms, and elucidated transition pathways which are validated by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), revealing differences in their energy landscapes through single molecule imaging. We analyzed domain motions at nanometer resolution, cross-validated against independent computational and experimental methods. Shifts in state equilibria and conformational adaptations were observed when proteins are mutated or during biomolecular interactions, such as target searching, binding, and cleavage with nucleic acids. Notably, changes in the energy landscape were observed when proteins with IDRs and RNA were within close proximity but not in apparent contact, suggesting that conformational redistribution may precede complete binding. This study shows how to characterize protein conformations and their time-dependent changes using instrumentation that is widely available at research universities but not yet used for these purposes.

papers.title: Solvent-free basic one-pot synthesis of 1,2,4-triazole derivatives
papers.abstract: The 1,2,4-triazole moiety is widely used in synthetic chemistry, however its synthesis presents several limitations. We developed a one-pot intermolecular reaction in basic conditions to afford the triazole scaffold from a wide range of amides and hydrazides. The use of an adjusted 4-dimethylaminopyridine quantity ensured basic and solvent-free conditions, in accordance with Green Chemistry principles. A systematic study of the steric, inductive and resonance effects together with hypothesis on the reaction intermediates allowed to optimize the co-activator and reduce the reaction time (1-2h). Our work introduces a rapid basic solventfree one-pot reaction to obtain 1,2,4-triazole containing compounds with broad applications in medicinal chemistry, as demonstrated by the synthesis of the precursor of an unnatural amino acid and a key intermediate of the maraviroc drug.

papers.title: Maintaining dynamic crosslink engagement under network perturbation preserves hydrogel viscoelasticity
papers.abstract: Dynamic hydrogels are widely used to emulate viscoelastic extracellular matrices, yet stabilization against dissolution does not necessarily preserve viscoelastic function under physiological swelling. Here, we interrogate how network topology governs retention of dynamic mechanics in swollen hydrogels. Using a modular thiol-ene platform in which a dynamic supramolecular guest-host network is architecturally decoupled from the stable covalent network, we first demonstrate that as-prepared hydrogels occupy a structured, low-dimensional viscoelastic manifold parameterized by the relative fraction of stable and dynamic crosslinks. This structured design space demonstrates that hybrid network viscoelasticity can be rationally parameterized by crosslinker composition across a broad range of relaxation behaviors. However, upon equilibration in aqueous media, this independently tunable viscoelastic space collapses; hydrogels spanning a broad range of relaxation extents converge toward a restricted mechanical regime despite preservation of macroscopic structure, consistent with swelling-induced dilution of guest-host bonding partners that were never architecturally coupled to the stable scaffold. To restore dynamic function without increasing permanent crosslink density, we introduce multivalent electrostatic interactions to enforce heteropolymer proximity. Increasing crosslinker charge preserves frequency-dependent elasticity and dissipation in the swollen state, with the maximally charged crosslinker retaining a normalized high-frequency modulus approximately five-fold greater than the uncharged control. Competitive disruption confirms that viscoelastic retention remains contingent on guest-host engagement. Together, these findings reveal that maintaining viscoelasticity under swelling requires architectural coupling of reversible motifs to a stable network, and that stabilization against dissolution alone is insufficient to preserve dynamic mechanical function.

papers.title: Wireless Bipolar Electrochemistry for Organic Electrosynthesis: Principles, Mechanistic Insights, and Emerging Autonomous Systems
papers.abstract: Wireless bipolar electrochemistry (BPE) has emerged as a powerful platform for organic electrosynthesis, enabling redox transformations on electrically floating conductors without direct electrical wiring. Through electric-field-induced polarization, bipolar electrodes simultaneously promote spatially separated oxidation and reduction reactions, offering unique opportunities for reaction design, miniaturized reactor architectures, parallel processing, and sustainable chemical synthesis. Recent years have witnessed significant advances in both exogenous and endogenous bipolar electrochemical systems, expanding the scope of wireless electrosynthesis to asymmetric transformations, flow chemistry, low-electrolyte conditions, autonomous microreactors, and selfpropelled electrochemical systems. This perspective review critically examines the fundamental principles governing bipolar electrochemistry, recent developments in organic synthesis, and emerging diagnostic methodologies, including split bipolar electrodes and electrochemiluminescence-based imaging, which have substantially improved mechanistic understanding of charge transport, polarization phenomena, and reaction control. The advantages and limitations of wireless bipolar systems are evaluated in comparison with conventional electrolysis, highlighting challenges associated with reaction selectivity, scalability, energy efficiency, and quantitative electrochemical characterization. Finally, future opportunities involving advanced materials, operando analytical techniques, artificial intelligence-assisted optimization, and continuous-flow processing are discussed. Collectively, these developments position wireless bipolar electrochemistry as a promising enabling technology for next-generation sustainable electrosynthesis and autonomous electrochemical manufacturing.

papers.title: Prediction of Kinetic Solvent Effects for SN2 Reactions using COSMO-RS
papers.abstract: Although ionic reactions comprise a major component of industrially-relevant reactions, the prediction of their rate coefficients remains a challenge. Furthermore, existing ab initio kinetic modeling methods are primarily suited for gas-phase conformers, and can be computationally expensive.
