We observed two distinct IR bands upon exposing reduced Ni/SiO2 sample to N2 at room temperature, located at ~ 2257 and ~ 2275 cm−1. Based on the use of 14N2 and 15N2 isotopes, we assigned these IR bands to N2 bound to Ni. Using Density Functional Theory (DFT), we calculated the vibrational and adsorption energies of N2 in various modes, which suggest the two IR bands are due to N2 bound in a ‘top’ binding mode on different Ni sites. We did not observe significant influence of Ni metal nanoparticle size on the IR absorption band properties, nor on the apparent ΔHads values yielded by van ’t Hoff analysis. Such unexpected apparent structure insensitive behaviour is explained by DFT results, which predict similar vibrational frequencies for N2 adsorbed on different Ni surfaces.

papers.title: Symmetry puts everything in order: Symmetry-governed crystal chemical modeling of the composition and structure of Nb3Sn alloy
papers.abstract: Symmetry and its manifestations are fundamental to nature. Symmetry concepts and principles are essential for developing advanced models and algorithms in materials theory. In this study, we examined the relationship between the physical properties of a crystal and its chemical composition. To do so, we combined symmetry theory methods with standard atomic-scale simulations of Nb3Sn alloy crystal chemistry. We exploited opportunities afforded by crystal symmetry laws and crystallographic methods to generate robust models of three-dimensional atomic arrangements and metallic element packing within solid solutions or binary intermetallic compounds. Our conceptual design scenarios are based on density functional theory computations, symmetrydetermined predictors, multiscale iterations, and theoretical space group methods. Key subjects addressed include an analysis of the outcomes of numerical simulations and the identification of critical points associated with potential phase transformations.

papers.title: Alanine-Rich Peptide for Spin-Dependent Transport: Synthesis of a 36-mer via Pentamer Assembly
papers.abstract: Alanine-rich peptides are of increasing interest in fields of spin chemistry and molecular spintronics due to their potential to exhibit the chiral-induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect. In particular, the 36-mer sequence H-C[AAAAK] 7 -OH has been identified as a promising model for inducing CISS. However, synthesizing this alanine-rich peptide is challenging due to its high hydrophobicity and lysine protection requirements, which typically result in low yields and significant side-product formation. Here, we report an optimized block-wise synthetic strategy employing Fmoc-[AAAAK(Boc)]-OH pentamers and DIC/Oxyma coupling, which significantly improves crude purity. A microwave-supported synthesis on Wang resin, combined with an acetyl capping step and 4-methylpiperidine deprotection, delivered crude peptide with 64% purity, confirmed by analytical reverse phase – high performance chromatography (RP-HPLC) and liquid-phase chromatography – mass spectrometry (LC-MS). By contrast, linear single-amino-acid synthesis and microwave-assisted protocols afforded low-purity or truncated sequences. Our protocol thus provides a robust and scalable route to this peptide, facilitating its application in CISS studies.

papers.title: Ion Gating of Charge Transport Across Phenothiazine Single Molecule Wires
papers.abstract: Electrochemistry is an important approach for controlling and modulating the electronic and electrical properties of molecular materials, even at the single molecule level. Recently, the combination of reliable methodologies for single-molecule measurements in electrochemical environments with increasingly refined computational modelling has greatly advanced understanding of charge transport through single molecules. It also reveals how this is impacted by the redox (electrochemical) state of the molecule and the electrochemical environment. In this study the single-molecule conductance of a phenothiazine-containing molecular wire PTZ-1 is shown to exhibit an electrode potential dependence characterised by a gradual rise over an unusually broad potential window (≈ 1 V). Significantly, the onset of the conductance rise occurs substantially negative of the reversible oxidation potential for the molecule, and therefore the data cannot be attributed to typical mechanisms for electrochemical gating. These processes are modelled using DFT computations, in which the increasing conductance is seen to result from the Fano resonance induced by the phenothiazine group which is gated by electrolyte ions. These electrolyte ions gate the conductance of the molecular wire even though the phenothiazine is not redox switched to its oxidised state. The significance of this work is in identifying this mechanism for gating conductance at the single molecule level, which recognises and includes the role of electrolyte ions in an ab initio computational model. This understanding is of great importance for nanoscale devices, where subtle ion migration plays a role in functionality.

papers.title: Engineering potent SNAr biocatalysts from de novo proteins featuring an activated arginine
papers.abstract: Arginine side chains play important roles in the catalytic sites of many natural and engineered enzymes. This versatility is further exemplified by the recent development of artificial enzymes for S N Ar processes, which rely on a key catalytic arginine embedded within a haloacid dehalogenase scaffold. Although powerful, the catalytic proficiency of these first generation S N Arases remains limited, meaning their activity is restricted to highly activated electrophile and nucleophile coupling partners. Here we address these limitations by developing miniature de novo S N Arases that offer far greater catalytic potency and synthetic scope. To this end, a computationally designed NTF2-like protein featuring an activated arginine embedded within its hydrophobic core was optimized over successive rounds of directed evolution. The enhanced catalytic proficiency offered by these optimized designs allows them to operate efficiently on poorly activated substrates and has enabled the development of unprecedented regio- and enantioselective S N Ar transformations. Structural and biochemical analysis of the most active enzyme reveals a remarkably sophisticated active site, whereby a key catalytic Arg17 embedded in an extended polar network works in synergy with an aromatic-rich substrate binding pocket to accurately position and activate the S N Ar coupling partners. This study provides new insights to guide the design of arginine-containing catalytic sites that will enable the future development of de novo enzymes for diverse chemical transformations.

papers.title: Phosphate-Mediated Proton Shuttling Governs Nitrate Electroreduction Selectivity on Copper
papers.abstract: The electrochemical reduction of nitrate (NO3RR) can be carried out at high reaction rates, yet selectivity to desired ammonia/ammonium remains challenging on catalysts like copper due to the presence of nitrite as a dissolved intermediate. We here find the local microenvironment of NO3RR can influence typical catalyst metrics of rate and selectivity to extents on par with those typically attributed to differences in catalyst formulation. Considering a phosphate buffered bulk pH 7 medium, we find the high NO3RR rates on Cu exceed the buffering capacity, leading to surface pH ~13. Accounting for the local proton activity to measure reaction rates at fixed overpotential demonstrates rates approximately an order of magnitude greater compared to a bulk pH 13 electrolyte. In the absence of phosphate, nitrite is kinetically more difficult to reduce on Cu than is nitrate. Inclusion of phosphate—regardless of the bulk pH—leads to the onset of nitrite reduction at comparable potentials to nitrate reduction, and ~2x higher electron selectivity to ammonia/ammonium compared to without phosphate. Grand 2 canonical density functional theory calculations demonstrate that adsorbed phosphate thermodynamically favors proton abstraction from water under reaction conditions, whereas nitrate and nitrite are incapable of doing so. This adsorbed phosphate—observed in operando surface enhanced infrared spectroscopy—thus stabilizes the intermediate nitrite and can promote the shuttling of protons from water to it, favoring selectivity to ammonia. The presence of a pH gradient further promotes proton shuttling from the bulk electrolyte to exacerbate these trends. Overall, these findings highlight the need to measure, control, and ultimately leverage the local environment around the active site in catalyst design.

papers.title: Decoupling Thermodynamic and Kinetic Moisture Instability Reveals a Critical Humidity Threshold for Sodium Thiophosphate Solid Electrolyte
papers.abstract: Sodium sulfide solid electrolytes are widely regarded as highly moisture-sensitive, requiring ultralow-humidity (typically 15-100 ppm) processing that imposes a major cost barrier to solid-state battery manufacturing. Yet the actual moisture-stability limit of these materials remains poorly quantified, and the mechanistic origin of degradation, whether thermodynamic or kinetic, is unresolved. Here, using sodium thiophosphate, Na3PS4, as a model system, we establish a quantitative moisture-stability framework that decouples thermodynamic and kinetic contributions to apparent instability. Controlled exposure studies across 13-38% relative humidity, correlated with H2S evolution, mass uptake, structural evolution, and ionic conductivity recovery, reveals a critical humidity threshold near 15% relative humidity, below which, Na3PS4 undergoes reversible hydration with minimal hydrolysis on surface, fully recovering its ionic conductivity at 13% relative humidity after brief heat treatment. Density functional theory shows that hydration is thermodynamically favorable (ΔG = -0.76 eV), whereas hydrolysis is kinetically gated by a 1.78 eV activation barrier, rationalizing the unexpected tolerance. By defining a practical humidity-tolerance window and a reproducible benchmarking protocol, this work provides a transferable foundation for the rational design of moisture-tolerant sulfide electrolytes toward substantially relaxed humidity requirements for all-solid-state battery manufacturing.

papers.title: N2 Oxidation to Nitrate via a Phase Transition-Based Pathway
papers.abstract: Nitric acid is essential in fertilizer production, yet its current industrial synthesis via the Haber-Bosch and Ostwald process accounts for 1 % of the chemical sector’s energy consumption and produces significant greenhouse gas emissions. Despite considerable efforts, previous attempts at electrochemical nitrogen oxidation have proven unsuccessful due to competition with the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and the inherent difficulty of activating the nitrogen (N 2 ) bond under ambient conditions. In this work, we propose a phase transition-based approach inspired by electrochemical ammonia synthesis to circumvent these challenges. The strategy is centered around formation of a metal nitride by direct nitridation of a suitable metal, followed by an oxidation step employing molecular oxygen (O 2 ). Li and Ca are identified as particularly promising candidates to mediate such a pathway based on reaction thermodynamics, and we show experimentally that Li nitride can indeed be oxidized to yield nitrate in the presence of O 2 . The proposed concept demonstrates considerable potential for direct N 2 oxidation, encouraging further computational and experimental investigation.

papers.title: Virtual screening of an orexin receptor ligand library identifies lemborexant analogs with favorable CNS drug-likeness and dual-receptor binding profiles
papers.abstract: Orexin receptor modulators (ORMs) are an emerging class of drugs that address insomnia using mechanisms distinct from those of conventional GABAergic sedatives. The unmet demand for safer insomnia drugs, especially in vulnerable populations such as patients with dementia, has brought ORMs into the spotlight. ORMs are also showing promise for treating type 1 narcolepsy. To further study ORMs, a PubChem-derived library of 80 structural analogs of four known orexin ligands was assembled, deduplicated into 79 unique compounds, and subjected to physicochemical filtering (Ro5), in silico ADMET prediction, and a composite CNS-weighted scoring scheme prioritizing BBB penetration. The top 20 candidates were docked against OX1R and OX2R crystal structures. Seventy-eight of 79 compounds satisfied Lipinski's criteria. Lemborexant-derived analogs dominated the shortlist, with seven analogs exceeding lemborexant in composite score. One analog (CID 56944043) achieved the most balanced dual-receptor binding profile (OX1R −8.796 kcal/mol, OX2R −7.780 kcal/mol), while three suvorexant-derived analogs failed to locate either binding pocket. A significant negative correlation between CNS drug-likeness and OX1R docking score (ρ = −0.54), and a positive correlation between OX1R affinity and predicted hERG liability (ρ = 0.58, p = 0.008) were observed. This pipeline effectively prioritized CNS-relevant orexin ligands while revealing a trade-off between BBB-oriented drug-likeness and receptor engagement, identifying safety considerations for high-affinity OX1R binders. All code and data are available at https://github.com/TheoreticalHarpist/orexin-ligand-virtual-screening (DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20599023)

papers.title: Directional Alternating Current Electrophoresis on Paper Driven by Spatially Non-Uniform Electric Fields
papers.abstract: Electrokinetic mechanisms are known to enrich a variety of analytes in paper-based media, yet localized, membrane-free enrichment of small charged analytes has remained an unmet capability. Recently, we reported biased–alternating current electrophoresis (b-ACEP), a new electrokinetic mechanism, different from dielectrophoresis, in which spatially non-uniform AC electric fields generate time-averaged, directional electrophoretic migration of small charged analytes. Here, we establish the first paper-based implementation of this mechanism (pb-ACEP) and demonstrate that b-ACEP remains operative in aqueous, porous cellulose substrates. Using screen-printed orthogonal electrodes to generate controlled AC field gradients, pb-ACEP enables rapid and localized enrichment of diverse charged analytes, including dyes, proteins, and nucleic acids. We observe up to 410-fold enrichment of xylene cyanol blue, 240-fold for hemoglobin, 150-fold for immunoglobulin G, and 50-fold for double-stranded DNA within minutes. Systematic control studies confirm the electrophoretic origin of pb-ACEP by excluding convective flow, dielectrophoretic effects, and Faradaic reactions, while voltage–frequency sweeps reveal tunable enrichment behavior consistent with theoretical predictions for AC-field–driven electrophoresis. Together, these results establish pb-ACEP as a fundamental and generalizable electrokinetic mechanism that enables high-efficiency, membrane-free, and spatially localized enrichment of charged analytes in porous media. This work expands the capabilities of AC-field electrophoresis and provides a new modality for chemical and biochemical sample manipulation, with implications for improving the sensitivity of paper-based assays and other point-of-care analytical systems.

papers.title: Four-Electron Reduction of O2 at a Single Metal Center: Redox Chemistry of a Uranium(II) Synthon
papers.abstract: Supporting Information Placeholder ABSTRACT: One-electron reduction of the N,N’-tethered U(III) complex κ2:η6-LArUI(THF) (A), featuring a ligand imposed η6arene-metal interaction, generates the reduced species [K(2.2.2-cryptand)][(κ2:η6-LAr)UI] (1) in good yield. Complex 1 exhibits severe structural distortion of the anchored arene moiety, indicating ligand-based rather than metal-centered reduction. In line with this, close inspection of the structural parameters of 1 reveals bond localization consistent with two-electron reduction of the arene concomitant with reduction-induced oxidation of the metal center, giving a formally U(IV) complex. Nonetheless, 1 is a potent U(II) synthon capable of four-electron transfer chemistry, activating the small molecules PhN3, PhNO, and O2 to yield the multiply bonded, hexavalent products trans-(κ2:η6-LAr)U(NPh)2 (3) and trans-(κ2-LAr)U(E)(E’)(THF) (E = NPh, E’ = O (4); and E = E’ = O (5)). The formation of mononuclear uranyl complex 5 is especially significant, as it constitutes the first reported example of O2 activation via four-electron transfer from a single f-element center.

papers.title: Ultrahigh Molecular Weight Fluorescent Copolymers as Injectable Biomaterials
papers.abstract: Injectable fluorescent polymers enable real-time surgical guidance and bioimaging, but simultaneously achieving high transparency, low cellular uptake, clinically practical viscosity, and long-term hydrolytic stability remains challenging. We report ultrahigh molecular weight (UHMW, > 106 g mol-1) fluorescent copolymers synthesized by photoiniferter reversible addition-fragmentation chain-transfer (RAFT) polymerization as injectable biomaterials, with a focus on fluorescent ophthalmic viscosurgical devices (OVDs). Dissipative particle dynamics (eDPD) simulations of diblock and random architectures revealed that fluorophore-rich segments collapse and drive aggregation and self-quenching, identifying random monomer distribution and low fluorophore loading as key design levers. Guided by these simulations, N,N-dimethylacrylamide (DMA) was copolymerized with fluorescein acrylate (FluA) at low loading (0.1–1 mol%) to yield poly(DMA-co-FluA) with molecular weights from ∼50 kDa to 1.4 MDa and bright green fluorescence under blue illumination. Comparison with (meth)acrylate analogues (OEGA, CEA, DMAEMA) showed that the acrylamide backbone uniquely combines hydrolytic stability, optical clarity, and access to UHMW. The 1.4 MDa copolymer matched commercial Healon GV viscosity at ∼30 wt%, retained shear-thinning injectability, and exhibited markedly lower HEK293 cellular internalization than the 50 kDa analogue while preserving viability. Ex vivo porcine-eye cataract surgery confirmed intraoperative visualization under cobalt-blue light, enabling OVD removal verification.

papers.title: Signal-performance physics is redundant with structure for predicting realized moth pheromone chemical space: a pre-registered honest-negative and the biosynthetic bound that remains
papers.abstract: Why does the chemical space of insect sex pheromones look the way it does? A natural hypothesis, implicit in six decades of chemical ecology, is that realized pheromones are the molecules that are both biosynthetically reachable and good signals: that signal-performance physics (volatility, active-space range, channel specificity) selects which reachable molecules nature uses. We test this directly and pre-registered, for the Type-I fatty-acyl pheromones of moths (the ~75% of species using C10-C18 acetates, alcohols, and aldehydes). We build a validated forward biosynthetic enumerator (a mechanistic desaturase / chain-shortening / terminal toolkit, checked against a 7-route enzymology panel) that defines the reachable set, and three validated performance oracles: vapor pressure (SIMPOL.1), a Bossert-Wilson active-space manifold (continuous-source range and equal-burst persistence, with Fuller-Schettler-Giddings diffusivity), and a combinatorial channelspecificity axis. Against a gold-curated, primary-cited sample of 35 distinct realized components from 11 genera (34 within the reachable set), we ask whether performance predicts which reachable molecules are realized, beyond molecular size and unsaturation. It does not. Volatility and active-space specificity add no cross-validated skill over structure; the lone apparent volatility signal is collinear with unsaturation and carries no unique information; the directional Bossert-Wilson specificity prediction is not supported. This reproduces, in chemical ecology, the RNA-morphospace result that arrival/findability dominates selection. What does separate realized from reachable is biosynthetic: realized pheromones are reachable in few desaturase-enzyme events, and against a biosynthetically realistic background the residual structural separation is modest. We also report a completeness wall that makes the stronger “predict unrealized molecules” question infeasible from current pheromone data, and a methodological trap (an enumerator’s polyene tail can manufacture a false performance signal) that any chemical-morphospace occupancy study must control. The contribution is a validated, reusable reachability-and-performance pipeline and a rigorous negative: in single-component Type-I space, realized pheromone identity is bounded by biosynthesis and dominated by findability, not tuned by signal-performance physics.

papers.title: Unlocking Temperature Insights in Mechanochemistry by Raman Thermometry
papers.abstract: Temperature critically influences mechanochemical reactivity, yet the thermal conditions experienced by molecules during ball milling remain largely unknown because reactions occur in sealed, dynamically agitated vessels that preclude direct measurement. Here, we introduce Raman thermometry as a powerful new, contactless, in situ method for mechanochemistry that enables direct measurement of the temperature of reaction mixtures inside a ball mill. The approach exploits the temperature dependence of the anti-Stokes to Stokes Raman intensity ratio, enabling temperature determination from the material under milling without perturbing the reaction environment. We confirm the stability and accuracy of the method through systematic calibration and demonstrate its efficacy across a diverse range of representative reactions. By enabling the first direct look at the thermal evolution of milling processes, this method paves the way for the mechanistic understanding, rational design, and scaling of mechanochemical synthesis.

papers.title: A Tale of Two Titanocenes: Distinct Ultrafast Relaxation Pathways across Titanium(IV) Chloride LMCT Photocatalysts
papers.abstract: Recent interest in ligand-to-metal charge transfer photocatalysts (LMCT PCs), which generate radical species upon photoinduced bond homolysis, has manifested in a variety of chemical transformations leveraging distinct combinations of high valent metals and redox-active ligands. Recent work on Ti(IV) complexes, both titanocenes and homoleptic titanium chlorides, provide a lens for investigating how variation of the ligand identity, molecular structure, and symmetry affects ultrafast photochemical reactivity and decay pathways. This work employs a combination of ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy and computational modeling to elucidate the photophysical relaxation pathways in TiCl62-, TiCpCl3, and TiCp2Cl2. The pathways that compete with photoinduced bond homolysis vary within this series from ultrafast relaxation to the GS to relaxation within the ES manifold, and in some cases depend on the wavelength of visible light used to excite the photocatalyst. Together, these results emphasize how LMCT photoreactivity can be switched or augmented with rational ligand selection.

papers.title: In Silico Study of Degradation in Host Molecular Materials for OLEDs
papers.abstract: We perform an in-depth computational study of degradation processes occurring during OLED operation for three commonly used emissive-layer host molecules: TBSO (4-(mtolylsulfonyl)-1,1-biphenyl), DPPCarba (9-(3,5-diphenylphenyl)carbazole), and DPPTriphen (2-(3,5diphenylphenyl)triphenylene). The investigation is carried out from both static and dynamic viewpoints. In the static framework, we evaluate thermodynamic descriptors that allow us to analyze possible chemical degradation pathways in the ground state, charged states, first excited states, and after exciton–polaron annihilation (EPA) and exciton–exciton annihilation (EEA). In the dynamic framework, non-adiabatic molecular dynamics (NAMD) simulations are used to follow degradation starting from both the first excited state and a higher-lying excited state representative of an EEA process. Furthermore, machine-learning-accelerated NAMD (ML-NAMD) simulations are employed to enhance the sampling of degradation pathways in TBSO. Combining static descriptors with direct and ML-accelerated dynamics provides molecular-level insight into chemical degradation mechanisms in OLED host materials and highlights the importance of going beyond static stability criteria when assessing degradation. These findings can support the rational design of more stable host materials for next-generation OLEDs.

papers.title: Heat or Speed? Decoupling Thermal and Motion Contributions to Er3+ Upconversion
papers.abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated that upconverting nanoparticles (UCNPs) can be used as nanoscale motion sensors exploiting motion-induced changes in luminescence intensity ratios (LIRs). In addition, UCNPs are well established as powerful luminescent probes for LIR-based thermal sensing. This work investigates aspects of angular motion and temperature and elucidates mechanisms of cross-coupling with the goal of designing decoupling strategies, including dual-readout schemes for orthogonal sensing. To this end, Er 3+ /Yb 3+ -codoped NaGdF 4 UCNPs were systematically investigated, confirming that the green-to-red LIR of the Er 3+ emission is affected by stirring, allowing for motion sensing, however, only under known thermal conditions. Conversely, the population and depopulation kinetics of the Er 3+ ion’s 4 F 9/2 → 4 I 15/2 transition show stirring dependence that is unaffected by temperature, with relative angular motion sensitivities (S r rpm ) of up to ca. 3% per 100 rpm. In parallel, the commonly applied green-to-green LIR using the Er 3+ ion’s 2 H 11/2 → 4 I 15/2 and 4 S 3/2 → 4 I 15/2 transitions for thermal sensing is found to be more robust than the green-to-red LIR under varying stirring conditions. For this to hold true, it is crucial to eliminate any contribution of the 2 H 9/2 → 4 I 13/2 transition at 558 nm, being affected by motion. Overall, we here unveil the underlaying mechanism of stirring-dependent Er 3+ upconversion and propose a strategy to decouple thermal and motion contributions, thereby opening new avenues toward dual sensors and nanotechnologies with potential relevance for, e.g., biomedical or microfluidic applications.

papers.title: High-Performance, High-Angular-Momentum K Engine on Graphics Processing Units
papers.abstract: Exchange matrix construction remains one of the main bottlenecks in GPU-accelerated Hartree-Fock and hybrid density-functional calculations, particularly when high-angular-momentum basis functions are used. Traditional recursive electron repulsion integral (ERI) algorithms minimize operation counts on CPUs, but on GPUs they generate a large number of intermediates, leading to high register pressure, memory traffic, and poor hardware utilization. Here, we present a novel GPU engine for the exchange matrix ( K ) construction designed to circumvent these limitations specifically for high-angular-momentum ERIs. The central component is a reformulation of the McMurchie-Davidson (MD) scheme as a fused double-Matrix Multiply (MatMul), allowing the most expensive high-angular-momentum contractions to be mapped onto the high-throughput Tensor Core hardware of modern accelerators while eliminating intermediate global memory traffic. Using low-level control over matrix multiply-accumulate instructions, we further introduce a specialized primitive-screening strategy that reduces unnecessary work while preserving the dense arithmetic structure required for high throughput. By combining this MD-MatMul engine with a Head-Gordon-Pople scheme for low-angular-momentum classes, our hybrid approach provides a high-performance approach for K-matrix formation up to g -functions. Benchmarks on NVIDIA H200 GPUs demonstrate that our K -engine, integrated with our previously developed J -engine, consistently outperforms existing GPU implementations in QUICK and GPU4PySCF. Across a variety of linear and globular systems, we observe speedups ranging from 1.1-3.1x over GPU4PySCF and 10.7-58.5x over QUICK across triple- and quadruple-ζ basis sets.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Automated Mass Spectral Analysis using NucleoSpec for Compositional Assignment of Nucleic Acid-Silver Complexes and Nanoclusters
papers.abstract: Nucleic acid–metal complexes, such as DNA-stabilized silver nanoclusters (DNA-Ag N ) and Ag(I)-mediated DNA duplexes, show promise for applications ranging from biomedical imaging to bioelectronics and sensing. Electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI-MS) is a powerful tool for precisely resolving their compositions, but the data analysis procedure can be challenging and time-consuming. No general-purpose software can automatically assign compositions of nucleic acid-silver complexes, most notably for DNA-Ag N , whose masses depend on the oxidation state of the silver core. We address these challenges by developing an automated data analysis workflow for ESI-MS of nucleic acid–silver complexes. This tutorial presents the analysis workflow and introduces NucleoSpec, an open-source, web-based platform that consolidates charge state determination, constraint-based composition enumeration, isotope-pattern matching, and adduct/conjugate handling into a single browser-accessible interface. The platform is benchmarked on published molecular formulae determined by manual analysis for DNA-Ag N , xeno-nucleic acid stabilized Ag N (XNA-Ag N ), nucleic acid–Ag(I) complexes, and chemically modified DNA-Ag N , reproducing assignments to single-proton precision (median centroid offset of 0.03 m/z) for spectra of adequate signal-to-noise. Low-signal peaks for which adjacent valence electron counts become difficult to distinguish are flagged by NucleoSpec for user inspection. By lowering the barrier to high-resolution compositional analysis and supporting integration into high-throughput pipelines, NucleoSpec addresses a key experimental bottleneck in informatics-guided design of nucleic acid–metal complexes.

papers.title: Cooperative Water Sorption with Size-Dependent Phase Changes in Copper Triazolate Nanoparticles
papers.abstract: Passive, sorption-based atmospheric water harvesting technologies (AWHTs) are hotly pursued as a strategy to replace energy intensive condensation-based technologies. Chemically tunable metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) offer an effective solution, but current design strategies are bottlenecked by high enthalpies of adsorption and structural requirements such as large pore volumes. Here, we report that phase-change induced water sorption in copper-triazolate MOF nanoparticles is facilitated by structural flexibility imparted by Cu2+ centers and demonstrates low adsorption enthalpies (48 kJ/mol) and excellent cyclability. Together, these results present a novel water sorption mechanism for MOF nanoparticles that underscores the importance of sizedependent lattice flexibility in porous materials.

papers.title: Humidity-Robust Antisolvent Search for Perovskite Thin-Film Fabrication via Human-AI-Robot Collaboration
papers.abstract: Reproducible fabrication of halide perovskite thin films remains challenging due to humidity-sensitivity, limiting translation from controlled laboratory processing to robust ambient manufacturing. Antisolvent engineering is central to controlling perovskite crystallization, yet selection remains empirical, literature-biased, and difficult to generalize because many commercial solvent candidates lack curated physical-property data. This study reports a robot-validated artificial intelligence (AI) workflow for discovering humidity-robust processing windows of perovskite thin films using darkness and heterogeneity metrics. Starting from over 10,000 commercial solvent products, human-guided data-source screening identifies liquid, chemically defined candidates compatible with antisolvent processing. A molecular-descriptor-based classifier, trained on a literature-derived baseline of reported perovskite antisolvents, then prioritizes candidates without requiring complete physical-property data. Subsequent practicality screening based on cost, hazard, handling feasibility, and humidity-relevant properties identifies ethyl 4-chlorophenylacetate for robotic validation. Under controlled spin coating at 5% and 75% relative humidity, this antisolvent produces phase-pure, dark, and macroscopically uniform films, outperforming chlorobenzene, a benchmark antisolvent, under high humidity. An automated image-derived darkness–uniformity score combined with Gaussian process regression reveals a broader low-score processing window across antisolvent volume, drop time, drop height, and humidity. This work reframes antisolvent selection as a robot-validated AI search for robust processing windows in environmentally sensitive solution-processed semiconductors.

papers.title: Facile Approach to Geminal Bisperoxides via BR3/O2-Enabled Peroxidation of Aldehydes
papers.abstract: A trialkylborane/O 2 -enabled peroxidation of aldehydes for the selective synthesis of geminal bisperoxides is reported. A range of geminal bisperoxides was obtained in high yields (up to >99%) from simple precursors. The synthetic utility was demonstrated through their diverse transformations into azidoperoxides, cyanoperoxides, peroxyesters, esters, and carboxylic acids. Mechanistic studies support the involvement of a radical pathway.

papers.title: Tensor–Guided Lattice Exploration (TGLE): Directed Crystal Structure Search Based on Elastic Eigenmodes
papers.abstract: The discovery of crystal structures that combine thermodynamic stability with superior mechanical performance remains a central challenge in materials science. We introduce Tensor–Guided Lattice Exploration (TGLE), a physics-informed crystal structure prediction framework that employs elastic eigenmodes derived from the computed 6× 6 stiffness tensor to drive directed lattice deformation along the softest (or hardest) modes. This physically motivated pathway systematically steers the exploration toward structures with enhanced mechanical properties—including increased Vickers hardness and elastic moduli—which constitutes a distinctive feature of the method. We demonstrate TGLE through six chemical systems: four transition-metal borides (Nb–B, Cr–B, Mo–B, and Mn–B) relevant to superhard materials design, and two wellcharacterised validation systems (Ni–Al and Si–O). In Nb–B, a single steering step triggers a symmetry-increasing phase transition (P31m→ P 6̄2m) that triples the predicted hardness from 10.7 to 30.9 GPa. Across all boride campaigns, TGLE identifies seven candidate structures with MLIP-predicted Hv > 30 GPa. To validate the MLIP-based screening, we perform full DFT calculations (VASP, PBE, stress–strain elastic tensors) on all seven candidates, followed by phonon stability analysis using the finite-displacement method (Phonopy + VASP). Four candidates are confirmed as both mechanically and dynamically stable hard materials: Mo2B8 Immm (Hv = 36.4 GPa), Nb3B5 P 6̄2m (Hv = 33.4 GPa), Cr2B6 P 3̄m1 (Hv = 32.8 GPa), and Mo4B8 R3̄m (Hv = 28.1 GPa). The three unstable candidates—both Mn-containing structures and the thermodynamically metastable Mo2B10—exhibit imaginary phonon modes, underscoring the importance of multi-level validation (MLIP → DFT elasticity → phonon stability). DFT formation energies agree with MLIP predictions to within |∆Ef | = 0.018 eV/atom. A direct benchmark against the USPEX evolutionary algorithm in the Nb–B system shows that TGLE recovers 3 of 6 known experimental phases with exact space group symmetry (vs. 0/6 for USPEX) and discovers hard candidates that energy-driven search overlooks, while USPEX provides more thorough thermodynamic coverage. The two approaches are complementary. TGLE is calculator-agnostic; the present implementation uses the GRACE-2L universal potential for rapid screening, with DFT validation of the top candidates.

papers.title: How Does Termination Proceed in Methacrylate Radical Polymerization?
papers.abstract: Radical polymerization termination mechanisms fundamentally govern polymer properties, yet remain contentious for methacrylate despite decades of study. Through systematic synthesis of model compounds and polymers, we establish definitive NMR fingerprints (e.g., 51.23 ppm for head-to-head quaternary carbon) to distinguish all potential termination pathways in methacrylate polymerization. Multidimensional characterization (1H/13C/DEPT135 NMR, HSQC, HMBC, MALDI-TOF, SEC) of BPO/AIBN-initiated poly(alkyl methacrylate)s reveals three key findings: First, chain transfer (kct) dominates the pathways through which propagating radicals are converted into dead polymers (51-85% contribution), generating saturated chain ends without radical consumption. Second, minor pathways include primary radical disproportionation (ktd-pi) between primary radicals and propagating radicals, and bimolecular disproportionation (ktd-ij) between propagating radicals via β-methyl hydrogen transfer. Third, no detectable evidence exists for either bimolecular combination (ktc-ij) or primary radical combination (ktc-pi), contradicting classical paradigms. The findings demonstrate that the dominant chain transfer pathway, by maintaining radical populations without consumption, provides a plausible alternative explanation for the observed runaway polymerization phenomena in industrial MMA systems. This contrasts with the classical 'trapped radical' hypothesis and could offer new insights for process safety optimization. The invariant NMR fingerprints across PMMA/PEMA/PtBMA establish a universal termination framework for 1,1-disubstituted monomers, enabling safety optimization in industrial processes.

papers.title: Electron-catalysed supramolecular assembly with high efficiency, robustness and versatility
papers.abstract: Although catalysis is widely exploited by nature to orchestrate noncovalent supramolecular assembly and build up complex living systems, its utilisation in synthetic chemistry has conventionally been limited to accelerating covalent reactions. Consequently, the development of artificial systems for catalytic assembly remains a formidable and largely unexplored challenge. Here, we present a rationally designed strategy of electron-catalysed supramolecular assembly, wherein the electron acts as an efficient, robust, and versatile catalyst to accelerate the formation of a donor–acceptor complex. Optimisation of the elementary steps and intermediate stability yields an efficient catalytic cycle, furnishing the process with both a high turnover number and operational robustness in open air. Furthermore, the electron catalysis can be readily triggered by diverse external stimuli—including electricity, light and mechanical force—enabling precise spatiotemporal control over the assembly process and near-quantitative synthesis of supramolecular complexes. Collectively, this work establishes a well-elucidated strategy of catalytic assembly with remarkable practicality, advancing the frontiers of noncovalent synthetic chemistry.

papers.title: Technoeconomic and Geospatial Analysis of Biogas Utilization for Enhancing Ammonia Production Competitiveness of the United States
papers.abstract: The US ammonia industry faces vulnerabilities, including volatility in the prices of natural gas – the primary feedstock for ammonia – and geopolitical risks, given that the US is a net importer of ammonia. This paper presents detailed studies on the prospect of partially offsetting these risks by boosting local ammonia production from waste-derived biogas, such as landfill gas and agricultural waste. Rigorous process design in Aspen Plus and technoeconomic evaluation were used to contrast emerging technologies (autothermal reforming, catalytic partial oxidation, methane pyrolysis, chemical looping) with the conventional technology, steam methane reforming (SMR), for hydrogen generation to produce biogas-derived ammonia. The results show that the energy efficiency of producing ammonia from biogas feed ranges from 33.6 to 67.7% on a methane basis, encompassing the reported value for natural gas feed (57%), demonstrating a pathway to standalone and retrofit drop-in solutions. Production costs varied considerably across technological pathways, with common drivers such as feedstock costs and capital investment accounting for 40%+ and 22%+, respectively. Biogas-based SMR shows the lowest minimum ammonia selling price (MASP) of $510 t⋅NH 3 -1 , followed by chemical looping reforming ($568 t⋅NH 3 -1 ). Methane pyrolysis showcases the highest energy efficiency of 60.7% (biogas basis) by combusting carbon black byproduct to meet thermal energy demand, followed by SMR (59.4%). Further, we show through geospatial sensitivity studies that economies of scale are the major driver for state-level differences in MASP, with electricity cost also playing a significant role in states with high electricity prices, such as California. The state of Texas shows the lowest MASP for four out of five technology options. This work has practical relevance to stakeholders looking to develop new ammonia facilities in the US or retrofit existing ones. Our technology evaluations are also relevant to other ammonia projects worldwide. This study outlines a comprehensive methodology for comparative technology evaluation, including energy efficiency and economic analyses, that is extensible to other processes for manufacturing commodity chemicals or fuels.

papers.title: A Vision-Language Agentic Pipeline for Lead Optimization: Defence-in-Depth Chemistry Gates and Cross-Provider Model Evaluation
papers.abstract: Background: Lead optimization in small-molecule drug discovery is a constrained search problem: from a chemical starting point and the structural cues of its binding pose, propose analogs that preserve the pharmacophore, satisfy ADMET liabilities, and remain synthetically accessible. Individual components such as pharmacophore alignment, SMIRKS transformation libraries, ADMET predictors, scaffold analysis, and structural-alert filters are mature, but the orchestration of these tools into a reproducible workflow that takes a lead and its ligand interaction diagram (LID) as input and returns a ranked, filtered analog set is non-trivial. Methods: We describe a twelve-stage agentic pipeline that combines a vision-language classifier of LIDs with a per-instance SMARTS construction step, deterministic structural gates, a curated 479-entry SMIRKS transformation library, an upstream ADMET-prediction backbone, and a synthetic-accessibility-anchored ranking. The architectural contribution is defence-indepth: each agent stage is wrapped by a deterministic gate (chemistry-validity allowlists, soft Murcko ring-topology check, PAINS / Brenk structural-alert filters, ADMET-screen thresholds) so that perception errors cannot corrupt the downstream analog set. Results: Across five evaluations: (i) a curated single-edit bioisosteric matched-molecular-pair pilot on which the library exact-recovers 16/30=53.3%of documented improving transformations; (ii) an unbiased ChEMBL-37–derived MMP scale-up of 2,000 pairs on which it exact-recovers15.5% with mean best Tanimoto-to-target 0.755 in misses;(iii)a129marketed-drug scaffold-preservation and structural-alert audit showing the soft Murcko gate cuts the analog set roughly in half while raising scaffold preservation to 100 %; (iv) a vision language classifier self-consistency study on a fixed LID (pairwise Jaccard 1.00 across all 28 pair-comparisons, zero chemistry-validator drops); and (v) an end-to-end case study on two contrasting leads (DYRK1A kinase inhibitor and Linezolid antibacterial), in which a LID-aware run improves the rank-1 analog on both Pareto-style score (0.586 →0.638) and synthetic accessibility (2.51 → 2.32). The defence-in-depth design preserves end-to-end output quality despite intermediate-stage variability. We additionally benchmark eleven language models across the three agent stages and report which configurations achieve reliable strict-JSON adherence and self-consistency, providing measured rather than asserted recommendations for the production default. Conclusions: The pipeline demonstrates that a small set of deterministic structural gates around language-model agent stages is sufficient to absorb vision-classifier errors and produce constrained, pharmacophore-preserving lead optimization output on multiple target classes. The platform is implemented as production software; the code, data, manifest-stamped raw outputs, and reproduction scripts are released open source under the MIT licence at https:// github.com/Nimieeee/lead-optimizer-paper.

papers.title: Thermally Activated Modification of Polylactide with Reactive Polysiloxanes: The Role of semi-IPN Structure in the Brittle–Ductile Transition
papers.abstract: Polylactide (PLA) has garnered significant attention as a potentially sustainable substitute for conventional petrochemical polymers. This attention is attributed to several factors, including its renewable origin, biodegradability, and its compatibility with conventional polymer processing techniques. However, its inherent fragility restricts its broader utilization as an engineering plastic. In this study, the investigation focused on the thermally activated reactive modification of PLA with two functional polysiloxanes of varying molecular architectures. This modification was explored as a toughening strategy, with the objective of promoting the brittle-to-ductile (BD) transition through the formation of a semi-interpenetrating polymer network (semi-IPN) within the PLA matrix. Extraction, thermal, spectroscopic, and morphological analyses were conducted to confirm the formation of semi-IPN structures entangled with PLA. The micromechanical deformation mechanisms of pristine and toughened PLA under tension, bending, and impact forces are discussed, revealing that the dispersion level, size of dispersed phase, molecular weight, and reactivity of the introduced soft phase strongly influence rheological and mechanical performance, leading to markedly improved mechanical performance. For instance, impact strength reaches 37 kJ/m2 at 1 wt.% MOD1 and elongation at break increases to 90% at 5 wt.% MOD2.

papers.title: Engineering Conditional Peptide Self-Assembly Using AlphaFold
papers.abstract: Programming self-assembly from peptide sequence remains difficult because existing design rules are only weakly predictive of emergent supramolecular behaviour. Here, we show that AlphaFold Multimer can be used to engineer conditional peptide self-assembly by simultaneously selecting for co-assembly and against assembly of the individual components. Using model confidence metrics as proxies for assembly propensity, we designed peptide pairs that largely remain unstructured in isolation, but form defined tape-like nanostructures upon mixing. Experimental measurements including circular dichroism, small-angle X-ray scattering and cryo-electron microscopy validate the predicted behaviour across multiple systems. These results establish artificial intelligence-guided design as a practical route to programmable supramolecular peptide materials.

papers.title: Effect of Surface Topography and Hydrophobicity on the Entropy of Individual Interfacial Water
papers.abstract: Water entropy plays a crucial role in solvation thermodynamics and influences processes such as hydrophobic collapse, molecular recognition, and ligand binding. Understanding how local water entropy responds to surface geometry and chemistry is key to developing molecularly interpretable models of the hydrophobic effect. Here, we employ a method developed in our group to compute the translational and rotational entropies of individual water molecules in the hydration layer of three classes of model interfaces: hydrophobic cavities, curved nonpolar sheets with controlled curvature, and graphene based interfaces with tunable water–surface interactions. Within hydrophobic cavities, the translational water entropy exceeds that of bulk water and increases with cavity depth up to 0.75 nm, beyond which it declines as dewetting reduces water occupancy at greater depths, whereas the rotational entropy is reduced near the surface but partially recovers at greater depths. For curved hydrophobic sheets represented by hexagonal lattices with curvature values κ = 0, 0.61, and 1.23 nm −1 , both entropic components vary with curvature, with water near concave (negative curvature) surfaces exhibiting higher entropy than near convex ones. Likewise, for graphene sheets with different curvatures and hydrophobicities, the water entropy increases near the more hydrophobic and concave regions. Overall, our results demonstrate that curvature and hydrophobicity act together to shape the structure and dynamics of the hydration layer, with concave nonpolar surfaces promoting higher water entropy than flat or convex surfaces.

papers.title: Simulated Chain-Growth Polymerization of PEG Nanogels: Understanding the Formation of Network Topology
papers.abstract: The structure of a network polymer determines its properties and behavior. And the formation of network topology depends on the chemistry and process during the polymerization. In this study, we described an in silico polymerization approach based on molecular dynamics simulation. The approach also incorporated the description of network topology using graph theory to monitor and even control the network formation. As a study case, the chain growth polymerization of poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) nanogels is simulated and the impact of the reaction time and concentration of reactants on the topological features of the nanogels are analyzed. When the monomer concentration increases, the percentage of defects, including dangling chains, primary loops and excessive chains in secondary loops, decreases. Moreover, the reactant concentration also has a strong influence on the resulting network topology, leading to a higher percentage of smaller cycles.

papers.title: Phenol-Driven Modulation for the Synthesis of a Plant-based Titanium Metal-Organic Framework
papers.abstract: Titanium-based metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) stand out owing to their hydrolytic stability and promising photocatalytic properties. However, the high reactivity of titanium precursors has limited their discovery to a comparably small number of structures reported to date. Strongly coordinating chelate linkers, such as ellagic acid (EA), amplify the synthetic difficulty of controlled crystal growth. To tackle this challenge, we employed an untapped modulator in MOF chemistry – phenol – which enabled the isolation of a new Ti-based MOF. TUW-11 (TUW = TU Wien) is built up of monometallic Ti4+ centers strongly bound by EA, resulting in a layered, honeycomb-like microporous framework. The underlying structure was determined by three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED), together with synchrotron X-ray techniques and scanning transmission electron microscopy. Furthermore, optoelectronic properties were studied thoroughly, and promising performance towards light-assisted dye removal reactions could be demonstrated using visible light.

papers.title: Repurposing GC-MS as a High-Temperature Micro-Reactor for the Catalyst-Free, Gas-Phase Synthesis of Vitamin E
papers.abstract: Gas-phase synthesis offers a transformative, solvent-free alternative to traditional solution-based organic reactions, aligning with the growing demand for sustainable and atom-economical chemical processes. Vitamin E is a critical bioactive molecule essential for antioxidant defense, cardiovascular health, and cellular signaling; however, its traditional synthesis remains resource intensive. In this study, we demonstrate a novel, catalyst-free, gas-phase synthesis of vitamin E analog by repurposing Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS) as both a high-temperature micro-reactor and an analytical platform. By leveraging the thermal environment of the GC injector port, the precursor hexa-2,4-dienal undergoes a rapid molecular assembly—likely via a thermally induced Diels-Alder [4+2] cycloaddition and subsequent dehydrative cascade—to form the chromane scaffold. Structural confirmation was achieved through high-resolution chromatographic retention data and mass spectral analysis, yielding a 947-match factor against the NIST Mass Spectral Library.

papers.title: Twelve Precisely Arranged Components in a Switchable Cyclic Molecular Daisy Chain
papers.abstract: Cyclic molecular daisy chains (DCs), which function as prototypical artificial molecular muscles in mechanically interlocked molecules (MIMs), hold substantial potential for advancing bio-inspired molecular machines and smart materials. However, the precise synthesis of DCs with more than 4 components remains a significant challenge, and strategies for sequence control are still underdeveloped. Here we report a controllable growth strategy employing tailored [2]rotaxane building blocks to achieve two key advances: the synthesis of DCs comprising up to 12 components and precise sequence control that allows for the formation of sequence-isomeric structures. These programmable molecular architectures demonstrate anion-responsive behavior, establishing them as ideal platforms for next-generation smart materials and nanoscale devices. Our method provides a general route for engineering complex molecular machines with customized functions. Introduction As recognized by the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, mechanically interlocked molecules (MIMs),[1-10] particularly rotaxanes and catenanes, have proven to be privileged platforms for the construction of molecular machines.[11-23] Since first proposed by Stoddart in 1998[24] and explored as molecular muscles by Sauvage in 2000[25], cyclic molecular daisy chains ([cn]DCs, where n represents the number of individual components), especially the [c2] type, have emerged as the most typical molecular muscle units.[26-31] These have been further employed as key building blocks for constructing novel (supra)polymeric materials with attractive stimuli-responsive or mechanical properties for various applications.[32-40] Moreover, for [cn] daisy chains with even more components (n≥3), due to their unique cyclic interlocked structures, rich co-conformations, and controllable motion behaviors, they could serve as ideal candidates for mimicking biomolecular machines such as the tail complex of bacteriophages.[41-44] Primarily owing to synthetic difficulties, they have been, however, rarely explored (Figure 1a).[45-47] In addition, multicomponent [cn] daisy chains with defined sequences similar as the sequence isomerism in biomacromolecules were not reported, though sequence engineering has evolved as an efficient strategy towards the creation of matters with tunable properties and functions. Given their potential, developing a new synthetic strategy for cyclic molecular daisy chains, particularly with controlled size and sequence, is highly important.

papers.title: The environmental impact of mycotoxin analysis: Evaluating the greenness of liquid chromatography mass spectrometry
papers.abstract: Food safety relies on extensive analytical measurements, while the environmental impact caused remains unclear. In this study, we evaluated the greenness of liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS), the analytical workhorse for mycotoxin screening, using the AGREE metric paired with a carbon footprint (CF) estimate for instrument operation and solvent use. Using manufacturer specifications for a routine setup, we estimate that a single system emits 30 t CO2 per year at 8,000 samples, with 6 t arising from the instrument being on standby, as operated by authors in their laboratory. We show that electricity consumption dominates the CF, whereas solvent consumption contributes 2% to the estimated total CF. Supplying the same workload with solar electricity can lowers annual emissions to ~4 t (≈86% reduction), emphasizing the usage of decarbonized power. Only a moderate influence of multi analyte LC-MS based screening on the AGREE metric was found. Contrary to that the CF estimation showed that increasing the number of analytes per analysis can markedly reduce emissions. We show that LC-MS sustainability can be improved through method optimization by expanding the number of target analytes, shortening analysis times, and reducing system stand-by, when screening food and feed for residues or contaminants such as mycotoxins. In this way, analytical laboratories can already lower their environmental footprint without investing into new equipment or switching to greener solvents.

papers.title: Optically Addressable Spins in a Metal−Organic Framework
papers.abstract: Molecular spins supporting optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) offer unique opportunities for quantum sensing and many body physics by combining the sensitivity and spatial resolution offered by optical spin detection with the capacity for bottom-up assembly and chemical control. Metal−organic frameworks (MOFs) are a promising architecture to leverage such opportunities since they offer control over spin placement, tunable porosity and large internal surface areas for efficient integration with sensing targets, and a richly tunable chemical space. However, optical spin readout has not been demonstrated in a MOF. Here, we report the first successful optical detection of spins in a MOF. We use a porphyrin-based aluminum MOF (Al-PMOF) which supports efficient triplet generation on the porphyrin chromophore ligands. Using electron paramagnetic resonance, we demonstrate that these triplet states support a spin coherence time ( T 2 ) on the order of a few microseconds at 50 K. Importantly, we successfully detect optically detected magnetic resonance of these triplets, using nearinfrared ODMR at 77 K. Optical spin readout in a MOF paves the way for next-generation quantum sensing applications which leverage bottom-up assembly.

papers.title: Engineering Near-Quantitative Bidirectional Switching and Z-isomer Stability in Arylazopyrazoles through Cooperative Non-Covalent Interactions
papers.abstract: The limited thermal stability of Z -isomers in reversible E / Z photochromic systems deters their broader functional applications. Here we report a family of arylazo-1,3,5-triphenylpyrazole photoswitches that exhibit rapid E → Z , red-light-induced, and near-quantitative bidirectional switching with tunable Z -isomer thermal lifetimes. Notably, the nitro-substituted derivative enables bidirectional visible-light-mediated switching, exhibiting blue light-activated forward isomerization and far-red (740 nm) light-induced reversal within the biological optical window. Single-crystal X-ray structures of both the E - and thermally metastable Z -isomers were resolved for all halogen-substituted derivatives, providing rare structural insight into T-type photochromic systems. The crystal structures reveal distinct "favorably twisted” conformations of the Z -isomer stabilized by cooperative noncovalent π···π stacking, C-X···π, and C-H···X interactions, establishing a general strategy for Z -isomer stabilization. Theoretical studies support that the thermal Z → E relaxation proceeds via a ground-state in-plane inversion mechanism.

papers.title: Isolation and Structure Elucidation of Cytotoxic Compounds, Sukumolides A-C, derived from Deep Sea Marine Invertebrates Collected in Kochi
Computation of the D1 Excited-State Formation Mechanism in Radical-Based Organic Light-Emitting Diodes
papers.abstract: Radical-based organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) emit from a doublet excited state, D1, enabling spin-allowed radiative decay without the singlet-triplet exciton constraints of closed-shell emitters. However, the charge-mediated pathways by which D1 is populated under electrical excitation from D0 remain unclear. Here we investigate, by means of quantum-chemical calculations and Marcus-type theoretical modelling, how competing charge-mediated pathways populate the emissive D1 state in three TTM-based radical emitters: TTM-1Cz, TTM-3PCz, and TTM-3NCz. We compare anion-mediated, cation-mediated, charge-charge annihilation, and excited-charge pathways within a minimal CBP-host model. The calculated energetics and rates suggest that D$_1$ formation probably proceeds via an S0 anion intermediate, D0 —>S0- —>D1, while excited state anion pathways may also contribute. In contrast, cation-mediated routes are generally disfavoured and, undesirable relaxation pathways returning charged species to D0 are very far in the Marcus inverted regime and therefore kinetically unfavourable. Overall, this work provides a computational framework for determining the D1 formation mechanism in radical OLED emitters and highlights anion-mediated pathways as the most plausible route to emissive doublet-state population.

papers.title: Boundaries of the Hammett Equation: Critical Window and Defenestration Window in CMS
papers.abstract: Since 1937, the Hammett equation has been the cornerstone for quantifying substituent effects, yet its applicability to open-shell single electron transfer reactions involving high-valent metal oxides has never been tested. Here, through systematic density functional theory calculations of the SOMO–SUMO energy gaps between MnO42- and a series of para-substituted pyridines, we show that the Hammett linear free energy relationship completely fails in this prototypical open-shell d1 system, replaced by a nonlinear, nonmonotonic response—within the σp range of –0.66 to 0.00, the energy gap remains constant at 0.28 eV, forming a “quantum critical window”. Through systematic comparison with non-open-shell and non-metal analogues, it is confirmed that this immune window is specific to metal d orbitals. On this basis, we further investigate the mechanistic nature of single electron transfer in this system: the OAT epoxy configuration is identified by frequency analysis as a higher-order saddle point rather than a stable minimum. Electron transfer exhibits a continuous spin population spectrum from 0.85 to 0.002, rather than a simple on/off switch. The study shows that oxygen atom transfer and single electron transfer, traditionally viewed as competing pathways, are not independent channels but two stages of the same cascade reaction—oxygen first transfers from manganate to pyridine to form a transient epoxy saddle point, then electrons flow through this oxygen bridge to the pyridine, and finally oxygen returns to the metal center to complete net SET. Substituents modulate the stability of the epoxy saddle point through σ-inductive and π-conjugation effects, precisely controlling the on/off switching of this cascade process. This “oxygen ferrying electron” mechanism provides a unified kinetic framework for SET reactions of high-valent metal oxides.

papers.title: Microplastics alter the fate of inland-derived microbial contaminants transported into coastal environments by tropical cyclones
papers.abstract: Tropical cyclones transport diverse contaminants, including microbial contaminants and microplastics, from inland to coastal environments. However, the fate of these inland-derived contaminants after transport remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the mechanisms by which microplastics affect the fate of inland-derived microbial contaminants in coastal waters. Field observations following Hurricane Milton revealed substantial transport of microplastics from inland areas to Florida’s Gulf Coast, where antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) associated with particles larger than 25 µm accounted for approximately 25% of the total ARG abundance introduced during the hurricane event. We confirmed that biofilm formation on microplastics reduced the decay rates of inland-derived bacteria to about half under simulated coastal conditions. We also confirmed that inland-derived bacteria coexisted with indigenous marine bacteria in coastal environments, facilitated by microplastics, for extended periods (weeks to months), posing a potential risk of horizontal gene transfer of ARGs from inland to coastal environments. Consequently, microplastics may extend the impact of storm-introduced microbial threats beyond what is captured by conventional fecal indicator bacteria-based assessments. This study highlights the need to reconsider microbial water quality recovery in coastal environments by accounting for particle-associated processes following extreme events.

papers.title: Acetylcholinesterase Activity Modulation by Proteinogenic Amino Acid Ester Ferulates salts with Enhanced Solubility and Antioxidant Properties
papers.abstract: Ferulic acid (FA) is a phenolic antioxidant whose application is restricted by poor aqueous solubility and limited bioavailability. Novel ferulate salts based on ethyl, isopropyl, and propyl esters of the natural proteinogenic amino acids L-tyrosine and L-phenylalanine were synthesized and characterized in terms of their structural, physicochemical, solubility-related, and antioxidant properties, as well as their influence on AChE activity and molecular interaction profiles. All derivatives exhibited higher solubility in aqueous media than unmodified ferulic acid, with tyrosine ethyl ester ferulate, [TyrOEt][FA], showing the highest solubility. The synthesized salts retained or enhanced the antioxidant potential of the parent compound, and tyrosine alkyl ester derivatives displayed nearly twofold higher activity than FA in the ORAC assay. The analyzed compounds also showed stronger AChE inhibitory activity than ferulic acid itself, with phenylalanine isopropyl ester ferulate, [PheOiPr][FA], exhibiting the strongest inhibitory effect. Molecular docking indicated that the derivatives bind within the aromatic gorge of AChE through hydrophobic contacts, π–π stacking interactions, and hydrogen bonding. More lipophilic isopropyl and propyl derivatives displayed more favorable interaction patterns, consistent with their enhanced inhibitory activity. The results demonstrate that salt formation with amino acid esters modulates both the physicochemical properties of ferulic acid and its interactions with AChE. Enhanced inhibitory activity was associated with favorable accommodation within the enzyme gorge, highlighting the role of lipophilicity and non-covalent protein–ligand interactions in determining biological activity.

papers.title: NEVPT2 Multiple Spawning Molecular Dynamics Simulations for Uracil
papers.abstract: The quasidegenerate n-electron valence state second-order perturbation theory (QD-NEVPT2) for complete active space reference wavefunctions has been implemented in the OpenMolcas package. The implementation utilizes the efficient formulation of Kollmar et al. for the electronic energy, which is extended here to the calculation of analytic derivatives. To demonstrate its utility, the method is applied to classical and non-adiabatic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of uracil. The non-adiabatic MD simulations describe the ultrafast deactivation from the ππ∗ to the nπ∗ state, demonstrating the applicability of the method to photochemical processes. Furthermore, a machine learning-based analysis of the trajectory data extracts key geometrical parameters that are associated with the magnitude of the time-derivative coupling.

papers.title: Lessons Learned on Obtaining Reliable Conductivity Estimates from Molecular Dynamics Simulations
papers.abstract: The calculation of reliable ionic conductivities from molecular dynamics simulations is not a straightforward task, especially for strongly correlated systems, such as ionic liquids or highly concentrated electrolytes, where the Nernst-Einstein approach tends to fail. In this manuscript, we present the newly implemented conduct module for TRAVIS. It allows the calculation of the ionic conductivity using the Einstein-Helfand and Green-Kubo approaches, which explicitly include ionic correlations in their formalism. We provide a broad overview of accessible transport properties and compare methods and best practices for obtaining statistically reliable estimates of ionic conductivity and other physicochemical properties derived from electrolyte molecular dynamics simulations, including transport numbers and the inverse Haven ratio. To validate our implementation and demonstrate the conduct module's capabilities, we simulated the ionic liquid 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium dicyanamide ([EMIm][DCA]) as well as the ether-based electrolyte lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide in ethylene glycol dimethyl ether (LiFSI/DME).

papers.title: Deep Inverse Design of Patchy Particles for Mesoscale Assembly of Superlattices
papers.abstract: The rational design of mesoscale superlattices with prescribed architectures remains a fundamental challenge in materials science. While self-assembly of patchy colloidal particles offers a powerful route to such structures, the combinatorial complexity linking patch number, placement, and interaction properties to emergent assembly architecture has hindered systematic inverse design. Here, we present a discrete neural-adjoint framework that enables direct optimization of building-block design for target superlattice formation. Leveraging a Gumbel–Softmax relaxation, our approach renders discrete patch configurations differentiable, allowing efficient gradient-based exploration of an otherwise intractable design space. Applied to a model system of self-assembling two-dimensional tiles, our method discovers patch designs that robustly assemble into complex superlattices, including multiple Archimedean tilings as well as previously unrealized Pythagorean and gyrated truncated hexagonal tilings. These results establish differentiable inverse design as a powerful approach for programming self-assembly, opening new avenues for the discovery of architected materials with tailored structure and function.

papers.title: Substrate-Adaptive Decarboxylative Olefination Enabled by Active Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: Generality in synthetic chemistry is rarely achieved through a single universal protocol. Instead, widely adopted transformations derive their utility from a well-characterized reaction space that enables rapid substrate-adaptive optimization. Here, we demonstrate how expert-guided reaction-space design combined with user-friendly machine-learning tools can accelerate the construction of such reaction spaces. Using the organocatalytic decarboxylative olefination of malonic acid derivatives as a model system, Bayesian optimization was used to generate a compact, transformation-specific dataset that served as transferable prior knowledge for substrate-adaptive optimization. This approach addresses key limitations of traditional fixed-condition substrate-scope studies by enabling rapid identification of high-yielding conditions for previously unseen and challenging coupling partners. Importantly, the learned reactivity landscape proved transferable beyond the substrate classes represented in the original reaction-development dataset, enabling efficient optimization of related nucleophile families. The resulting platform provides a mild, atom-economical, and highly stereoselective alternative to classical phosphonate-based olefinations, enabling access to diverse α,β-functionalized unsaturated thioesters, esters, and amides, including complex molecular architectures. More broadly, this study demonstrates that reaction-development datasets can serve as transferable reaction knowledge, enabling efficient substrate-adaptive optimization and accelerating the maturation of emerging synthetic methods into practically general transformations.

papers.title: Time-resolved investigation of photocatalytic allene deracemization with kinetic modeling and force-field-based molecular dynamics
papers.abstract: Chiral thioxanthones were shown to be promising energy transfer catalysts for the photoinduced catalysis of organic molecules. In recent years, they were successfully applied in photocatalytic deracemization and kinetic resolution reactions with high enantiomeric excess rates. Previous computational investigations have focused on static investigation mostly using density functional theory (DFT). In this study, we use force field-based molecular dynamics to explore the dissociation dynamics of a photocatalyst-substrate complex comprised of a primary allene amide (substrate) and a functionalized chiral thioxanthone (catalyst). Leveraging the quantum mechanically derived force-field (QMdFF) framework enables the efficient simulation of the molecules in the ground and the excited states. We derive kinetic parameters for the complex dissociation and use them in a kinetic reaction model. Our study indicates that the experimentally observed temperature optimum results from a different temperature dependence of the photo-induced energy transfer and the dissociation and association processes of the substrate-catalyst complexes.

papers.title: Impact of catalyst functionalization, framework defects, and guest loading on nitrobenzene diffusivity in Zr-based metal-organic framework UiO-67 investigated by molecular dynamics and PFG-NMR
papers.abstract: Molecular diffusion in metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) is a key factor controlling their performance in catalysis, gas storage and separation, sensing, and drug delivery applications, where the rate and selectivity of molecular transport directly influence efficiency, selectivity, and the kinetics of molecular recognition. To elucidate critical features of existing MOFs and unravel design principles of novel MOFs, we combine all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with pulsed field gradient NMR (PFG-NMR) measurements to systematically investigate how linker functionalization by proline-derived catalyst, framework defects, and guest loading influence the diffusion of nitrobenzene in the Zr-based MOF UiO-67. We reveal that increasing the fraction of catalystfunctionalized linkers in a mixed-linker MOF reduces nitrobenzene mobility due to steric hindrance in the pore windows and increased surface to volume ratio. Notably, also the position of the functional group on the linker modulates diffusion. Molecular insight provided by MD simulations reveals, that missing linker defects enhance guest diffusivity by enlarging the pore windows of the framework. We furthermore show that an intermediate guest loading maximizes diffusivity, while both lower and higher loadings drastically reduce it. Our combined approach, utilizing MD simulations and PFG-NMR, demonstrates how subtle changes in the framework architecture govern molecular diffusion processes and how a mixed-linker strategy can be employed to mitigate some of these drawbacks.

papers.title: Interplay of Catalyst and Electrode Design Governs C–C Coupling in Ag-Doped Cu Loaded Gas Diffusion Electrodes
papers.abstract: Electrochemical carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) reduction has been intensively studied as a promising route for converting CO 2 into value-added multi-carbon products such as ethylene (C 2 H 4 ). To date, most efforts have focused on the development of highly active electrocatalysts, particularly through alloying and heteroatom doping of Cu, to enhance C–C coupling and C 2 H 4 formation. However, in gas diffusion electrode (GDE) systems operated at industrially relevant current densities, CO 2 reduction proceeds at complex gas–liquid–solid triple-phase interfaces, where the structure of the catalyst layer critically governs the reaction microenvironment and product selectivity. However, how this interfacial structure affect the performance of alloyed catalysts and whether such effects can be generalized across different catalyst compositions remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that CO 2 reduction selectivity in Ag-doped Cu catalyst-loaded GDEs is governed by the cooperative interplay between catalyst and electrode design. Using Ag-doped Cu nanoparticles as a model system, we systematically investigate how Ag doping and catalyst loading collaboratively define the reaction microenvironment and CO 2 reduction selectivity. We demonstrated that moderate catalyst loadings maximize C 2 H 4 selectivity by establishing a balanced reaction environment with appropriate CO accumulation and efficient CO 2 transport, whereas excessively low or high catalyst loadings result in suppressed C 2 H 4 formation also in the alloyed catalysts. These results reveal that alloy catalyst performance is determined not only by inherent electronic and atomic properties but also by the catalyst layer configuration at the triple-phase interface. In GDE systems, optimizing this local environment is essential to fully unlock the catalysts' intrinsic activity.

papers.title: Annealing-aware screening of Co–Ir–Ni–Rh–Ru alloys for ammonia decomposition
Natural Orbital Correlation Analysis of Cluster Bonding: From Aromatic Clusters to Metallic Superatoms with Quantum Topology Probes
papers.abstract: We present a systematic study of electron correlation across 11 molecular and cluster systems using the number of effectively unpaired electrons ND = P i ni(2 − ni), the Takatsuka–Head-Gordon index, computed from coupled-cluster natural orbital occupations over the complete correlated orbital space. Computed at the CCSD/def2-SVP level, all systems studied exhibit substantial total electron correlation when the full natural orbital space is retained: aromatic Al4 2 – (ND = 3.84), antiaromatic Al4 4 – (4.03), planar and icosahedral B12 clusters (4.42 and 4.99), heteroatomic B6N6 (5.11), and cesium–aluminum superatoms Cs3Al8 – and Cs3Al12 – (5.58 and 7.10, respectively), and the B12N12 cage (7.18, the largest in the set). We show that ND is an extensive quantity dominated by the dynamic correlation tail over many weakly occupied virtual orbitals, and introduce the per-electron correlation density fe = ND/Ncorr as a complementary intensive measure. This intensive measure reveals a correlation-density trend: small clusters (Al4, B12, B6N6) exhibit fe ≈ 0.08–0.14 at CCSD/def2-SVP, while metallic superatoms show fe ≈ 0.03–0.05. The separation is clearest between the regime extremes and in matched-element comparisons (Al4 vs. Cs3Aln – family means differ by ∼2× at comparable orbital density); at the larger def2-TZVP basis the boundary-adjacent Al4 2 – /Cs3Al8 – pair narrows to ∼1.1×, so we frame this as a trend in per-electron correlation density rather than a sharp two-regime boundary. We demonstrate that truncation of the natural orbital space to a small active window dramatically underestimates ND, and that complete occupation data are essential for physically meaningful correlation diagnostics. In a separate, exploratory study we map atomic coordinates of ten molecular systems onto Rydberg atom registers and measure entanglement on an analog neutral-atom emulator (Pasqal). We observe topology-dependent entanglement, but within this ten-system set no graph-theoretic metric reaches statistical significance; we therefore present this component as preliminary and hypothesisgenerating, not as a demonstrated structure–property relationship.

papers.title: Digital infrastructure to support and share daily high-throughput experimental materials research
