The proposal converts the current time-limited approvals of pesticide and biocide active substances (typically 10 to 15 years, followed by mandatory renewal) into time-unlimited approvals by default, replacing periodic reassessment with a reactive, case-triggered review mechanism initiated at the Commission's discretion. This paper sets out the proposed amendments, surveys the positions taken by the principal stakeholder groups (EU institutions, industry associations, farming organisations, civil society, and the scientific community), and finally presents our own analysis. The Commission justifies the suggested changes largely with the removal of administrative inefficiency. Industry and farming organisations broadly endorse this perspective, whereas civil society organisations oppose the proposal as a weakening of public safety and a disregard of environmental concerns. We find the Commission's justifications insufficient. The proposal was adopted without a full impact assessment and without a public consultation, and the Commission's claim that "no viable alternatives" exist disregards the obvious options of extending renewal periods, leveraging the One Substance, One Assessment framework, or reforming the Biocide Review Programme. Substantively, unlimited approval freezes the evidence base at the date of each substance's most recent evaluation, which for many active substances predates the 2018 endocrine disruption criteria, the 2023 EFSA bee guidance, and ongoing revisions of aquatic and terrestrial ecotoxicology guidance. It also removes the self-selection mechanism through which industry currently withdraws substances expected to fail renewal, which might hamper marked access for innovative solutions. Finally, the proposal introduces legal uncertainty through the deemed mutual recognition between Member States. The replacement of periodic review by Commission-triggered reassessment makes regulatory action dependent on political will and on the monitoring capacity of under-resourced agencies, neither of which past practice gives reason to consider sufficient. A further structural consequence, not assessed by the Commission, is the displacement of scientific disputes from administrative procedure to judicial review.

papers.title: Reimagining acylation chemistry with nucleophilic indicator organocatalysts that uncover a temperature-dependent mechanistic switch
papers.abstract: Acylation reactions are a cornerstone of synthetic organic chemistry with amide bond couplings as one of the most central and frequently employed reactions in medicinal chemistry. However, the availability of a wide range of specialized activation reagents and catalysts necessitates time-consuming and resource-intensive screenings to perform and optimize certain acylation reactions. To streamline this process, we report a new class of nucleophilic acylation catalysts based on the azopyridine scaffold that combine an enhanced catalytic activity with an intrinsic indicator function. The two catalysts, DMAAP and PPAY, enable the direct optical detection of the catalytically active N-acylpyridinium species through a pronounced, reversible color change. This indicator system revealed that N-acylpyridinium formation is enhanced at low temperatures. Subsequent kinetics analyses uncovered electrophile- and catalyst-dependent behavior which does not correlate with literature models: While pyridine and DMAP show opposing trends with respect to temperature, highly unusual parabolic Eyring plots were obtained for DMAAP and PPAY in combination with benzoyl chloride. Microkinetic simulations and NMR titration studies support a mechanistic rationale involving competing steps concerning the temperature-dependent N-acylpyridinium equilibria and the subsequent acyl transfer to the terminal nucleophile. Overall, our studies showcase that DMAAP and PPAY significantly outperform the predominantly used DMAP in esterification and amidation reactions, with rate accelerations of up to ~50-fold at low temperatures. Their function as indicators allowed to streamline the performance and optimization of acylation reactions by providing a visual confirmation for the formation of the catalytically active intermediate. These findings establish azopyridines as a powerful nucleophilic catalyst class with an exceptionally rare ability to reversibly self-report catalytic states.

papers.title: Balancing Diversity and Efficiency in Training Datasets for Robust Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials enable atomistic simulations at near first-principles accuracy. As model architectures mature, their reliability is increasingly constrained by training data quality. Here, we introduce Automated Training with Latent-space-Aware Sampling, ATLAS, a unified and multifunctional framework based on reversibly compressed latent space and online reliability verification. By co-designing diversity and efficiency criteria with a diversity-aware database generator and a manifold-aware active learning workflow, we steer exploitation toward sparse configurational regions in the structural space while preventing premature convergence. ATLAS produces compact datasets that allow MLIP training with high accuracy reducing up to 300 times fewer structures. To test ATLAS-trained MLIPs, we looked for high-temperature properties such as melting (physical) and decomposition (involving chemical reactions), demonstrating that our methodology consistently brings down prediction errors for temperature below 175 K, for Cu, CuZn and IrO 2 . ATLAS provides a principled and transferable strategy for building robust, similarly accurate and well-balanced MLIPs across diverse material classes.

papers.title: The Redox Array: Streamlined Ion-Electron Balancing
papers.abstract: The Redox Array (RA) is presented as a compact variation of the ion-electron method for balancing redox equations. The approach organises half-reaction-derived integers into a simple array structure, reducing intermediate transcription and repeated notation during balancing procedures. The RA is designed to consolidate intermediate simplification into a single stage, and provides a unified bookkeeping framework for both acidic and basic systems. The method is intended as a supplementary procedural tool for practitioners already familiar with conventional half-reaction balancing.

papers.title: Activation-Induced Turbostratic Ordering in pDCPD-Derived Hard Carbon Enables Stable Carbonate-Based Sodium-Ion Storage
papers.abstract: Sodium-ion batteries are widely considered a promising alternative to lithium-ion batteries, due to the abundance and low cost of their raw materials. However, the development of high-performance and cost-effective electrode materials remains a significant challenge, particularly when competing with lithium iron phosphate systems. Herein, we present a hard carbon material derived from readily available poly(dicyclopentadiene) for use as a negative electrode in SIBs. This study investigates the influence of carbonization temperature and subsequent CO2 activation on the HC’s structure and electrochemical performance. The impact of activation proved to be dependent upon the first stage carbonization temperature, creating greater local ordering for samples carbonized at higher temperatures. The removal of defects and increase in interlayer distance resulted in a turbostratic structure that enhanced rate performance and capacity retention when compared with non-activated samples. The optimized HC exhibits a reversible capacity of 352 mAh/g at 0.1 C and a capacity retention of 88.1% after 500 cycles with a carbonate based electrolyte. This work introduces a cost-effective approach for producing hard carbon materials with distinctive nanostructure and provides valuable insights into achieving long cycle life in sodium-ion batteries.

papers.title: Toward Resolving the RuO2/IrO2 Oxygen Evolution Activity Puzzle: Critical Roles of Spin Polarization and Exchange-Correlation Functional Accuracy
papers.abstract: The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity ordering of RuO2 and IrO2 is well established experimentally, yet density functional theory calculations have persistently failed to reproduce this trend, undermining computational catalyst design. Here, we investigate this discrepancy by evaluating OER thermodynamic and kinetic activities of IrO2 and RuO2 using four exchange-correlation (XC) functionals (PBE, RPBE, r2SCAN, and MS2-rVV10) under spin-polarized and spin-unpolarized conditions. Spin polarization selectively stabilizes the O* intermediate on IrO2 while leaving RuO2 comparatively unaffected, and neglecting spin effects yields unphysically low kinetic barriers for IrO2. Among the four functionals, only MS2-rVV10 reproduces the experimentally observed thermodynamic activity ordering; however, all functionals fail to capture the correct kinetic barrier ordering. We trace these failures to a systematic correlation between adsorption-energy errors and deviations in the predicted activity trend. Notably, the OOH*-OH* scaling offset and theoretical limiting potential are themselves XC-functional dependent, cautioning against cross-functional comparison of overpotentials. Cross-code benchmarks rule out numerical implementation as the error source, while higher-rung functionals progressively overestimate Ru local magnetic moments in RuO2, introducing additional errors. This work establishes accurate exchange-correlation functionals and proper spin-polarization treatment as prerequisites for reliable OER catalyst design.

papers.title: Is a bit over okay?–Overcomplete sets of localized molecular orbitals
papers.abstract: Quantum chemical bases are mostly linearly independent, whether orthonormal or not. However, in certain applications, using an overcomplete set of functions, not forming a basis in the strict sense offers distinct advantages. Localized molecular orbitals (LMO) projected from atomic orbitals (PAO) are a primary example. Use of redundant LMOs is facilitated by the mathematical theory of frames. Along with a systematic presentation of the necessary background, it is shown that the trace of one-electron operators can be obtained by a formula analogous to the orthonormal case. For instance, the electronic dipole moment can be expressed as a sum of frame LMO centroids multiplied by their fractional populations as weights. An advantage of frame LMOs is demonstrated when following reaction coordinates. When a system passes through a high-symmetry point between lower-symmetry arrangements, orthogonal LMOs often exhibit abrupt changes. This occurs when a specific set of localized orbitals does not represent the molecular point group of the highsymmetry structure, resulting in equivalent sets of orthogonal LMOs that may induce discontinuities in LMO based quantities. It is shown that PAO related frame LMOs transition smoothly in these scenarios, without any extra algorithmic effort.

papers.title: Reshaping Ru Polypyridyl Photochemistry With Choline-Geranate (CAGE) Ionic Liquids
papers.abstract: Choline-geranate (CAGE) ionic liquids are emerging as powerful topical delivery media, yet their impact on the photochemistry of metal-based phototherapeutics remains unexplored. Here we show that CAGE ILs can substantially reshape the excited-state landscape of Ru polypyridyl complexes, promoting ligand photorelease in a prototypical PDT scaffold while preserving the expected behaviour of photo-labile and photo-inert analogues. These findings highlight CAGE ILs as both an enabling delivery platform and an active medium that can tune Ru photoreactivity, with implications for designing PDT and photoactivated chemotherapy strategies.

papers.title: Reaction-aware control of autonomous batch synthesis
papers.abstract: Autonomous experimentation is transforming materials discovery; however, information gained from widely used batch synthesis and characterization workflows is limited by endpoint measurements and fixed robotic protocols that treat chemical reactions as black boxes. Here, we introduce a reaction-aware autonomous framework that incorporates crystallization trajectories into the adaptive experimental design, enabling kinetics-informed decision-making in self-driving laboratories. These trajectories, collected through in situ optical monitoring, are converted into kinetic descriptors that simultaneously adapt measurement intervals, batch sizes, and formulation variables. Using the solution-phase crystallization of ZIF-67 as a model system, we built a DIY robot that autonomously identified synthesis conditions yielding nucleation rates over five-fold higher than static maximin sampling while tripling information gains per experiment. This work showcases a new design principle for autonomous experimentation: measurement protocols are not passive settings, but active components of the decision-making process that determine how a closed-loop system observes, interprets, and optimizes a reaction landscape.

papers.title: Unified Mechanistic Insights into Hydrogen Evolution and Oxidation from Homogeneous to Heterogeneous Molecular Electrocatalysis
papers.abstract: Direct comparisons between homogeneous and heterogeneous electrocatalysis using the same molecular system remain rare, despite their importance for catalyst design and device integration. Here, we investigate the heterogenization of the DuBois–Shaw nickel catalyst [Ni(P Cy ₂N Arg ₂) 2 ] 2 ⁺ (NiCyArg), a well-characterized molecular electrocatalyst for reversible H₂/H⁺ interconversion, and assess whether its established homogeneous mechanistic framework can be extended to surface-confined conditions. The catalyst was successfully immobilized onto edge-plane graphite electrodes via noncovalent interactions. Cyclic voltammetry over a range of pH values under Ar and H₂ demonstrates that the heterogenized catalyst retains its reversibility and bidirectional catalytic activity near the thermodynamic H₂/H⁺ potential, with a pronounced bias toward hydrogen oxidation. Pourbaix analysis reveals redox potentials and p K ₐ values of key intermediates that closely match those obtained under homogeneous conditions, indicating minimal perturbation of the thermodynamic landscape upon immobilization. Kinetic analysis using a simplified ECrECr model shows that the same chemical step remains rate-limiting in both regimes, while internal proton transfer processes are modestly slowed upon surface confinement. Overall, this work provides a quantitative bridge between homogeneous and heterogeneous systems and demonstrates that solution phase mechanistic models can in some conditions be applied to surface immobilised systems.

papers.title: N-Heterocyclic Carbene-Carbodiimide (NHC-CDI) Adducts as a Tunable Scaffold for Distonic Radical Cation and Dication Stabilization
papers.abstract: Reactive organic intermediates – particularly radical cations and dications – possess unique structural and electronic properties significant for the advancement of fundamental chemistry and materials. However, stabilizing motifs for these highly reactive species have limited synthetic accessibility and tunability. N-Heterocyclic carbene-carbodiimide (NHC-CDI) adducts are a promising platform to stabilize these intermediates due to their tunability and synthetic accessibility. Herein, we report a simple NHC-CDI framework – containing substituted diphenyl CDIs with one radical stabilizer (4-dimethylamino) and one tunable handle – that can stabilize distonic radical cation and dication species. We synthesized six systematically-varied adducts that undergo two sequential, reversible oxidations with half-wave potentials (E1/2,1 = −0.528 to −0.205 V; E1/2,2 = −0.005 to 0.115 V) correlating strongly to the electronics of the CDI (i.e., Hammett σp parameters). Electrochemical studies confirmed each redox event as a reversible, one-electron, and diffusion-controlled process. Additionally, spectroscopic experiments of a chemically-oxidized NHC-CDI support the formation and stability of the radical cation and dication species. The facile synthetic tunability and accessibilty make this platform promising for the study and development of reactive intermediates for catalysis and energy materials.

papers.title: Spin-polarized oxygen evolution driven by a honeycomb quantum magnet
papers.abstract: The spin state of electrocatalysts has recently emerged as a critical factor governing the kinetics of the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). Here, we show that intrinsic magnetic anisotropy in frustrated quantum magnets provides a route to spin-selective OER without external magnetic fields or engineered spin-filtering interfaces. Using the honeycomb cobaltate series Na 2 Co 2 – x Ni x TeO 6 (0 ≤ x ≤ 1.0), we systematically tune magnetic interactions through chemical substitution while largely preserving the par ent crystal symmetry. Experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that the parent compound Na 2 Co 2 TeO 6 , a Kitaev-type frustrated antiferromagnet, exhibits a spin asymmetric electronic structure associated with strong magnetic anisotropy, together with limited, framework-preserving electrochemical reconstruction during OER. Consistent with this spin-active framework, electrochemical measurements show a monotonic decline in activity per active Co site with increasing Ni content; NCTO delivers an overpotential of 290 mV, a Tafel slope of 40 mV dec −1 , and the highest turnover frequency per active site in the series. Notably, all compositions exhibit cycling-induced stability enhancement, most pronounced in NCTO. Raman, XPS, and magnetometry suggest that this anomalous durability originates from controlled Co-centered reconstruction and lattice-coupled magnetic evolution within a largely retained honeycomb framework. These findings point to frustrated quantum magnets as a promising mate rials platform for spin-informed electrocatalysis, where magnetic anisotropy, spin-state modulation, and controlled lattice adaptability can be jointly leveraged to improve OER activity and stability.

papers.title: Scalable and Printable Three-Phase Ion Gel Electrocatalyst Device
Chemoselective Hydrogenation of Technical-Grade Fatty Acid Esters to High-Purity Oleyl Alcohol: Systematic Evaluation of Homogeneous Catalysts
papers.abstract: The catalytic hydrogenation of esters is a promising route to fatty alcohols due to its efficiency, safety, and environmental compatibility. Oleyl alcohol is particularly relevant because it is accessible from renewable resources and combines high stability with versatile functionalization potential. However, its selective synthesis remains challenging, as catalytic systems must differentiate between C=O and C=C bonds during fatty acid ester hydrogenation. In this study, commercially available homogeneous ruthenium catalysts were systematically screened for the hydrogenation of high oleic sunflower oil methyl ester (HOSOME) under technically relevant conditions. Technical-grade feedstocks were used without prior purification to evaluate catalyst tolerance towards natural impurities. Catalyst systems were compared regarding chemo- and regioselectivity, revealing distinct ligand, solvent and base effects on reaction outcome. Time-resolved analysis of the reaction progress provided insight into the underlying reaction network. Under optimized conditions (80 °C, 30 bar H2, 0.4 mol% 2 [Ru-MACHO], 5.0 mol% KOtBu), quantitative conversion (>99%) and oleyl alcohol selectivities of up to 87% were achieved. Furthermore, the direct conversion of trioleate and conjugated methyl linoleate demonstrated the robustness and versatility of the catalytic system. These results establish a basis for the selective hydrogenation of fatty raw materials under mild conditions and provide a sustainable route to unsaturated fatty alcohols.

papers.title: Realizing Ultrathin Amorphous Borophene: Characterization and Surface Functionalization
papers.abstract: Amorphous nanomaterials are an interesting subset of materials with properties that are derived from the lack of long-range atomic order found in crystalline structures. The absence of an ordered lattice provides distinct advantages, such as high isotropic conductivity, superior mechanical toughness, and a high density of unsaturated surface sites that open pathways for surface modification. Borophene (BP) is a synthetic, two-dimensional allotrope of boron that has captured intense scientific interest because it is stronger, lighter, and more flexible than graphene. While crystalline forms of BP have been widely explored, the amorphous phase of BP has remained experimentally elusive. Here, we report the first synthesis of ultrathin amorphous BP (aBP) via liquid-phase exfoliation of amorphous boron nanoparticles and the covalent 2 modification of the surface of the resulting nanomaterial. The aBP nanodisks are less than 2 nm thick and do not exhibit long-range order. The reaction of the aBP nanodisks with aryl diazonium salts results in the spontaneous attachment of aryl groups to the nanomaterial surface, as confirmed by several techniques. We propose a radical-mediated mechanism in which surfacegenerated aryl radicals react with electronically active, defect-rich sites on aBP. This mild and versatile strategy establishes a new platform for engineering aBP properties and expands its potential in electronic, sensing, and catalytic applications.

papers.title: Why quasicrystals conduct poorly: a combinatorial selection principle on K5
papers.abstract: Aluminium, copper, and iron are excellent conductors. Alloy them into a quasicrystal and the resistivity rises by a factor of 106. Anneal the alloy to perfection and it conducts worse. Remove the Drude peak: there is none. Forty years after Shechtman’s discovery, no model explains these three facts together. We show that one equation does: ( n 2 ) = ( n 3 ) , whose unique solution is n = 5. Five vertices force a lattice in four dimensions, a five-fold rotation forbidden in periodic 3D, and quasiperiodic order in any three-dimensional observation. The 4D lattice is a crystal—periodic, fully conducting, with ten open channels per cell. Projected into 3D, six of those channels become invisible: the observer sees only four, and those are the shallowest. The quasicrystal does not conduct poorly. We observe it poorly.

papers.title: Polymer Immobilization Governs Mediated Bioelectrocatalysis and Enables Automated Redox Mediator Screening
papers.abstract: Enzymatic bioelectrocatalysis relies on redox mediators to shuttle electrons between enzymes and electrode surfaces when direct electron transfer is inaccessible. However, mediator performance is highly enzyme-specific and difficult to predict, which makes identifying effective mediators dependent on experimental screening. Enzyme immobilization offers a practical route to reduce enzyme consumption in such studies, but polymer matrices can significantly influence electrochemical behavior, complicating interpretation of screening results. Here, we systematically evaluate how polymer immobilization environments affect mediated bioelectrocatalysis using glucose oxidase and diaphorase as model enzymes. Across a panel of naphthoquinone mediators, polymer-dependent differences in catalytic activity and electrochemical reversibility were observed, even for mediators with similar redox potentials. These effects arise from coupled influences of mediator transport, local chemical environment, and enzyme–polymer interactions, leading to a tradeoff between maximizing catalytic current and preserving intrinsic mediator–enzyme reactivity trends. While pyrene-functionalized LPEI films yielded the relatively high current densities, alkyl-modified LPEI better reproduced solution-phase mediator behavior. A redox polymer, dimethylferrocene-modified LPEI (Fc-LPEI), provided a balance of high activity and favorable electrochemical characteristics, enabling reliable comparison across mediators. Leveraging this platform, Fc-LPEI–immobilized enzymes were integrated into an automated electrochemical screening system, demonstrating reproducible, high-throughput evaluation of mediator performance. These results establish polymer matrix selection as a critical parameter in bioelectrocatalysis and provide a framework for the development of scalable, data-driven mediator discovery workflows.

papers.title: Characterizing protein-excipient interactions for the development of high concentration protein formulations Authors: Asuka A. Orr1, Xun Li1‡, Chaowang Zeng1, Daniel J. Deredge1, Alexander D. MacKerell, Jr.1*, Stephen W. Hoag
papers.abstract: High-concentration protein formulations (HCPF) with concentrations exceeding 50 mg/mL have gained significant attention due to their potential to reduce injection volumes, improve patient comfort, and lower administration costs by enabling subcutaneous self-administration. However, the thermodynamic instability of proteins at high concentrations, which can lead to aggregation, poses significant formulation challenges and regulatory concerns. This study emphasizes the critical role of excipients in stabilizing HCPF by attenuating self protein-protein interactions (PPIs). In this study, chymotrypsin and lysozyme were chosen as model proteins. A systematic experimental characterization, including temperature scanning viscometry, particle size distribution analysis, pH evaluations, zeta potential determinations, and visual inspections was performed to evaluate the physicochemical properties of the HCPF prototype during the stability study. In conjunction, the computational methodology, Site-Identification by Ligand Competitive Saturation (SILCS)-Biologics, was applied to perform comprehensive analysis of buffer and excipient binding occupancies and associated total system charge to interpret experimental data for the development of predictive models. Stabilization is shown to be associated with the number of sites to which an excipient binds, with consideration of the participation of those sites in PPI. This interdisciplinary approach enhances our understanding of HCPF development and optimization, offering predictive solutions to mitigate protein aggregation there by improving the efficiency and cost-effectiveness of biopharmaceutical product lifecycles.

papers.title: Hantavirus ANDV Glycoprotein Gc: Multi-Site Computational Analysis of Remdesivir Binding Under pH-Dependent Fusion Conditions
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic pathogens responsible for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), diseases associated with substantial mortality and limited antiviral treatment options. Andes virus (ANDV), a highly pathogenic New World hantavirus, utilizes the glycoprotein complex composed of Gn and Gc proteins to mediate host-cell entry and membrane fusion. The Gc glycoprotein undergoes pH-dependent structural rearrangements during endosomal trafficking, making it an attractive therapeutic target. In the present study, a comprehensive molecular docking analysis of Remdesivir against multiple functional regions of the Andes virus glycoprotein Gc was performed using AutoDock Vina under physiologically relevant pH conditions (7.4, 5.5, and 4.6). Five structurally and functionally important regions were investigated, including the fusion-loop pocket (Region 1), Gc homodimer interface (Region 2), pH-sensing interface (Region 3), GnB–Gc stem accommodation interface (Region 4), and conserved aromatic groove stabilization region (Region 5). Remdesivir exhibited strong multi-site binding with affinities ranging from −9.1 to −7.0 kcal/mol. These findings suggest that Remdesivir may interfere with viral fusion machinery through simultaneous constitutive and pH-sensitive mechanisms. The study provides mechanistic insights into hantavirus fusion regulation and highlights the potential value of multi-site antiviral targeting strategies against emerging RNA viruses.

papers.title: First-principles data for solid-solution Nb–Zr, Ta–Zr, and V–Zr binary alloys with body-centered-cubic structures
papers.abstract: We present three open-access datasets containing density functional theory (DFT) calculations for refractory solid-solution binary alloys niobium–zirconium (NbZr), tantalum–zirconium (TaZr), and vanadium–zirconium (VZr) in 128-atom body-centered-cubic (BCC) supercells. These datasets extend our previously published first-principles collections for NbTa, NbV, TaV, and NbTaV alloys and were generated with the same automated high-throughput workflow based on the Vienna Ab-Initio Simulation Package (VASP). For each of the three NbZr, TaZr, and VZr systems, we uniformly sample 31 chemical compositions across the full composition range in 4-atom increments. For every composition we construct 100 distinct disordered atomic configurations by randomizing the element assignments on the BCC lattice sites. All structures are fully relaxed, and the released data include complete input files, detailed VASP outputs for each relaxation stage, and derived physical quantities such as ground-state formation energy and root mean-squared displacement (RMSD) relative to an ideal BCC reference. These Zr-containing binaries are motivated by our earlier demonstration that graph neural networks (GNNs) trained on binary NbTa, NbV, and TaV data can interpolate formation enthalpies and structural descriptors in ternary NbTaV alloys while dramatically reducing the required number of ternary DFT calculations. The new NbZr, TaZr, and VZr datasets increase the diversity of available binary training data, in particular in systems with larger size mismatch and stronger lattice distortion due to Zr, and are intended to support the development of transferable machine learning (ML) interatomic models for accelerated exploration of high-dimensional multicomponent alloy spaces.

papers.title: Quantum-accurate strain energy estimation of saturated ring systems in drug-like molecules via equivariant deep learning
papers.abstract: Accurate estimation of conformational strain in small-molecule ligands is critical for successful structure-based drug design. While torsional strain in acyclic bonds is readily assessed, evaluating strain in saturated ring systems currently necessitates conformational sampling and compute-intensive quantum-mechanical calculations. To address this limitation, RingAnalyzer is introduced, i.e., a machine learning framework predicting conformational strain directly from single three-dimensional molecular geometries. The method introduces a ring-centric 3D equivariant neural network trained on a rigorously curated dataset of 4’226 drug-like molecules and 27’581 conformations. Calculated at the high-fidelity ωB97XD/Def2TZVP level of theory, this dataset captures diverse stereoelectronic effects. Following extensive data augmentation strategies yielding 76’636 conformations, the computational model accurately predicts strain energies with a mean absolute error of 0.54 kcal/mol, demonstrating robustness to structural artifacts and incomplete structures. Prospective application of RingAnalyzer across diverse structural repositories, including small-molecule conformer generators, 3D generative models, co-folding architectures, docking datasets, the Protein Data Bank, and the Cambridge Structural Database, highlights a widespread occurrence of high-energy ring artifacts. As a computationally efficient and quantum-accurate geometric filter, RingAnalyzer enables the rapid identification and elimination of strained ring systems to streamline structure-based molecular design.

papers.title: Computational Pedagogical Modeling as a New Empirical Category in Chemistry Education
papers.abstract: Chemistry education research has evolved into a mature discipline, yet its taxonomy of publication categories has not kept pace with the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven research practices. This Perspective introduces Computational Pedagogical Modeling (CPM) as a formally defined research methodology and proposes its recognition as a new empirical category within chemistry education. Bridging validated cognitive taxonomies with a direct epistemological parallel from within the chemical sciences—namely, the accepted empirical status of computational chemistry despite the absence of wet-laboratory procedures—the argument is made that AI-generated pedagogical artifacts produced through systematically designed, parameter-documented prompt architectures constitute legitimate empirical data. Two concrete exemplars ground the argument: (1) the Bridging the Macroscopic, Microscopic, and Symbolic Domains of Chemistry (/bq/) prompt architecture, which guides students across these domains, recently detailed in the preprint Bridging Johnstone’s Triangle with Generative AI via the Pedagogical Evaluation, Design, and Analysis Laboratory (PEDAL) Archive at ChemRxiv; and (2) the NExAIE scholarly writing and AI-augmented evaluation ecosystem, implemented in a functioning journal infrastructure. The PEDAL Archive itself—a research-grade platform assigning citable DOIs and 24-plus documented research parameters to every prompt architecture—provides the instrumentation layer that satisfies reproducibility standards analogous to parameter reporting in computational chemistry. Implications for editors, reviewers, authors, and the field’s methodological development are discussed.

papers.title: Design and validation of a dual-atmosphere X-ray diffraction cell for operando analysis of solid oxide cells
papers.abstract: Operando X-ray diLraction measurements of solid oxide cells require simultaneous access to high temperature, separated gas atmospheres, electrical polarisation and an unobstructed X-ray path. Here, we report the design and validation of a dual-atmosphere operando X-ray diLraction cell developed for structurally resolved studies of electrochemical ceramic devices. The cell operates up to approximately 850 °C, maintains independent fuel- and air-side atmospheres, and allows open-circuit voltage measurements and controlled electrical biasing during diLraction. Key design elements include a glass-sealed sample mount, spring-loaded electrical contacts, a thermally optimised heater assembly, and a half-cylinder window geometry providing diLraction access over a wide angular range. The cell was validated using a model solid oxide cell containing a dense gadolinia-doped ceria (GDC) fuel electrode on a 3YSZ electrolyte. Under applied electrolysis bias, the GDC diLraction peaks shifted systematically to lower 2θ, while the 3YSZ and Ni reference phases remained invariant at fixed temperature. Rietveld analysis showed a monotonic GDC lattice expansion reaching approximately 1% at the highest applied bias. By correlating this expansion with the eLective oxygen partial pressure estimated from electrochemical measurements, the experiment demonstrates that the structural state of GDC is governed by the electrochemically imposed oxygen chemical potential rather than by the inlet gas composition alone. The developed cell therefore provides a platform for linking operating conditions directly to redox-driven structural changes in solid oxide cell materials.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Assessing Models of Reactor Pressure Vessel Steel Embrittlement
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of ductile-to-brittle transition temperature shifts (TTS) of steel alloys used in reactor pressure vessels (RPVs) is critical for informing safe and reliable nuclear reactor operation. Recently, numerous physically-motivated semiempirical and data-driven machine learning (ML) models of TTS for RPVs have been developed. Here, we present detailed benchmarks of the most widely used models and discuss their pros and cons based on statistical metrics on key data subsets (e.g., predicting TTS of steels under reactor life extension conditions of low flux and high fluence) and their physical trends with key variables (e.g., irradiation flux and fluence). In addition, we develop an ensemble neural network ML model that includes a physics-informed loss function component which penalizes unphysical changes in TTS with flux and fluence. We show that this model overcomes shortcomings in a similar earlier model related to extrapolation to higher fluence over a range of flux values from low flux life extension conditions up to high flux test reactor conditions. We show detailed per-alloy and highest fluence data predictions, and provide life extension predictions for the US nuclear reactor alloys. Finally, we have developed a codebase to make the use and evaluation of all models readily accessible to the broader community. It is our hope this codebase can grow to encompass new models developed by the community and function as an informative benchmark for modeling of RPV steel embrittlement in the future.

papers.title: Entropic and Enthalpic Contributions to Streptavidin–Biotin Unbinding
papers.abstract: The streptavidin–biotin complex is one of the strongest known noncovalent interactions and is widely used in biotechnology. Here, we quantify the entropic and enthalpic contributions governing streptavidin–biotin unbinding using molecular simulations combined with force spectroscopy–based theoretical modeling. Steered molecular dynamics simulations were performed over a broad range of pulling velocities and temperatures to generate dynamic force spectra, from which the most probable rupture forces were extracted. Analysis within the Dudko–Hummer–Szabo framework yielded an activation free energy of (28.8 ± 4.3) kJ mol -1 , consistent with the lower bound of experimental reports. By introducing our temperature-dependent extension of the DHS model, we further decomposed the unbinding free energy into enthalpic (42.6 ± 5.9 kJ mol - 1 ) and entropic (12.4 ± 6.0 kJ mol -1 at 300 K) contributions. These results reveal a substantial entropic component that modulates complex stability and helps reconcile discrepancies among previous measurements. The computational framework is general and applicable to other receptor–ligand systems.

papers.title: Learning chemically transferable protein-protein binding energetics from peptide potential of mean force building blocks
papers.abstract: Conventional all-atom molecular dynamics (AAMD) simulations can expedite exploration of protein-protein interactions and the resultant design space but are too costly to span the time and length scales relevant to protein oligomerization and self-assembly. In this work, we define a framework for a chemically transferable coarse-grained (CG) force-field for interprotein interactions by matching nonbonded interaction potentials to the potential of mean force (PMF) governing small peptide association using a two-body Lennard-Jones-Gaussian (LJG) potential; we refer to our model as PEBBLE (Potential of mean force Estimator from Building BLock Energetics). Parameters are learned via relative entropy minimization (REM) from AAMD of GXG tripeptides (with guest residue X) for all 210 amino acid pair combinations. Application of these parameters yields good agreement with AA potentials of mean force (PMFs) and experimental binding free energies across three benchmarks: dimerization motif QVVAG, heterodimeric coiled-coil E3/K3, and globular barnase/barstar (both wild-type and mutants). We further reproduce assembly outcomes for experimentally characterized tripeptides: fibrillar (VFF) and non-assembling (ECG). These results show that a simple LJG basis trained only on tripeptide statistics can generalize from molecular PMFs to higher-order structures and energetics relevant to protein-protein interactions and ultimately, protein-based materials design. In the future, we envision that the PEBBLE CG model will be used to (i) enable sampling of protein oligomers when AAMD is too costly and (ii) accelerate development of low-resolution CG models.

papers.title: ChemDistill: Hierarchical Graph Attention Distillation with Parameter-Efficient Multi-Task Adapters for Molecular Property Prediction and Chemical Reaction Analysis
papers.abstract: Molecular property prediction and chemical reaction analysis are fundamental tasks in computational chemistry with critical applications in drug discovery and materials design. While large pre-trained molecular models have achieved remarkable performance, their computational cost severely limits deployment in resource-constrained environments. Moreover, existing methods struggle with cross-domain knowledge transfer, multi-task learning for diverse molecular endpoints, and the integration of spectral data with molecular graph representations. In this paper, we propose ChemDistill, a unified framework for chemical knowledge distillation with hierarchical graph attention that addresses these challenges through three complementary modules. First, the Hierarchical Graph Attention Distillation module transfers knowledge from large teacher models to lightweight student models through flow-based distillation with a calibration mechanism that corrects systematic biases inherited from the teacher. Second, the Chemistry-specific Parameter-Efficient Multi-Task Adapter enables simultaneous prediction of multiple molecular properties with only ten percent of full fine-tuning parameters through task-shared and task-specific adapter components. Third, the Spectrum-Molecular Joint Representation module fuses spectral data including infrared spectroscopy and nuclear magnetic resonance with molecular graph features via cross-modal attention, enabling end-to-end prediction from raw spectral inputs to molecular properties. Extensive experiments on MoleculeNet, QM9, and USPTO benchmarks demonstrate that ChemDistill achieves state-of-the-art performance across all tasks while requiring only 1.6 million parameters, approximately a 3.3 times compression ratio compared to the teacher model. On the Tox21 benchmark, ChemDistill achieves a ROCAUC of 0.879, outperforming the teacher model ChemBERTa while being significantly more compact. For chemical reaction prediction on USPTO, ChemDistill attains a Top-1 accuracy of 51.6 percent, surpassing existing methods by a substantial margin. Keyword: Knowledge Distillation, Molecular Property Prediction, Graph Neural Network, Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning, Spectral Analysis

papers.title: Determination of reduced nitrogen by 4-Toluenesulfonyl Chloride (TsCl) Derivatization and HPLC-MS
papers.abstract: The potential environmental and health impacts of reduced nitrogen have drawn significant research interest in recent decades. While various analytical techniques exist for detecting specific reduced nitrogen compounds in air and liquid matrices, given the diverse research interests across scientific disciplines, there remains a need for a widely applicable, selective, and affordable method. In this work, a high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS) method that incorporates a simple precolumn derivatization procedure using p-toluenesulfonyl chloride (TsCl) was optimized for the analysis of small reduced nitrogen compounds. This derivatization method is selective for the N–H bond and exhibits high sensitivity and calibration linearity for a diverse range of reduced nitrogen compounds. Key derivatization parameters, including reaction pH and time, were optimized, and the stability of the derivatization products was investigated. This derivatization method was further applied to particulate matter samples collected from a poultry research center and biomass burning samples from wood combustion. Using an ultra-high resolution MS and its MS2 function, we identified MS2 fragments unique to TsCl derivatization. This finding enables the detection of various reduced nitrogen compounds in complex environmental matrices.

papers.title: Non-Covalent Metal–Water Polarization Governs Helmholtz Capacitance
papers.abstract: Electrified metal–water interfaces govern charge storage and electrochemical reactivity, yet the microscopic origin of their metal-dependent Helmholtz capacitance has remained unresolved. Here we use extensive density-functional theory-based ab initio molecular dynamics simulations to reproduce and explain the long-established experimental capacitance trend at fcc(111) metal–water interfaces. We show that this trend is governed primarily by the electrode-side electronic response of the explicit metal–water interface, which controls the effective electron-spillover length and hence the bias capacitance. This relation remains predictive for cross-geometry bimetallic-like systems. Our findings clarify the microscopic origin of metal-dependent Helmholtz capacitance and suggest a physically grounded design principle for electrode materials in sustainable-energy technologies.

papers.title: Mapping Nanoscale Confinement and Water Properties Inside Peptide-Nucleotide Biomolecular Condensates
papers.abstract: Biomolecular condensates formed by liquid–liquid phase separation create dynamic, water-rich microenvironments that are essential for cellular organisation, yet it is challenging to understand their internal aqueous phase. Here, we introduce Brønsted photoacids and photobases as a new class of environmental fluorescent probes to interrogate the water phase inside biomolecular condensates. Using in vitro condensates formed by intrinsically disordered poly-lysine or poly-arginine peptides with nucleotides, we combine steady-state and time-resolved fluorescence to resolve the probe’s excitedstate proton transfer and subsequent proton recombination dynamics. We show that both photoacids and photobases remain largely solvated within poly-lysine-based condensates, with only modest slowing of proton transfer relative to bulk water, consistent with a moderately more viscous aqueous environment. We mainly focus on photoacids, which exhibit strongly enhanced geminate proton recombination, attributed to nanometre-scale confinement of water within the condensates, inducing reflective boundaries for the dissociated proton. By modelling the recombination kinetics, we use the photoacid as a molecular ruler to estimate the dimensions of confined aqueous nanocavities, revealing characteristic maximum radii of ~6 nm. Altering condensate composition systematically modulates these properties, with ATP- and poly-arginine–based condensates displaying denser, less hydrated interiors. These findings establish excited-state proton transfer probes as powerful tools for quantifying nanoscale water confinement in biomolecular condensates, with implications for condensate function and molecular sequestration.

papers.title: Enveda-180: generation of a large open multimodal MS/MS and ion mobility spectral library for drug-like small molecules
papers.abstract: Small-molecule characterization depends heavily on annotated MS/MS spectral libraries for reference matching and, in the case of open-source libraries, for training machine-learning-based structure elucidation. A primary bottleneck is the scarcity of such open data: current libraries such as GNPS, MSnLib, and MassBank, combined, contain spectra for approximately 150,000 unique compounds, representing a small fraction of known chemical space. These libraries are also sparse in complementary measurements such as liquid chromatography retention time (RT) and collisional cross section (CCS) from ion mobility mass spectrometry, the latter of which is seeing growing adoption in the field. To address these gaps, we present Enveda-180, an open spectral library built from high-throughput, pooled characterization of 184,330 structurally diverse small molecules, more than doubling the combined structural coverage of MS/MS open libraries, and more than 5x the combined open CCS values. Compounds were profiled at three collision energies in both positive and negative ion modes. We describe our profiling methods in detail, including the use of ion mobility to resolve multiple species of the same nominal ion structure. Enveda-180 substantially expands the chemical space covered by open MS/MS libraries and enables multimodal learning by integrating retention time, CCS, MS/MS, and metadata within a single resource.

papers.title: Visualizing the Interplay between Etching and Sulfidization of Cu2O nanocubes via in situ X-ray ptychography and X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: From solar cells to hydrogen evolution catalysts, metal sulfides are at the heart of the clean energy transition, yet translating the simplicity of liquid-phase synthesis into nanostructures with controlled morphology, composition, and crystallinity remains far from trivial. Copper sulfide (CuS) nanostructures are a prime example, where hollow morphologies are particularly desirable but their formation mechanism remains poorly understood. Here, we employ a multimodal in situ X-ray approach to investigate the transformation of Cu 2 O nanocubes into CuS in the liquid phase. In situ X-ray ptychography and diffraction resolve the morphological and structural transformations during sulfidization, revealing the formation of hollow CuS structures. Complementary high-energy resolution fluorescence detected X-ray absorption near-edge structure (HERFD-XANES) spectroscopy shows that at room temperature the transformation proceeds via etching accompanied by the formation of Cu 2 S, whereas at elevated temperatures sulfidization dominates. These findings uncover the temperature-dependent competition between dissolution and sulfidization and provide mechanistic insight into hollow CuS nanostructure formation. While such hollow morphologies are often attributed to the Kirkendall effect, our findings reveal a more complex mechanism involving the interplay of etching and sulfidization during the transformation process. More broadly, this work demonstrates the power of complementary in situ X-ray techniques to probe chemical transformations in solution beyond the limits of conventional electron microscopy.

papers.title: Iron-digermanium cluster: synthesis, Lewis-base-induced isomerization, dihydrogen activation, and alkene cycloaddition
papers.abstract: Heterometallic complexes containing multiple heavier tetrylidyne ligands (RE; E = Si, Ge, Sn, Pb) are promising for cooperative bond activation but are rare because RE units tend to oligomerize. We present the synthesis, electronic structure, and reactivity of an irondigermanium complex, [Fe(GeAr’)2] (1, Ar’ = 2,6-Dipp2-C6H3, Dipp = 2,6-iPr2-C6H3), featuring adjacent Ar’Ge units bonded to Fe through double and single Fe–Ge bonds, respectively. Complex 1 reacts readily with tBuNC, H2, and styrene via coordination, bond activation, and cycloaddition pathways, producing diverse structural outcomes. Coordination of tBuNC to Fe induces a formal reductive elimination of the two Ar’Ge units, forming an iron-digermyne complex (2) with a rare σ,σ-type double-bonding mode. Under mild conditions, H2 is activated, forming a germyl(IV)-iron-germylidyne complex (3). The reaction with styrene involves a [3+2] cycloaddition, yielding a bis(germylene)-iron complex (4). Notably, the reaction with 2,3-dimethyl-1,3-butadiene (DMB) proceeds via an unusual kinetic [3+4] cycloaddition pathway to produce a bis(germylene)-iron species (5), which then irreversibly rearranges into the thermodynamically favored [1+4] product (6). In contrast, the heavier iron-tin analog exhibits distinct reactivity towards these substrates, highlighting fundamental differences between Fe–Ge and Fe–Sn bonding and reactivity.

papers.title: Contouring mitigates voiding at the lithium/ceramic electrolyte interface on discharging solid-state batteries
papers.abstract: Voids form at the interface between the lithium metal anode and ceramic electrolyte of a solidstate battery when discharged at practical rates (current densities) and stack pressures, leading to voltage polarisation and ultimately cell failure. Contouring the interface can increase the current density at which polarisation occurs and voids form. An egg-box contoured topography with peak height and separation of 5 and 30 µm respectively at the Li/Li 6 PS 5 Cl interface, increases the discharge current at which voiding commences ten-fold, from 0.2 to 2 mA cm −2 for a 2 MPa stack pressure at 30 °C. In practical applications, cells are typically subjected to short periods at higher discharge rates, e.g. electric vehicle (EV) acceleration. Contoured cells at 2 MPa stack pressure can sustain pulsed currents of 3 mA cm −2 at 30 °C and 8 mA cm −2 at 60 °C without cell failure. To assess practically relevant discharge demands, the Worldwide Harmonised Light Vehicles Test Procedure (WLTP), which is designed to represent typical driving conditions that a passenger car would experience in real-world use, was translated into a sequence of discharge current profiles equivalent to approximately five hours of driving (3.31 mAh cm −2 ) involving currents as high as 9 mA cm −2 . At 2 MPa and 60 °C, an egg-box contoured Li/Li 6 PS 5 Cl can sustain the WLTP discharge sequence without polarisation, whereas a non-contoured interface polarises by 5 V before completing two cycles. These results serve to demonstrate the significance contouring the Li/solid electrolyte interfacial can play in raising discharge currents to practically relevant levels. The results stand in stark contrast to the effect of contouring on the critical current before dendrites form on charging, which is only increased by ~50%.

papers.title: In situ visualization of adaptive linker redistribution and phase transformation in multivariate zirconium MOFs
papers.abstract: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) can form multiple phases under nearly identical conditions, limiting reproducible phase isolation and predictive design. This is particularly challenging in multivariate MOFs, where heterogeneity introduces additional compositional and dynamic disorder during crystallization. However, it remains unclear how linker competition and incorporation are resolved, and whether phase formation occurs through dynamic evolution or direct assembly. Here, we show that transient linker availability directs structural evolution in mixed-linker Zr–MOFs, enabling programmable access to fcu, hcp, hxl, and hns phases. By combining in situ SAXS/WAXS with experimental and computational analyses, we reveal highly dynamic self-assembly pathways involving anisotropic growth, fcu-to-hcp phase transformation, and real-time linker redistribution during crystallization, demonstrating that composition is reshaped throughout synthesis, leading to thermodynamically favored plane-selective linker distributions. This establishes a molecular-level mechanistic pathway for predictive control of multivariate low-dimensional MOFs by revealing evolving linker redistributions during phase formation, enabling direct control over self-assembly.

papers.title: Generative Glide: A De Novo Workflow for Ultra-large Library Screening
papers.abstract: In the past few years, chemical vendors have embraced enormous virtual spacesoften exceeding 1010 molecules. The sheer size of these spaces presents a formidable computational challenge for traditional structure-based virtual screening. Exhaustive docking of such spaces is computationally prohibitive, and even modern active learning docking algorithms, which leverage fast ligand-based machine learning to identify the most promising candidates for docking, struggle to achieve an acceptable turnaround time. Methods based on de novo molecular generation using the reactions that define the virtual space can bypass the challenge of scoring every molecule in the space, but will often yield candidates where the synthesis as described will not work in the lab. To address these challenges, we present the Generative Glide workflow, an integrated framework that bridges the gap between in silico generation and physical acquisition. Generative Glide employs an ensemble of reinforcement learning agents optimized against a supervised GCN-based QSAR model to navigate toward chemical space regions with improved predicted binding likelihood. We implement a two-tiered strategy to ensure tractability: a high-throughput Bloom filter to rapidly identify molecules within ultra-large commercial catalogs and a retrosynthetic analysis engine to validate novel out-of-library candidates. Deployment across diverse protein targets and multiple ultra-large libraries demonstrates that the workflow consistently achieves a significant shift in docking score distributions toward better scoring compounds while maintaining a high level of scaffold diversity. Notably, the architecture is designed to be light-weight, enabling a relatively fast turnaround time compared to exhaustive enumeration. By incorporating active learning, Generative Glide further refines the scoring model’s predictive accuracy within high-potency domains, enabling the agents to effectively navigate and exploit the extreme negative tail of the docking score distribution that is poorly represented in the initial training data. This workflow provides a scalable, generative solution to augment and accelerate the virtual screening of modern chemical space.

papers.title: Estimation of thermodynamic quantities via in-situ monitoring and modelling at the early-stage of ettringite formation.
papers.abstract: Early stage of solid formation from solution is a matter of debate, particularly nucleation and early growth. Existing thermodynamic models based on bulk equilibrium assumptions often fail to capture these elusive stages and consequently the nature of early-stage formation. This work focuses on estimating key quantities, such as interfacial energy, early crystal growth rate, and the freshly formed solid solubility through in-situ monitoring and numerical modelling. As case study, we focus on ettringite, a critical solid formed during early hydration of cement. A highly controlled, dilute, titration-precipitation method was employed to deconvolute the early stages of solid formation. The process was monitored using Ca2+ ion selective electrodes (ISE), along with optical, pH, and conductivity probes. Their data were incorporated into a model based on classical nucleation theory (CNT) and monovariate population balance. This integrated approach provides a better baseline, offering meaningful insights into an essential reaction of real cement. In our study, where the growth is limited by Ca2+ diffusion, the fresh solid solubility (log Ksp,fresh) was found to be -40.7±0.02, and solid-liquid interfacial energies for primary and secondary nucleation were 22.7± 0.06 and 19.2±0.05 mJ/m2, respectively. Additionally, the evolution of needle dimensions was estimated in the experimental timeline. The proposed model was subsequently extended to describe ettringite formation in model cement, providing physically consistent estimation of nucleation and growth rates and insights into the complex dynamics of cement hydration.

papers.title: A Metal-Free C6N16 Primary Explosive with High Thermal Stability and PETN Initiation Capability
papers.abstract: A nitrogen-rich metal-free primary explosive, 4,10-diazidotetrazolo[1,5-d]tetrazolo[1’,5’:1,6]pyridazino[4,5-d]pyridazine (C6N16, DBTP), has been designed through strategic optimization of nitrogen isomerism and synthesized from simple precursors. The highly nitrogen-dense molecular framework features a planar crystal packing with high density (1.79 g cm-3), excellent thermal stability (Tonset = 201 °C), and high heat of formation (5631 kJ kg-1). Calculated detonation parameters (D = 8001 m s-1, P = 24.2 GPa) and successful initiation of PETN demonstrate its practical performance as a metal-free primary explosive. In addition, it has good UV light stability, near zero aqueous solubility and hygroscopicity, and significantly lower aquatic toxicity compared to lead-based systems. These combined properties position DBTP as a promising candidate for next-generation environmentally benign primary explosives.

papers.title: Photoredox/Copper-Catalyzed Enantioselective S‑Alkylation of Sulfenamides with Hydrocarbons Enabled by Commercial BOX Ligands
papers.abstract: Enantioenriched sulfilimines are valuable sulfur-stereogenic building blocks, but catalytic asymmetric S‑alkylation directly from hydrocarbons is still challenging. Here we report a dual photoredox/copper-catalyzed enantioselective S‑alkylation of N‑acyl sulfenamides with hydrocarbons enabled by commercially available chiral bis(oxazoline) (BOX) ligands. The reaction merges peroxide-based HAT with chiral copper catalysis to furnish sulfur-stereogenic sulfilimines from benzylic hydrocarbons and representative unactivated alkanes in good yields and enantioselectivities (up to 90% ee). A practical feature is that the hydrocarbon coupling partner is typically used in only 10 equivalents, improving substrate economy compared with related radical C(sp 3 )–H functionalizations. Stern–Volmer studies show efficient quenching of the photocatalyst by a copper/BOX/sulfenamide assembly, consistent with a cooperative initiation pathway.

papers.title: Small Science Agentic Models for Automated Perovskite Thin Film Exploration via Monte Carlo Decision Trees and Delayed Bayesian Optimization Feedback
papers.abstract: Autonomous materials discovery requires decision frameworks capable of handling process-dependent outcomes, delayed feedback, and sparse experimental data. We introduce Small Science Agentic Models (SSAMs), a distributed architecture for self-driving laboratories in which scientific reasoning is embedded across narrow, physically interpretable models tied directly to the experimental workflow. Implemented as an event-driven, agent-based closed loop, the SSAM framework integrates hypothesis generation, protocol construction, characterization-derived state representation, machine-learning decision-making, and orchestration, treating each experiment as an evolving process trajectory rather than an isolated parameter evaluation. We apply this framework to discover an effective Dion–Jacobson (DJ) organic spacer for stabilizing the photoactive 3D-like phase of FAPbI3. Through agent-guided hypothesis formation employing Socratic reasoning and Tree-of-Thought branching, furan-2,5-diyldimethanammonium (FuDMA) was identified as a previously unexplored DJ spacer compatible with the perovskite lattice. The binary FAPbI3/FuDMAPbI4 compositional system was then explored autonomously using a Monte Carlo decision tree with delayed-reward updating. Over ten iterations, the system achieved 95% predictive agreement between predicted and measured film quality, identified the highest-performing sample within three iterations, and converged toward focused exploitation by approximately seven iterations. Optimal film formation was localized to FA based compositions of 60–80% within a tightly constrained spin-coating and annealing regime. Time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) analysis of 96 films revealed two composition-dependent FuDMA interaction regimes through fast-component amplitude analysis. At intermediate spacer concentrations (20–40% FuDMA), FuDMA acts as a lattice-strain compensating additive that suppresses trap-mediated recombination and extends carrier lifetimes, while at higher fractions it drives quasi-2D phase formation accompanied by accelerated fast-decay dynamics. Complementary 1H NMR and FTIR spectroscopy provided mechanistic insight into these regimes, revealing composition-dependent changes in FA chemical environments and furan ring oxygen interactions with the inorganic framework in the precursor state. These results establish SSAMs as a transparent, workflow-grounded approach to trajectory-aware autonomous experimentation in dynamic materials systems.

papers.title: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering covalency analysis reveals non-Aufbau electronic configurations in low-valent lanthanides
papers.abstract: Divalent lanthanide ions can adopt complex 4fn5d1 electron configurations that formally violate the Aufbau principle. The blending of contracted 4f and diffuse 5d character strongly influences lanthanide frontier molecular orbitals, yet quantitative characterization of 5d electron participation in bonding remains challenging. To address this, we report L3-edge high energy resolution fluorescence detected X-ray absorption near edge structure (HERFD-XANES) and valence to core resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (V2C-RIXS) for a series of divalent lanthanide complexes [M(NHAriPr6)2] (M = Ce, Tb, Dy and Yb; NHAriPr6 2=N(H)C6H3-2,6-(C6H2-2,4,6-iPr3)2) and their trivalent precursors [M(NHAriPr6)2(I)], which all feature close metal–arene contacts. It is demonstrated that V2C-RIXS can be applied to quantify relative 5d covalency contributions to lanthanide–arene bonding. Analysis of divalent cerium, terbium, and dysprosium complexes reveals non-Aufbau (5d1) configurations, which show significant 5d–arene δ-bond covalency and stabilization of the associated bonding orbitals. V2C- RIXS spectra are accurately simulated and compared with UV-vis-NIR results using DFT/ROCIS calculations. A detailed assignment of spectral features and correlation to predicted electron configurations define a trend of increased 5d covalency for these complexes relative to their trivalent precursors. Conversely, the divalent ytterbium complex has an Aufbau configuration, 4f14, and shows markedly reduced 5d covalency relative to its trivalent precursor.

papers.title: Diversification of heteroleptic assembly topologies through covalent bridging
papers.abstract: Expanding the structural and functional diversity of metallosupramolecular assemblies remains challenging for selective recognition, catalysis, and materials science. Existing synthetic strategies often impose constraints on the size, shape, and functionalization of building blocks, limiting access to assemblies of certain geometries or higher nuclearity. Here, we demonstrate a versatile approach for accessing a variety of heteroleptic, metal-mediated architectures based on the covalent bridging of identical or unlike ligands via flexible or rigid tethers, thus enabling synthetic routes to previously unattainable di- and tetranuclear multicomponent structures. Depending on the type of bridge and counter-ligand combination, we achieved the non-statistical assembly of Pd 2 (AB)CD cages, singly-bridged Pd 4 A 4 (B 2 )D 2 double-cavity systems and doubly-bridged Pd 4 (B 2 ) 2 D 2 structures. Dynamic cage-to-cage transformations enable triggered separation of C 60 from fullerene mixtures, while incorporation of photoswitchable ligands allows reversible modulation of cage geometry and properties. Remarkably, all assemblies arise from ligands that, in their untethered form, fail to yield clean integrative self-sorting. The robustness of this modular strategy is demonstrated through comprehensive NMR spectroscopic and mass spectrometric characterization and six single-crystal X-ray structures. Methodological progress in the synthetic access to nanostructures of increasing complexity promises to advance the functionality of soluble receptors, stimuli-responsive life-like systems and porous materials with intricate morphology.

papers.title: Computer-Aided Bioprocess and Solvent Design for Industrial Methyl Ketone Production
papers.abstract: Methyl ketones have recently been identified as a promising candidate for biofuels among other uses. They can be produced via biomass fermentation using Pseudomonas taiwanensis VLB120 ∆6 pProd. However, the literature does not contain a complete early stage design proposal including upstream bioreactor design and downstream product purification at industrial scale. We present a model-based design approach for methyl ketone production based on renewable resources, including fermentation and product purification. We apply OptKnock [Burgard, Pharkya, Maranas: Biotechnology and bioengineering 2003] to propose beneficial gene knockouts in the strain and adapt our SimulKnockReactor methodology [Ziegler et int. Mitsos: Comp&ChemEng 2026] to optimize the bioreactor for the production of methyl ketones. We then apply an enhanced version of our COSMO-CAMPED framework [Polte et int. Leonhard: CIT 2023] for the downstream purification of the fermentation broth. Extraction-based separations offer substantial potential for efficient purification of chemical products, particularly from the dilute aqueous streams of biotechnological fermentations. Finding a solvent with the required thermodynamic properties, bio-compatibility, and benign environmental properties is vital for the overall process performance. We propose three gene deletions to P. taiwanensis VLB120 ∆6 pProd, namely, inorganic diphosphatase, polyphosphate kinase, and inorganic diphosphatase. We identify isopentyl-isopropylether as most suitable extraction solvent among several others that outperform our literature benchmark of Di-n-butylether. We present an optimized layout for the combined upstream and downstream process that produces methyl ketones at a bulk production capacity of 1× 107 kg/a for a total cost of 6.0USD/kg.

papers.title: Sprinkle, Don’t Dump: A Spectroscopic Analysis of Light Assisted-Pulsed Linear Sweep Voltammetry Enabled Copper (Cu) Single-Atom Dispersion on TiO2 Nanotube.
papers.abstract: Single atom photocatalysts (SAPCs) offer maximum atom efficiency and unique catalytic behaviour, presenting a promising path toward economically viable and sustainable catalytic systems. However, the rational design and optimization of such materials by gathering atomic-level evidence using high-end characterization tools remain challenging due to their cost and limited accessibility. In this work, we demonstrate a simple, integrated approach to fabricate, investigate and optimize SAPCs. An energy-efficient electrochemical approach for fabricating Cu-based single-atom sites on titanium dioxide nanotubes (TiNT) arrays was developed to achieve strong metal-support interaction. The immobilized TiNT framework provides ordered electron transport pathways and strong anchoring sites for Cu adherence, while the electrochemical conditions dictate whether Cu atoms evolve as isolated sites or aggregate into clusters. Although in general, electrochemical strategies for the synthesis of single atoms on oxide offer precise control over deposition, their effectiveness critically depends on the underlying deposition dynamics. Therefore, we have investigated the influence of deposition mode on the formation and dispersion of Cu single atoms, redox coupling strength and electronic structure within these systems, using X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS), Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) and Time-of-Flight Secondary Ion Mass Spectroscopy (ToF-SIMS). XPS and EPR analysis indicates that Linear Sweep Voltammetry (LSV) deposition produces clustered Cu species, whereas pulsed LSV (pLSV) leads to atomically dispersed Cu centres. ToF-SIMS spectra suggest increased CuO-/Cu- ratio consistent with evidence seen in XPS and EPR. Together, these complementary observations confirm that pLSV enables efficient stabilization of atomically dispersed Cu sites through interfacial redox coupling strength modulation and clustering suppression. With this we have shown that a multi-modal approach with the strategic and integrated use of XPS, EPR, and ToF-SIMS can enable efficient screening of single-atom catalysts during the design stage.

papers.title: Integrating Dispersive Liquid-Liquid Microextraction with HPLC-MS/MS for Simultaneously
De Novo Design of Intramolecular Cage-locking NIR-II Luminogens with Aggregate-Caused Quenching and Aggregate-Induced Emission Properties for Highly Efficient Surgical Antitumor Phototheranostic
papers.abstract: Highly brightness fluorophore in the second near-infrared (NIR-II) window is promising for noninvasive and rapid-response clinical surgical phototheranostics. However, it is an appealing yet significantly challenging work to develop such fluorophores with advancements of ACQ/AIE dual properties and brightness emission to overcome the influence of in vivo internal microenvironment. Herein, we first propose two superior brightness NIR-II luminogens (named as CTU4 and CTU5) with such properties to bridge the gap between surgical requirements and molecular development. The luminogens were constructed via the introduction of two cage moieties to locking their intramolecular motion, endowing the fluorophores with brightness NIR-II emission in the molecular and aggregate states. The CTU5 was demonstrated that reveals this characteristic with quantum yield of 1.7% in molecular state and 7.1% in aggregate state. Moreover, the water-dispersible CTU5 nanoparticles process a tumorto-background ratio of 12.4 for tumor removal, photothermal conversion efficiency of 59.2%, and efficient type-I reactive oxygen species generation ability, contributing to its photoluminescent/photothermal dual images-guided surgical anti-tumor phototheranostics. This work highlights the intramolecular locking strategy to achieve NIR-II diagnostic agent with ACQ/AIE dual properties and their potential surgical antitumor phototherapy.

papers.title: Room temperature alcohol-mediated surfactant-free synthesis of alloys and core-shell nanoparticles: the example of Au-Ag nanomaterials
papers.abstract: Core-shell nanoparticles present unique properties that their monometallic counterparts do not express. Unfortunately, the simple and environmentally friendly preparation of such advanced structures can be challenging. A method that by-pass typicall challenges in the synthesis of such materials is proposed based on a room temperature mono-alcohol mediated synthesis without the need for surfactant. The concept is demonstrated with the straightforward synthesis of goldsilver alloys and core-shell nanostructures. The results pave the way to complex materials obtained by more sustainable surfactant-free approaches.

papers.title: Polylasso Network
papers.abstract: Synthetic polymer networks face a fundamental trade-off: high energy dissipation and rapid recovery are mutually exclusive in conventional designs. Herein, inspired by the topological architecture of lasso peptides, we report the de novo synthesis of a polylasso network (PLN) that reconciles this long-standing conflict. Using a recognition-first interlocking-cyclization strategy, we construct stable lasso monomers that are subsequently cross-linked into a bulk network via thiol-ene click chemistry. The resulting topology establishes an intrinsic coupling between sliding-mediated high energy dissipation and entropy-driven rapid recovery. Under deformation, controlled tail sliding through the macrocyclic cavity, accompanied by host–guest dissociation and molecular friction, enables efficient energy dissipation, while geometric constraint limits excessive displacement and maintains structural integrity. Upon unloading, the elastic potential energy stored within the loop is rapidly released to drive tail retraction, while host–guest reassociation further promotes rapid restoration of the original lasso configuration and the overall network structure. Consequently, the PLN exhibits pronounced hysteretic energy dissipation (damping capacity, 90.2%) and rapid mechanical recovery under cyclic loading. These results establish molecular lasso topology as a general design principle for decoupling the conventional trade-off between energy dissipation and recovery, opening a route toward resilient soft materials with biological tissue-like mechanical adaptability.

papers.title: Unlocking Cation-π Interaction in A 3D Porphyrin Covalent Organic Framework for Efficient Gold Extraction
papers.abstract: Recycling precious metal gold from electronic waste is not only environmentally beneficial but also economically attractive. Adsorption-based processes are appealing for their low energy requirements and minimal secondary waste generation. However, current adsorbents suffer from low adsorption capacities. Even the most promising porous adsorbents, such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and covalent organic frameworks (COFs), typically have capacities less than 2 g g-1 for gold. Herein, we report a thiazole-linked 3D porphyrin-based COF, which shows an unprecedented adsorption capacity of 32.6 g g-1 towards gold via an adsorption-reduction mechanism. Such high capacity originates from the full exposure of various adsorption sites in the 3D open channels and their strong interaction with gold. DFT calculations reveal that the porphyrin motif is the strongest adsorption site through cation-π interactions. Transient absorption spectroscopy discloses the COFmediated photo-reduction process. The presented results establish noncovalent interactions in 3D COF scaffolds as a key principle for efficient and selective metal recovery, paving the way for urban mining of precious metals.

papers.title: Synthesis-Aware Molecular Generation via Reaction-Driven Global Search
papers.abstract: Synthesizability remains a central challenge in de novo molecular generation. Conventional goal-directed molecular optimization methods, where molecules are generated by optimizing target properties often suffer from low synthetic accessibility. Existing strategies typically address this gap through post hoc filtering or by restricting generation to predefined reaction schemes. The former decouples synthesis from optimization, whereas the latter improves feasibility at the cost of restricting molecular exploration. We present RxnMol, a synthesis-aware molecular optimization framework in which each candidate is encoded as a synthetic-route representation: an ordered sequence of readily available molecular building blocks. A pretrained reaction prediction model converts these building blocks into a product molecule through sequential reaction prediction, while a population-based global optimization algorithm modifies the route representation and evaluates the resulting molecule against the target objective. Thus, molecular optimization operates on synthetic routes rather than solely on final molecular structures. Each selected molecule is obtained from the optimized route representation by RxnMol; therefore, the improved objective values remain directly tied to the corresponding synthetic routes predicted by the model. Across protein target and bioactivity optimization tasks, RxnMol improves Top-1 performance on both generative baselines that optimize molecular structures directly and template-based synthesis-constrained methods in most benchmarks. Together, these results show that de novo molecular design can be formulated as route optimization, where reaction prediction translates route representations into product molecules for objective evaluation.

papers.title: Synthesis of spiro-1,2-dihydropyridine derivatives via cycloisomerization of 3-aza-1,5-enynes catalyzed by gold(I) complex/polyoxometalate hybrids.
papers.abstract: This study reports an optimized method for the synthesis of spiro-1,2-dihydropyridines via the cycloisomerization of 3-aza-1,5-enynes, catalyzed by heterogeneous gold(I)–polyoxometalate (POM) hybrids. By replacing traditional homogeneous catalysts with these hybrid systems, we achieved high yields (up to 82% isolated) and shortened reaction times, while minimizing product degradation. The reaction scope was demonstrated across a broad range of substrates, including aryl, alkyl, and heterocyclic derivatives, as well as variations in ring size and nitrogen substituents using 5 mol% of IPrAuI(MeCN).H5P2W18O64 as catalyst.
